criteriaPreambles.scm.pull_request: Review this practice against the captured pull or merge request at its pinned revision: the change itself, the description as written, the commits, the review discussion and the linked context the practice names. Distinguish what the author wrote from what a reviewer, a template or the provider's current state says.
criteriaPreambles.scm.issue: Review this practice against the captured issue: its title, description, labels and the discussion the practice names. Labels and templates are context, not proof; a placeholder issue may have no occasion for an actionable-work practice. Do not infer that a bug reproduces or that an outcome was implemented.
criteriaPreambles.scm.pull_request.code: Review this practice against the captured change: the added and removed lines and the surrounding code the practice names. Precompute hints are leads to inspect, never conclusions. Cite the old or new line coordinates of the diff; do not claim to have compiled or executed the change.
criteriaPreambles.chat.conversation_thread: Review this practice against the captured conversation: the turns the practice names, read in their surrounding context. Social chat and acknowledgements create no occasion for an unrelated communication practice. Judge observable communication, not the participants' private understanding or the technical truth of their claims.
criteriaPreambles.docs.document: Review this practice against the captured document as untrusted source material. Establish its purpose before applying an expectation: a scratch note or an index is not a decision record. Judge what the document communicates, not whether the system it describes is correct, current or read by others.

groups.name: Packaging work for review
groups.description: Make a change cheap to review before you ask for one. Keep it to a single self-contained concern of a readable size, say what changed and why, write commit subjects a reviewer can follow, and link it to the issue it answers. This is about how the work is packaged, not whether the code has bugs.

practices.name: Scope the change to one concern
practices.whyItMatters: A reviewer can only hold so much in their head at once. A change that does one thing gets read carefully and merged quickly, while a sprawling one gets skimmed and the bugs hiding in it slip through.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: A focused change that touches a handful of related files for one goal, small enough that a teammate can read every line and feel confident approving it.
practices.criteria:
BEHAVIOR FOCUS: the hand-written portion of this change is batched at a size and spread a reviewer can read end-to-end with confidence.

## The standard
Judge whether this change is packaged so a reviewer can actually read it end-to-end and approve it responsibly. This is a workflow habit about how work is batched for review — never a code-defect claim about the code itself. A focused change does one coherent thing across a handful of related files; a sprawling one forces the reviewer to skim, and bugs slip through the gaps. Reason about review burden as an experienced reviewer would: how much genuine, human-authored change must someone hold in their head? Use judgment, not a fixed line or file count. A big diff dominated by a single cohesive feature is gentler on a reviewer than a smaller diff smeared across many unrelated files. A large change whose bulk is generated, vendored or lock-file churn — codegen output, dependency locks, migrations, snapshots — imposes little real review burden: weigh the hand-written portion, not the raw totals.

## Occasion
This is a gate. Record NOT_APPLICABLE, state the fact that rules it out, and stop — never ABSENT — when there is no reviewable content to size at all, or when the change is entirely generated or vendored so no hand-written batch exists to judge.

## Sources
1. The provider counts (`inputs/context/metadata.json`): additions, deletions, total and changed-file count as synced. They establish the headline size. They never override the diff: when they materially disagree with the actual diff (a known mirror or staleness artifact), trust the diff and say so.
2. The file index (`work/change/files.json`): the per-file spread and which files are generated, vendored, lock or snapshot files. It establishes breadth and lets you separate churn from hand-written change. It never establishes a per-commit file mapping.
3. The annotated diff (`work/change/diff.patch`): ground truth for what was actually changed and how much of it is hand-written. It establishes the counts you report. It never establishes whether the code is correct.
You see file-level spread and totals, not per-commit patches; judge packaging from those. If the required size fields and the diff needed to derive them were not captured, report a collection gap and record no observation.

## Judge
Read the counts, the file index and the diff, and separate the hand-written portion from churn. Then test the cells in this order.
- PRESENT/GOOD (POSITIVE): the hand-written change is small and cohesive enough that a teammate could plausibly read every meaningful line and feel confident — a tight batch. Never grade an empty or unmeasurable change as a well-sized strength.
- PRESENT/BAD: no ordinary case.
- ABSENT/GOOD (NEGATIVE): the change is large or scattered enough that careful line-by-line review becomes impractical, so smaller or stacked changes would serve the reviewer better. Name the size and the spread you measured.
- ABSENT/BAD: no ordinary case.
- UNDETERMINED: the change plainly has hand-written content, but after reading the complete diff the generated bulk cannot be separated from the hand-written portion, so you cannot size it. The work was batched; you could not measure it. Name what would let you separate them. Having measured a sprawling change is ABSENT/GOOD, not UNDETERMINED.
One observation per review, over the whole change.

## Severity
Negatives only; formative, never a merge gate. MINOR, the usual band: a light nudge toward smaller batches. MAJOR: a recommendation to split or stack, reserved for sprawl across many files that almost certainly bundles unrelated concerns. Size or spread alone never exceeds MAJOR, and raw line count by itself never reaches it.

## Grounding
State the exact additions, deletions, total and changed-file count you used and where you read them; never invent a count. For ABSENT/GOOD, describe the observable packaging — "touches N files / ~M changed lines, spread across unrelated areas" — citing the file index lines and diff hunks that show the spread, and state which files you discounted as generated, vendored or lock churn. For PRESENT/GOOD, cite the counts and the file index that bound the batch. Never claim a per-commit file mapping you cannot see. Never impute intent, haste or character.

## Defer
Whether the touched files form one logical concern is a cohesion judgment owned by the area framing and by `commits-are-atomic-and-cohesive`; do not re-litigate single-concern semantics that a file index cannot decide. Whether generated artifacts belong in the change at all belongs to `excludes-generated-and-build-artifacts`. Here only: is the hand-written batch a size and spread one reviewer can read with confidence?

practices.name: Describe what changed and why
practices.whyItMatters: Your reviewer was not in your head when you wrote the code. A sentence on why you made the change spares them from reverse-engineering your intent from the diff, and missing that rationale is one of the most common things that leaves a reviewer confused.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: A title like 'Cache user lookups to cut the dashboard load time' with a body that opens 'The dashboard re-fetched every user on each render, so it stuttered on large teams.'
practices.criteria:
BEHAVIOR FOCUS: the title and description state what this change does and a concrete reason why it exists, so a reviewer is oriented before opening the diff.

## The standard
Judge ONE thing: can a reviewer understand WHAT this pull request changes and WHY from the title and description alone? Good orientation is a specific, imperative title naming the concrete change, plus a quotable clause in the title or description stating the motivation — the problem it solves, the prior pain, the user impact, the goal or a constraint. A story-id or tag prefix such as "[Feat] US5.2: …" does not make a title generic; only a truly contentless title does — "fix", "wip", "update", a bare branch or issue reference. The WHY is why the CHANGE exists — the problem, user goal, request or constraint the whole change answers. A reason attached to one sub-decision inside it ("moved the helpers into their own folder to match the naming", "chose API X because it is not deprecated") explains that choice, not the change, and does not supply the WHY on its own; a requirement or user-story line quoted in the body ("As a runner I want to see my route on a map") does, because it names the goal the change serves. Reason connectives ("so that", "because", "to avoid", "in order to") are common but NOT required: a clause that simply names a problem or goal ("the dashboard re-fetched on every render") states the WHY. A rationale inside a bullet, a details block or a checklist item counts exactly as one in prose; a dedicated heading is welcome but not required. A title such as "Cache user lookups to stop dashboard stalls" already supplies both action and reason; do not demand a second reason in the body. Repetition does not erase a stated reason, and a brief description needs no extra prose to fill a heading. A restatement of the action alone ("Update node" / "to update node") supplies no motivation, and neither does a schedule: a course day, a sprint, a milestone or a ticket number in the title ("Sprint 3: …", "Milestone 2: …") says when the work was due, not why it exists. Nor does a closing reference: "Closes #N" links the work, and the linked issue's objective is the issue's text, not the description's — the WHY is quoted from the title or description itself. A sentence that restates the title in the first person ("I created a glossary from the analysis") is the WHAT again, not a reason, and so is a sentence that describes what the feature now does ("the report can now be exported as CSV", "the user gets a chance to undo it"): the behaviour built is the WHAT in other words. A WHY survives when the change's own action is taken out of the clause and a problem, need or constraint is left standing. The description's own checked feature bullets name what the change does; they supply the WHY only where a bullet states a user goal or problem rather than a component built.

## Occasion
NOT_APPLICABLE has no ordinary case: every pull request calls for this description. Never record NOT_APPLICABLE, and never record ABSENT for text you could not read.

## Sources
1. The title (`inputs/context/metadata.json`): it establishes what the change is named and can itself carry the WHY. It never establishes a motivation that is not written in it.
2. The description as written (`inputs/context/description.md`): every section, bullet, nested list, details block and checklist item, not only a "Why" heading. It establishes the WHAT and the WHY the change states. It never establishes a reason the diff would suggest but the text does not say. `work/change/description.authored.md` lists which of its lines the author wrote and which are the merge request template's own (headings, checklist labels, placeholders, comments); a template line is not the author's word, and a WHY is quoted from the author's lines.
Judge from these two and nothing else. Never read the diff to supply a rationale the description did not write. A missing body is not an empty one: if the title or body were never captured, report a collection gap and record no observation. Also report a collection gap when the only motivation clause defers to a linked issue or document this review cannot read — "rationale in #412", a design-doc link that was not captured: quote the deferring clause, do not assume the WHY sits behind it, and do not count it ABSENT. Breadth of the change, when severity needs it, comes from the file and line counts in `inputs/context/metadata.json`.

## Judge
Scan the WHOLE description before deciding anything is absent. Then test the cells in this order.
- PRESENT/GOOD (POSITIVE): a title that names the actual feature, area or fix, AND a quotable clause in the title or body stating WHY. Read title and body together: a concrete problem, impact, goal or constraint in either supplies the motivation.
- PRESENT/BAD (NEGATIVE): an explanation is supplied but misleads — it orients the reviewer toward a different change than the one described. Quote the misleading clause.
- ABSENT/GOOD (NEGATIVE): the WHY is required and missing — the body is empty or template, or the only candidate clauses restate the action. Name which is missing: a title that names nothing, a body that names no reason, or both. An empty body and a restatement require different evidence and different feedback; say which you found.
- ABSENT/BAD: no ordinary case.
- UNDETERMINED: you genuinely cannot tell a restatement from a motivation AND that clause is the only candidate WHY. Quote it and do not resolve the doubt in either direction. Having read the whole title and body and found no reason is ABSENT/GOOD, not UNDETERMINED.
One observation per review.

## Severity
Negatives only; never above MAJOR on this practice alone — a formative habit, not a merge gate. Calibrate by review cost, not by counters. MINOR, the usual band: a small, single-file change with a thin description; a generic-but-harmless title atop an otherwise informative body, the lightest case; a body that enumerates what changed but omits the why — it still orients. Toward MAJOR: a contentless body on a broad, multi-file change, the heaviest cost. Do not inflate a small change with a thin description.

## Grounding
To claim the WHY is PRESENT, quote the exact rationale clause verbatim from the title or body. To call it ABSENT, cite the boundary: the title, and the body quoted or stated to be empty or template, with every bullet, nested list and checklist item read. Never fabricate a verdict on a field you cannot see. Never claim what the diff does; the description is the subject. Talk about the description — "the description names no reason" — never about the author, and never impute intent.

## Defer
Code quality belongs to the craft practices; how the commits are partitioned belongs to `commits-are-atomic-and-cohesive`; conduct in review threads belongs to `engaging-with-inline-review-comments`; whether a reviewer can verify the change belongs to `states-how-to-verify-the-change`. Here only: does the description orient a reviewer on what and why?

practices.name: State how to verify the change
practices.whyItMatters: A reviewer who knows where to start, what to do and what to expect can check the change in minutes and trusts what they see. Without that, they either guess at a procedure, skip the check, or ask — and the change waits.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: A change to the filter sheet whose description says: open Discover, apply two types, relaunch — the filters are still applied; clear them — the default list is back. The steps name the screen, the action and what success looks like, and the linked issue's acceptance criteria say the same.
practices.criteria:
BEHAVIOR FOCUS: for the material effect of this change, a reviewer who knows the repository's documented setup can find where to start, what to do and what to expect — from what the author supplied or explicitly adopted.

## The standard
Judge ONE check for the main material effect of the change. It is communicated when three elements are available across the permitted sources: an ENTRY (where a reviewer starts: a command, a screen, a named test, an authored preview or story, a documented setup step), an ACTION (what to do: run, tap, enter, configure, restart, or — for an appearance-only change — render and inspect) and an EXPECTED RESULT (what distinguishes success: a stated requirement, an assertion, a visible state, a persisted value). The three may come from different sources. A step phrased as a check states its expected result — "verify the list updates", "confirm the values persist after relaunch" name what the reviewer looks for; do not demand a literal value on top of it. "Testing: N/A" or an empty heading is NOT evidence of anything; read every source below before deciding.

## Occasion
This is a gate. When the change is one of these kinds and nothing else, record NOT_APPLICABLE, name the kind, and stop — never ABSENT: a diagram, a glossary, user stories or an introduction have no runtime result a reviewer could check, so "no verification instructions" is not a finding about them. The kinds: an empty diff; only whitespace, formatting or file moves with unchanged content; a self-introduction, biography, problem statement, user stories, glossary or other planning prose; a conceptual diagram (analysis object model, subsystem decomposition, UML — as image, JSON or Markdown) and the README text that embeds or describes it; README prose that explains architecture or tool usage without an operational procedure; the deletion of template or boilerplate files the project does not reference. Reading rendered prose is not a check. Judge the actual patch, not the title: a title that promises a feature does not make it present, and a documentation change that adds setup or run instructions IS material. Material effects: application behavior, appearance, navigation, persistence, configuration or project settings (build manifests, package dependencies, ignore patterns, editor settings that run commands), tests, build scripts, and operational documentation (how to set up, run, deploy).

## Sources
Read all of these before judging; an element found anywhere here counts as author-supplied.
1. The title and the WHOLE description (`inputs/context/description.md`): every section, checklist, acceptance-criteria list and step list, not only a "Testing" heading. Screenshots: a single one shows a visible state (an entry or an expected appearance); an ordered or captioned sequence can also show an action. You cannot open an image: read its caption, its filename and the sentence around it, and count the shown state as communicated when the text around it, or the title's own statement of the visible change, says what it shows — a screenshot under a "Screenshots" heading in a change whose title names a UI change shows that change. Never record ABSENT or UNDETERMINED because the image bytes are not available to you: the author supplied the picture, and what you cannot see is not what they failed to say.
2. A linked issue the author adopted (`inputs/context/linked_work_items/<n>.md`): the description names it with a closing keyword (Closes, Resolves, Fixes #N), or the title or branch was created from it, or the description says the change implements it. Its acceptance criteria, steps and title are the author's instructions. A bare "#N" left in a template, or an issue only found by number search, is NOT adopted.
3. The patch (`work/change/diff.patch`): an authored preview, story, runnable sample or executable test added or changed in the diff is an ENTRY for the view or unit it exercises. For an appearance-only change, rendering that preview is the ACTION and a stated or shown appearance is the EXPECTED RESULT. A preview does not establish interaction, navigation, callbacks or persistence.
4. The repository's documented setup (README, CONTRIBUTING, a documented generate/build/run route in `<repositoryRoot>`): prerequisites and generic run/build steps. Reuse them; do not demand them repeated in the description. For a project-configuration change (a renamed target, a build manifest, package additions), the documented generate/build/open route IS the check when it covers that configuration.
5. The author's own words in the discussion (`inputs/context/general_comments.json`, `inputs/context/review_threads.json`) where they state a check. A reviewer's report of testing is NOT the author's instructions.
The implementation can confirm reachability or contradict an instruction; it never supplies instructions by itself: a view's own source (its labels, its literal text) is not a stated expected result, and copying it would invent one.

## Judge
Test the cells in this order.
- PRESENT/GOOD (POSITIVE): the main material effect has an entry, an action and an expected result across the sources above, and following them would let a reviewer see the effect. This holds even when the description says "N/A", even when the elements are split between a preview, an issue and a screenshot, and even when secondary effects have no check. Do not turn an uncovered secondary effect into a negative.
- PRESENT/BAD (NEGATIVE): instructions exist but are materially misleading: it describes a different change than the patch makes, names a control or screen that is not in the code, requires an input, secret or device the reviewer cannot obtain from the documented setup, or declares "no UI change" when the patch changes the UI. Quote both the instruction and the contradicting code or fact.
- ABSENT/GOOD (NEGATIVE): no source supplies a usable check for the main material effect AND the effect cannot be confirmed by reading the diff alone — it needs running, interacting, configuring or observing. Name the missing element(s) and what the reviewer would need. A preview alone with no stated or shown expected result for an interactive change is ABSENT.
- ABSENT/BAD is exceptional: only when the author explicitly removed or refused a harmful or plainly unnecessary procedure. Never for an empty heading.
- UNDETERMINED only when the captured sources genuinely conflict or an adopted issue could not be captured; state the question that would settle it. Having read every source and found no usable check for a material effect is not undetermined: it is ABSENT/GOOD.
One observation per review; keep the same check in the summary, the evidence and the rationale.

## Severity
Negatives only; almost always MINOR: a bounded addition or correction fixes it — one missing element, one misleading detail, one undocumented prerequisite. MAJOR: a significant effect is unverifiable as communicated, or the instruction sends the reviewer to a materially wrong check. CRITICAL only for a communicated procedure that demonstrably risks production data loss or live-credential disclosure; never hypothetical.

## Grounding
Cite the exact lines: the description or issue lines that supply each element, the diff lines of a preview or test, the screenshot reference, the README lines. For ABSENT, the citations show the boundary you searched (the description, the adopted issue, the previews and tests in the patch, the documented setup) and the material effect (diff lines) that needs the check. Never claim a build, test or app run was executed. Judge the instructions, not correctness: a clear check that would expose a defect is still a GOOD check.

## Defer
Whether the description explains what and why (`describe-what-and-why`), whether tests exist (`ships-tests-with-the-change`), and whether the code is correct belong to other practices. Here only: can a reviewer verify the material effect from what the author communicated?

practices.name: Mark the change ready and link its issue
practices.whyItMatters: When you mark work ready, people start spending time on it. A leftover 'work in progress' tag or a missing issue link makes them guess whether it is really done and why it exists, small friction that adds up across a team.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: A change that is out of draft, has no 'do not merge' label left on it, and carries a 'Closes #482' line so anyone can trace it back to the need it answers.
practices.criteria:
BEHAVIOR FOCUS: how the change is handed off — presented as genuinely ready for others' time, and traceable back to the issue it answers.

## The standard
Judge two things about the handoff, combined into one observation. READINESS: is the change presented as actually ready for review, not silently still a work in progress? TRACEABILITY: can a reader follow it back to the motivating issue? Good: an out-of-draft pull request with no leftover "WIP" or "do not merge"-style signal and a quotable closing reference — "Closes #482", or an issue id embedded in the branch slug. Bad: a mixed-signal handoff — a draft-style marker in the title while the pull request is openly non-draft — or a substantive feature or fix change with no traceable reference anywhere a reader would look. Use the judgment of an experienced reviewer, never fixed lexical lists or counters. A genuine draft is a legitimate in-progress state, informational only and never a defect; a closing reference on a draft is exactly the traceability wanted, not a contradiction. A trivial chore — a dependency bump, formatting, a rename, docs and the like, by judgment — rarely needs a tracking issue, so a missing reference there is not a fault. A plain issue mention without a closing keyword is traceable but does not auto-close: say so rather than penalise it. A non-draft pull request that presents its own Definition-of-Done checklist entirely unticked asks for review while stating that nothing is done; weigh that as a mild mis-signal, judging whether the checklist is real or boilerplate.

## Occasion
NOT_APPLICABLE has no ordinary case: a pull request IS a handoff, so the occasion for readiness and traceability always arises. A trivial chore needing no tracking issue is a PRESENT handoff judged on its readiness, not an inapplicable one.

## Sources
Reason only from metadata that is actually present.
1. The pull request record (`inputs/context/metadata.json`): the draft flag, the title, the branch name. It establishes the declared state, any title marker, and an issue id in the branch slug. There is no CI, build or mergeability field and no structured linked-issue field here: never assert build, CI or merge state, or a linked-issue field you cannot quote.
2. The description (`inputs/context/description.md`): the closing reference or plain mention, the WIP-style signal, the Definition-of-Done checklist and its ticks. It establishes what the handoff says; it never establishes what was done.
3. The file index (`work/change/files.json`): file NAMES only — enough to tell a trivial chore from a substantive feature or fix. Never file contents, never per-commit patches. A file index cannot establish whether testing happened: manual verification, external test suites and existing unchanged tests need no test file in this diff. Never infer that a testing checklist claim is false from missing test filenames, and never ask for it to be unticked on that basis.
When the deciding fact is not observable — the draft flag was never populated, or the context is un-enriched — the handoff still happened and you could not read it: report a collection gap, name the fact you could not read, and record no observation.

## Judge
Test the cells in this order.
- PRESENT/GOOD (POSITIVE): the pull request is out of draft with no leftover draft-style signal, and a reference is quotable in the title, the description or the branch — or the change is a trivial chore that needs none. A genuine draft with a closing reference is also PRESENT/GOOD.
- PRESENT/BAD (NEGATIVE): a mixed signal — a draft-style marker in the title while the pull request is openly non-draft, or a real Definition-of-Done checklist left entirely unticked on a non-draft pull request. Quote the offending token or the unticked lines.
- ABSENT/GOOD (NEGATIVE): a substantive feature or fix change with no traceable reference on any of the three surfaces — title, description, branch — after scanning all of them.
- ABSENT/BAD: no ordinary case.
- UNDETERMINED only when a read surface genuinely cannot settle whether a change is a trivial chore or substantive; name what would settle it. A missing draft flag is a collection gap, not UNDETERMINED. Having scanned the three surfaces and found no reference on a substantive change is ABSENT, not UNDETERMINED.
One observation per review, combining the sub-checks by taking the most severe. A genuine draft never makes a NEGATIVE on readiness; note it as context, and it never lifts the severity.

## Severity
Negatives only; never above MAJOR on handoff alone — non-blocking and formative, a workflow habit to grow. MINOR, the usual band: a mixed marker alone, a missing reference alone, or an unticked checklist. MAJOR: a substantive handoff that is both mis-signalled and untraceable.

## Grounding
Quote the exact token relied on: the issue reference, the offending title marker, the draft flag value, the unticked checklist lines. For ABSENT/GOOD, name the surfaces scanned — title, description, branch — and the file names that make the change substantive. Never invent a clean bill, a reference or a contradiction you did not verify. Describe the observable signal; never impute intent or character.

## Defer
Test-suite adequacy and automated-test presence belong to `ships-tests-with-the-change`; scope cohesion belongs to `scope-one-reviewable-change`; commit-message quality belongs to `commit-subjects-explain-each-change`. Here only: is the handoff ready and traceable?

practices.name: Write commit subjects a reviewer can follow
practices.whyItMatters: Six months from now, someone, maybe you, will run git blame on a confusing line and read your commit subject to understand it. 'wip' and 'fix stuff' tell them nothing, while a clear subject tells the whole story.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: A history you can read top to bottom, where each subject names exactly what that step did, such as 'Extract the retry logic into a helper' then 'Add a timeout to the upload call'.
practices.criteria:
BEHAVIOR FOCUS: each authored commit subject names what that step did, so a reviewer can follow the history without opening the diff.

## The standard
Judge whether the pull request's commit SUBJECTS let a reviewer follow the change step by step. A legible subject is a specific summary of what that commit actually did, so someone reading the history — or a future `git blame` — understands the step without opening the diff. Judge clarity, not format: a `type:` prefix (feat, fix, refactor, chore) is acceptable but never required, and terse is fine when the object of the change is clear ("wire up depth buffer", "cache detection results", "split parser into lexer + reader" are all legible). Uninformative: a subject that carries no specific information about the change — a bare "wip", "fix", "update", "lint" or "stuff" with no object, a lone punctuation mark, placeholder junk, a bare issue reference or branch slug with no description, "address comments" with no specifics, a subject cut off mid-phrase, or the same subject repeated verbatim across commits. The test is the object: "update changelog", "rename settings tab" and "ignore build output" name what was touched and are legible however terse; "small changes", "fix" and "cleanup" name nothing. These are open examples, not a closed list; reason as an experienced reviewer would about whether each subject carries real information. A subject pairing a reference WITH a real summary ("#39: switch logging to the shared Logger") is legible, not noise. This is a workflow habit about how history is written, never a claim about the code itself.

## Occasion
This is a gate. Automatic merge commits ("Merge branch ...", "Merge pull request ...", or a `parent_count` of 2 or more) are git plumbing, not authored summaries; exclude them from the judgment. Record NOT_APPLICABLE, say so, and stop — never ABSENT — when only merge commits remain after that exclusion: no authored subject was written here.

## Sources
1. The commits (`inputs/context/commits.json`), derived in this container from the captured repository with git: each subject, its body and its `parent_count`. They establish what each authored subject says. Judge each subject on its own; the order is the order a reviewer reads the history in, nothing more. They never establish what the code does or whether it is correct.
2. The checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): per-commit diffs are not derived for you, but `git show <sha>` is available there. Use it only to say what the noisiest commit appears to have done, so the next reader could follow without the diff. Never re-judge a subject's accuracy against the code, and never assert the code is correct.
Precompute hints (`work/precompute-out/summary.md`), when present: every authored subject with the shape it has — bare, a repeat, a list of concerns, cut off — as places to look, never verdicts. If `inputs/context/commits.json` is unavailable, report a collection gap and record no observation; uncollected subjects are never authored silence and never UNDETERMINED.

## Judge
Test the cells in this order.
- PRESENT/GOOD (POSITIVE): every authored subject names what that step did; a reviewer can read top to bottom and follow the work.
- PRESENT/BAD (NEGATIVE): some authored subjects carry no specific information about the change. Quote the noisy subjects and, for the noisiest commit, say what it appears to have done.
- ABSENT/GOOD and ABSENT/BAD: no ordinary case. With one or more authored commits the subjects exist and are judged; with none, the occasion is NOT_APPLICABLE.
- UNDETERMINED: no ordinary case. A subject you have read is either informative or not; never invent a subject or a clean bill you did not read.
One observation per review, over every authored subject. State how many subjects you saw.

## Severity
Negatives only; never above MAJOR on subject quality alone — a formative habit to grow, never a merge gate. Scale to how much the noise degrades a reviewer's ability to follow the history, and weigh review burden proportionally: a single-commit change is inherently low-burden. INFO: a lone straggler in an otherwise clear history, the gentlest nudge. MINOR, the usual band: several uninformative subjects that make the history hard to follow. MAJOR: a history that is mostly noise, where a reviewer genuinely cannot follow the change commit by commit.

## Grounding
Every claim rests on the subject text you quote: the deciding subjects — the noisy ones for PRESENT/BAD, and the subjects you accepted for PRESENT/GOOD. Commit messages are not citable lines, and `inputs/context/commits.json` being derived here rather than staged is not a collection gap: the subjects were read. Quote the deciding subjects verbatim in the rationale, each with its short SHA, and cite `inputs/context/metadata.json` (`scm.pull-request.core`, the `title` line) as the location: the pull request the commits belong to. Never cite a diff line or a repository file for this observation — its evidence is subject text — and never record UNDETERMINED because the subjects have no line of their own to cite. Describe observable behaviour only; never impute intent or character.

## Defer
Legibility of the pull request title and description belongs to `describe-what-and-why`; the scope and cohesion of what a commit touches belongs to `commits-are-atomic-and-cohesive`; code correctness belongs to other practices. Here only: does each authored subject tell the reader what that step did?

practices.name: Say which acceptance criteria are done
practices.whyItMatters: When you close an issue, everyone assumes its whole checklist is done. A quick note on what you finished and what you left for later spares your reviewer from re-checking each item, and keeps the unfinished work from quietly disappearing.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: A line in the description such as 'Closes #57: login and reset are done here, the rate-limit item moves to #61', so the change can be checked against its own definition of done.
practices.criteria:
BEHAVIOR FOCUS: a pull request that closes a tracked work item with checkable acceptance criteria says which of those criteria it satisfies and which it defers.

## The standard
Judge ONE thing: when a change CLOSES a tracked work item that carries checkable acceptance criteria — a Definition-of-Done or acceptance-criteria heading, a task list, a Given-When-Then block, an enumerated must/should list — can a reviewer tell from the pull request itself which criteria this change satisfies and which are deferred? A good handoff maps the change to those criteria: "Closes #57: login and reset done here; rate-limit deferred to #61", or a checked task list mirroring the item's entries, so the change can be confirmed against its own done-list without reverse-engineering. This is a delivery and traceability habit about how the change is handed off — never a code-defect claim and never an assertion that a criterion is unmet.

## Occasion
This is a gate. The occasion exists only when the authored handoff claims to close a tracked item that carries a quotable, checkable criterion. Record NOT_APPLICABLE, name what ruled it out, and stop — never ABSENT — when the linked item you could read carries no closing entry with a checkable criterion: no closing reference at all, or an item that states no checkable criterion — a title alone, a user story ("As a …, I want …"), or prose with no list, checklist or acceptance section is not a checkable criterion. A candidate item alone does not open the occasion, and neither does a body that references an item without a checkable criterion. How an item is referenced — a closing keyword, a bare mention, a branch number — is a syntax fact, not adoption: inspect the exact mention in context, since examples, templates and code may name unrelated work.

## Sources
1. The description (`inputs/context/description.md`) and the title (`inputs/context/metadata.json`): the closing reference and any done/deferred mapping — a checked task list, a Given-When-Then or DoD block, a sentence naming what is done and what moves elsewhere. They establish what the handoff says. They never establish whether a criterion is met.
2. The source branch (`inputs/context/metadata.json`) and the commits (`inputs/context/commits.json`): further places a work-item number may appear. They establish how the item is referenced, nothing more.
3. Each linked item (`inputs/context/linked_work_items/<n>.md`: number, title, url, state, labels, body): the criteria block to map against. It establishes whether a checkable criterion exists and its exact wording. It never establishes that the pull request adopted it; the closing reference does that.
4. The diff (`work/change/diff.patch`): the touched-file set, read only to ground a heavier severity. It never establishes that a criterion is met or unmet.
5. The inventory (`inputs/context/project_inventory.json`): open it and state either the linked or closing issue you found, quoting its `#number "title" (state)`, or that you scanned the inventory and found none.
If the linked items were not captured, you cannot tell whether there was a done-list to map to: when the body carries a closing reference but no mapping and the item's criteria are unreadable, report a collection gap and record no observation. The POSITIVE path does not depend on that file: a body that carries a closing reference together with an explicit checked task list, Given-When-Then or DoD block mapping the change to enumerated criteria is judged from the body alone.

## Judge
Test the cells in this order.
- PRESENT/GOOD (POSITIVE): the closing pull request maps the change to the item's criteria — stating what is done here and what is deferred. The mapping may be implicit: a body whose statements name the substance of each criterion as done (or deferred) honours it, and a checklist that copies the criteria is a mapping; a checklist format is never required. A template's own Definition of Done — items about the merge request's form (title format, lint, a local build, screenshots) rather than the item's criteria — maps nothing, however many of its boxes are ticked. Quote the closing reference and the criteria span.
- PRESENT/BAD: no ordinary case. A stated mapping is never judged wrong here, because you never assert that a criterion is unmet.
- ABSENT/GOOD (NEGATIVE): a quotable closing reference to an item with a checkable criteria block, and the body neither names the substance of the criteria as done nor defers them — a restatement of the title, an empty template, or a body that speaks of something else. Frame it as a forward-looking handoff request — "state which of #N's criteria this satisfies and which are deferred" — never as a failure.
- ABSENT/BAD: no ordinary case.
- UNDETERMINED: the captured text leaves genuinely open whether the mention closes the item; name the question that would settle it. Having read the body and the item and found no mapping is ABSENT/GOOD, not UNDETERMINED.
One observation per review. Use your judgment as an experienced reviewer for cases not enumerated here.

## Severity
Negatives only; never above MAJOR on this practice alone — non-blocking. MINOR, the usual band: a single nudge to state coverage. MAJOR only when, having actually scanned the touched-file set in the diff, you can ground a plausible gap: a concrete quoted criterion has no corresponding surface in the touched files — the item requires an error state and the diff adds only the happy path — and the body does not mark it deferred. Phrase even this as "state whether <criterion> is in scope here or deferred". When you cannot ground a gap, stay MINOR. Identical inputs yield identical severity.

## Grounding
Every observation quotes the work-item number, its closing reference, and the exact criterion span from the linked item's body, citing the item's url. For ABSENT/GOOD, the citations show the closing reference, the criteria block, and the body read through without a mapping. You have the diff and an excerpt, not the running system: never claim to have run, compiled or verified the change, and never assert a specific criterion is unmet, missing or broken — you point at a handoff gap, not at correctness. Never invent or demand a criterion the item never stated. Describe what the body says against what the item states; never impute intent or character.

## Defer
Whether the issue itself is well written belongs to the issue-authoring practices (`issue-has-checkable-outcome`); the pull request description in general belongs to `describe-what-and-why`; marking the change ready and linking its issue at all belongs to `ready-and-traceable-handoff`. Here only: does the closing change say which stated criteria it covers?

groups.name: Acting on review feedback
groups.description: Close the review loop. When a reviewer leaves a substantive comment on a line, answer it with a reply that names what changed or a follow-up commit that addresses it, and resolve the thread before merging. Feedback only improves the work once someone acts on it.

practices.name: Respond to each review comment

appliesWhen.absentSays: nobody left a review comment on this pull request

practices.whyItMatters: A reviewer spent real attention pointing at a specific line. When the thread just sits there, they cannot tell whether you agreed, fixed it, or missed it, and they will hesitate before putting in that effort again.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: Every reviewer comment gets a visible response, either a follow-up commit that addresses it or a short reply like 'Good catch, switched to the shared client in a2b1c3', so no thread sits unanswered.
practices.criteria:
BEHAVIOR FOCUS: visible uptake of each substantive reviewer comment — the loop is closed by a reply, a stated decline, a question back, a pointer to a fix, or a resolution.

## The standard
Judge one habit: when a reviewer left a substantive inline or conversation comment — a question or a change request — did the author visibly engage with it rather than leave it sitting silent? The standard is ENGAGEMENT, not agreement. A loop is closed by any visible response: a reply that fixes it; a reply that declines with a stated reason; a clarifying question back; a pointer to a commit or SHA that addresses it; a thread the reviewer or the author marked resolved; or a global "Done" or "Addressed" posted after the review batch, which closes the loop even when unanchored and unresolved. Good: "Good catch — switched to the shared client in a2b1c3"; "Keeping this as-is because the input is a compile-time constant"; a resolved thread paired with a follow-up commit whose message anchors to the comment's file or its concrete wording. Bad: a reviewer change request or question with no reply, no resolution, and no commit that plausibly addresses it. Only a substantive reviewer comment that drew no response of any kind is an open loop.

## Occasion
This is a gate. Reviewer input is a note whose author login differs from the pull request author character-for-character; a note by the pull request author is never reviewer input, and the author gets no credit for replying to themselves. A comment the record flags `bot` (an access token, an app, a review service; this tool's own notes are never in the record) is reviewer input when it asks something of the change: the author's silence toward an automated finding is the same open loop, and an author who answers or resolves it engaged. Exclude only bare acknowledgements such as "LGTM" or "+1", which ask nothing. Treat a human's login as a real reviewer whatever its shape (a numeric or token-like login is still a person on a provider that anonymises accounts); the pull request author is the `author` of the record, and every other human login is a reviewer. An author who wrote no note at all is not an identity problem: the author's side is then the commits and the resolutions, and silence when neither answers. Record NOT_APPLICABLE, name the fact, and stop — never ABSENT — when, after excluding noise, no quotable substantive reviewer comment exists; the common case is a freshly opened pull request. One exception: when the same login is recorded on a comment and on the reply that answers it (a known mirror artifact that collapses identities), you cannot tell whether a reviewer spoke at all — that is UNDETERMINED, never NOT_APPLICABLE. A reviewer login that differs from the author's is never that case.

## Sources
1. The inline comments (`inputs/context/comments.json`: `path`, `line`, `body`, `author`, `created_at`, and `thread` and `in_reply_to` where the provider records them) and the threads (`inputs/context/review_threads.json`: each thread's `id`, resolution state and who resolved it). They establish who said what and whether a thread was resolved. A thread's comments are the ones sharing its `thread` id, or its path and line; scan the ENTIRE list for a later author note that answers a comment — agreeing, declining with a reason, pointing at a fix, or a global "Done" after the batch. The precompute summary (`work/precompute-out/summary.md`) lists every inline comment by someone other than the author, one row each, with whether the author replied in the thread, whether it was resolved and by whom, whether the change touches the line, and how many authored commits came after it, counting those that touched the same file apart: decide every row.
2. The general comments (`inputs/context/general_comments.json`): conversation-level questions and change requests, and author replies posted outside a thread. Same partition, same scan.
3. The pull request author and state (`inputs/context/metadata.json`): the login to partition by, and whether the work is merged or closed.
4. The commits (`inputs/context/commits.json`: each with its message, `committedAt` and the `files` it touched): a follow-up commit counts as uptake when it comes after the comment and touches the commented file, or when its message observably ties to the comment — a shared path or a shared concrete term. Uptake is judged on the request's substance, not its letter: a rename to a different space-free name answers "rename to remove spaces". A later commit on the file says the file moved, not that the ask was taken up: read the changed lines in the diff before crediting it.
An image: its caption and the sentence around it. An external link: nothing. When a substantive reviewer comment is visible but the facts that would settle its uptake are not — replies, thread state or commit subjects you could not read — report a collection gap and record no observation.

## Judge
Test the cells in this order.
- PRESENT/GOOD (POSITIVE): every substantive reviewer comment has a visible response of one of the kinds above. Quote the reply, the resolution marker, or the matching commit-message phrase.
- PRESENT/BAD (NEGATIVE): a response exists but its concrete content is harmful; only when the quoted content supports that judgment.
- ABSENT/GOOD (NEGATIVE): at least one substantive reviewer comment drew no response of any kind. Name the single most consequential open thread, quote it, and point forward to replying in-thread or pushing a fix. "Not replied on the same line", "thread not marked RESOLVED" and "no commit references it" are merge-gate facts and never the deciding clause.
- ABSENT/BAD: no ordinary case.
- UNDETERMINED only for the collapsed-identity case above; name the question. Having scanned every note and found no response to a reviewer comment is ABSENT, not UNDETERMINED.
One observation per review, over all reviewer comments.

## Severity
Negatives only; never above MAJOR on this alone — a formative habit, not a merge gate. MINOR, the usual band: an open question on still-open work. MAJOR: an ignored change request, or an open loop on work already handed off — merged or closed.

## Grounding
Quote the reviewer comment in every cell. When you assert uptake, quote the reply, the resolution marker, or the commit-message phrase that ties to it; never infer uptake from a commit's mere presence or timing. Never invent a reply, a resolution, or a clean bill you did not verify. Describe the state of the work — "this thread is still open" — never the person, and never impute intent or a causal outcome.

## Defer
Whether the resulting code is correct belongs to other practices. Merge timing and merging past unresolved threads belong to `merged-past-unresolved-review-threads`. Here only: was each substantive reviewer comment engaged with?

practices.name: Resolve open threads before merging
practices.whyItMatters: Merging while a reviewer still has changes requested skips the very check they asked for, and tells them their review did not count. It is also a quality signal, not just a courtesy: changes that land with little reviewer discussion tend to carry more defects that surface after release. Resolving the threads first keeps review worth doing.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: By the time you merge, every open thread is resolved and anyone who requested changes has come back with an approval, so nothing lands over an objection.
practices.criteria:
BEHAVIOR FOCUS: the change merged while a reviewer's change-request or an unresolved review thread still stood.

## The standard
At the moment the change MERGED, was the review loop closed first — every reviewer's gate either resolved or superseded — or did the change land while a reviewer's request or an open thread still stood? This is a process habit about closing the loop before merge, never a claim that the merged code is wrong: the code may be perfectly correct and still have skipped the re-review a reviewer asked for. A later approval supersedes a change-request only if it occurred before the merge; a resolution after merge does not establish that the loop was closed beforehand.

## Occasion
This is a gate. If the change did not merge, record NOT_APPLICABLE, name that fact, and stop — never ABSENT: there is no merged loop to assess. NOT_APPLICABLE has no other ordinary case.

## Sources
1. The pull request record (`inputs/context/metadata.json`): `state`, and `merged_at` when the provider recorded it. It establishes that the change merged and when. It never establishes the review state.
2. The review-decision and thread-resolution records (`inputs/context/review_threads.json`): each reviewer's decision, each thread's path, line and resolution, and their dates. They establish the review state at the merge timestamp when read as dated events. A current decision or resolution field is a current-state fact, not automatically a historical one; a latest-state snapshot, a filename or a record count never by itself proves the historical record is complete.
3. The discussion (`inputs/context/general_comments.json`, and the inline comments in `inputs/context/comments.json`, each carrying the `thread` it belongs to): dated comments that explain a supersession or a resolution. They establish why a gate was lifted, when dated. They never establish a decision a reviewer did not record. The precompute summary (`work/precompute-out/summary.md`) lists the merge — who, when — and one row per thread the record does not mark RESOLVED, with its `id`, anchor, opening time and whether it is outdated; it says whether the threads file was captured at all.
The diff (`work/change/diff.patch`) establishes nothing here: never use the code to infer a reviewer's decision. If the change merged but `inputs/context/review_threads.json` is absent or truncated, the loop had some state at merge and you could not read it: report a collection gap and record no observation. Never treat a missing file as an empty loop.

## Judge
Test the cells in this order.
- PRESENT/BAD (NEGATIVE): merged with the loop still open — a reviewer's change-request still stood at merge (name the reviewer, quote the decision), or an unresolved thread that nobody resolved remained (quote its path:line).
- ABSENT/BAD (POSITIVE): merged with the loop closed — no reviewer's change-request still stood and no unresolved thread was left open. State the evidence relied on: "merged; reviewer X's change-request superseded by their later approval; no unresolved thread".
- PRESENT/GOOD and ABSENT/GOOD: no ordinary case. Merging over a standing gate is not desirable, and a closed loop is not a lapse.
- UNDETERMINED when the qualified sources were inspected but cannot establish the state at merge — for example, a change-request with no date that could precede or follow the merge; name the unresolved historical question. A complete record with no standing gate is ABSENT/BAD, not UNDETERMINED: when every thread is resolved and the last recorded decision is an approval, the loop is closed whether or not the record carries a merge or resolution timestamp — a missing timestamp is not a standing gate. A missing required source is a collection gap, not an observation.
One observation per review, on the single at-merge question.

## Severity
Negatives only; never above MAJOR on loop closure alone — non-blocking. MINOR, the usual band: a merely open thread with no standing request, the lighter lapse. MAJOR: landing over a reviewer's still-standing request-changes gate, the heavier miss. Equivalent observed states get equivalent treatment.

## Grounding
For PRESENT/BAD, quote the deciding review evidence and the dated facts that show it still stood at the merge timestamp. For ABSENT/BAD, cite the complete bounded review record — the merge timestamp, every decision and every thread's resolution with dates — that shows none remained. Describe only the observable state: "merged with N request-changes still standing; thread at <path:line> unresolved at merge". Never "you ignored the reviewer" or "you merged broken code"; never a claim about the code's correctness; never a current open or resolved state offered as proof of the state at merge.

## Defer
Whether threads on an OPEN pull request are being taken up belongs to `engaging-with-inline-review-comments`. Here only: was the loop closed at the moment of merge? Do not double-flag.

groups.name: Writing issues a maintainer can act on
groups.description: Write issues someone can pick up without coming back to ask what you meant. State the problem clearly, what you saw versus expected plus steps to reproduce for a bug, or the who and why for a request, keep each issue to one concern, say how to tell when it is done, and link the design or decision the work depends on.

practices.name: State a problem a maintainer can act on
practices.whyItMatters: A maintainer cannot fix what they cannot picture. An issue that leaves out what you saw versus what you expected, or the who and why behind a request, comes straight back with 'can you clarify?' and you both lose a day.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: A bug report that reads 'uploading a 0-byte file returns 500, I expected a clear validation error' and lists the exact steps to reproduce, so a maintainer can start straight away. Or a request that names one concrete capability with who it helps and why, such as 'reviewers lose track of which files changed in large diffs, so add a per-file changed-lines summary to the review view'.
practices.criteria:
BEHAVIOR FOCUS: the issue, read on its own, gives a maintainer enough to start work without a clarification round-trip.

## The standard
Judge whether this issue lets a maintainer picture what is wrong or what is wanted, and begin. The bar is the one a senior triager applies. A reader must be able to identify the kind of work and find the concrete substance it needs. For a defect report: the actual or observed behaviour, the expected behaviour, and how to reproduce it — a concrete reproduction path (numbered steps, or a stack trace, an exact error or a failing test) is the single most valuable and most-often-missing element, so weight it accordingly. For a capability request: a concrete capability stated clearly, ideally with who benefits and why. A specific title that locates the work — not a bare slug, an empty template or "it's broken" — is part of being act-on-able. Use judgment for forms not enumerated here: an issue that ships a quotable acceptance-criteria, Definition-of-Done or Given-When-Then block is act-on-able on that block alone; do not then demand a beneficiary or a "so that" clause. An epic, umbrella or requirement card carrying substantive prose is act-on-able at the requirement level; its detail lives in child stories, so judge it as a requirement, never as a thin story. An untyped issue that nonetheless asserts a malfunction IS a defect report; judge it as one.

## Occasion
This is a gate. Record NOT_APPLICABLE, name the fact, and stop — never ABSENT — when there is no work-kind to judge: a pure question or open discussion that asserts no defect and requests no capability. Do not demand reproduction steps of a discussion. A title that names a task or a capability ("Add App icon", "Edit README and diagrams") is engineering work even when the body is empty: the gate passes and the empty body is the lapse, never NOT_APPLICABLE.

## Sources
1. The title and the WHOLE body (`inputs/context/description.md`): every section, template field, step list and criteria block. It establishes the kind of work and the substance stated inline. An image: read its caption and the sentence around it. An external link: nothing.
2. The title and labels (`inputs/context/metadata.json`): a deliverable-type label names the kind of work. It never establishes substance by itself; an empty template echoing the title under such a label is still empty.
3. The comments (`inputs/context/comments.json`): part of the observable artifact; substance stated there counts. They never establish substance you cannot quote from them.
4. Linked design, decision or spec documents (`inputs/context/outline/`): when the issue delegates its substance to a document materialized here, read it. A concrete capability or interface the document actually specifies is substance an implementer can start from; count it as PRESENT rather than demanding the issue restate it inline. A generic document or a placeholder marker that does not concretely pin THIS work supplies nothing.
When the issue delegates its substance to a specific named document that was NOT materialized, you cannot tell whether that substance exists: report a collection gap and record no observation, never a claim against prose you were never shown. If the issue text was not captured completely, the same.

## Judge
Test the cells in this order.
- PRESENT/GOOD (POSITIVE): the kind of work is identifiable and the substance it needs is genuinely present and quotable — inline, in a comment, or in a materialized document the issue delegates to.
- PRESENT/BAD: no ordinary case. An act-on-able statement is never undesirable.
- ABSENT/GOOD (NEGATIVE): a required element of the act-on-able core is missing, because the issue delegates to nothing and states none itself, or the materialized document is generic or a placeholder. Name the missing element.
- ABSENT/BAD: no ordinary case.
- UNDETERMINED: no ordinary case. A complete but empty or vague body is an assessed gap — ABSENT/GOOD — not UNDETERMINED; an incomplete capture is a collection gap, not an observation.
One observation per review, over the whole issue.

## Severity
Negatives only; never above MAJOR — a non-blocking authoring-habit nudge, not a merge gate. Severity reflects HOW MUCH of the act-on-able core is gone, judged from the evidence, never from a feeling. MINOR, the usual band: the work is clear and only one secondary element is missing. MAJOR: the issue is effectively unstartable — a defect with neither a concrete symptom nor reproduction steps; a request naming no concrete capability, such as a bare title or an empty template echoing the title under a deliverable-type label.

## Grounding
Every element you call present must be quotable from the artifact — the body, a comment, or the materialized document; an element you cannot quote is absent. For ABSENT/GOOD, the citations show the boundary you searched: the whole body, the labels, the comments, and the `inputs/context/outline/` documents or their absence. Never invent content and never grant a clean bill you did not verify. Describe the observable gap — "the body names a symptom but no reproduction path" — never the reporter's intent or character.

## Defer
Whether the issue has a checkable or measurable outcome belongs to `issue-has-checkable-outcome`. Whether it duplicates another filed issue, beyond noting an evident restatement, belongs to `issue-scoped-to-single-concern`. Here only: can a maintainer picture the work and start?

practices.name: Keep the issue to one concern
practices.whyItMatters: An issue that quietly bundles three unrelated asks cannot be assigned, estimated, or closed cleanly. One part lands, the rest linger, and the whole thing stays open forever, tracking nothing.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: One issue, one deliverable, such as 'add CSV export to the reports page', rather than 'add CSV export, fix the date picker, and bump the chart library' crammed into one ticket.
practices.criteria:
BEHAVIOR FOCUS: how the issue is scoped — one cohesive deliverable at the issue's intended level, rather than unrelated asks stapled into one ticket.

## The standard
A good issue tracks ONE cohesive deliverable: something that can be picked up, worked and closed as a single unit. Judge cohesion as an experienced reviewer would: is there a single thread of intent, or have unrelated asks been stapled together so that part can land while the rest lingers? The test is whether a maintainer would naturally assign, estimate and close it as one thing, or would be fighting to. One feature, one bug, one question is one concern. Internal decomposition is still ONE concern: implementation sub-steps, a checklist that builds up one capability, a sub-issue rollup that breaks one feature into trackable children. An epic that bundles several RELATED facets of the same feature area (create, rename, delete plus search for one entity) is ONE concern at its altitude; that breadth is what makes it an epic. The tell of bundling is separable threads of intent targeting different concerns, never the mere presence of "and" or a long checklist.

## Occasion
This is a gate. Record NOT_APPLICABLE, name the fact, and stop — never ABSENT — when there is no concrete deliverable to scope at all: a pure question, a support request, an open discussion, an empty or title-only body, or an untouched template. Do not manufacture a POSITIVE from that absence.

## Sources
Judge only from the issue body, its labels and its sub-issue rollup as captured.
1. The title and the WHOLE body (`inputs/context/description.md`): every section, checklist and step list, and the sub-issue rollup when the capture carries it. It establishes the deliverable(s) named and how they relate. It never establishes what the author meant beyond the written spans.
2. The labels and title (`inputs/context/metadata.json`): the issue's intended level — epic, feature, bug, task. They establish the altitude at which to judge cohesion. They never establish cohesion by themselves.
3. The workspace inventory (`inputs/context/project_inventory.json`): sibling issues. Open it and state either the overlapping or duplicate issue you found — quote its `#number "title" (state)` — or that you scanned the inventory and found none. A bundled concern that clearly warrants its own existing or separate sibling is evidence of multiple concerns; confirm against actual titles and bodies, never from sibling count alone.
An image in the body: read its caption and the sentence around it. An external link: nothing. If the issue was only partly captured, report a collection gap and record no observation.

## Judge
Test the cells in this order.
- PRESENT/GOOD (POSITIVE): one cohesive deliverable, including any internal decomposition or related-facet epic described above.
- PRESENT/BAD (NEGATIVE): genuinely unrelated deliverables fused into one ticket — "add CSV export, fix the date picker, and bump the chart library". Feed forward the single most consequential split: name the concerns to break into linked issues. Never enumerate every clause.
- ABSENT/GOOD and ABSENT/BAD: no ordinary case. An issue with a deliverable has a scope to judge; one without is NOT_APPLICABLE.
- UNDETERMINED only when the complete text genuinely leaves one journey versus separate deliverables unresolved; quote the ambiguity and say what would settle it. A partly captured issue is a collection gap, not UNDETERMINED.
One observation per review, over the whole issue.

## Severity
Negatives only; never above MAJOR on scoping alone — a formative habit, never a merge gate. MINOR, the usual band: separable asks that a maintainer could still split without stranding work. MAJOR: clearly unrelated bundling that will genuinely strand work, with part landing and the rest lingering open.

## Grounding
Quote the actual span(s) that name the deliverable(s) you are judging; for PRESENT/BAD, the spans that name each separable concern. State the inventory result in every observation. Describe the observable bundling — "the body names three deliverables with no shared thread" — never carelessness or intent. Never invent a deliverable, a clean bill, or a bundling you did not read.

## Defer
Whether an epic should itself be split into tracked child stories belongs to `breaks-large-work-into-trackable-subtasks`; do not double-count it. Here only: is this issue one concern at its level?

practices.name: Define a checkable outcome
practices.whyItMatters: Without a clear line for 'done', nobody can tell when the work is finished, including the person doing it. A checkable outcome turns 'improve performance' from an open-ended wish into a task someone can actually complete.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: A short acceptance checklist a maintainer can tick off when the work is truly finished, such as 'export downloads a valid CSV' and 'an empty result shows a friendly message', rather than a vague hope of improvement.
practices.criteria:
BEHAVIOR FOCUS: a quotable finish line — an outcome a maintainer could later verify as DONE from the issue alone.

## The standard
Judge one thing: does this issue define an outcome a maintainer could later verify as done? A good issue draws a clear finish line: a reader can tell, from the issue alone, what state of the world means the work is complete. The line can take many shapes — an acceptance checklist, a Given-When-Then block, a story's who/what/why phrased so the result is testable, or, for a bug, a stated expected behaviour a fix must restore. The form does not matter; the testability does. Use judgment as an experienced reviewer would; do not hunt for a keyword or label. Good: "export downloads a valid CSV; an empty result shows a friendly message". Bad: "improve performance" with nothing that could ever read as done, or a body that only echoes its title. For an umbrella, epic or requirement card, the right checkable outcome is a definition of done that decomposes into child work, not an inline checklist: bundling many capabilities is expected of it.

## Occasion
This is a gate. Record NOT_APPLICABLE, name the fact, and stop — never ABSENT — when there is nothing whose "done" this practice could define: a question, a support request, an open discussion, or a bare board or ceremony placeholder with no asserted problem and no requested capability. A missing checklist on something that was never engineering work is not a defect. A title that names a task or a capability ("Add App icon", "Add package") with an empty body is engineering work whose done was never defined: the gate passes and ABSENT is the answer, never NOT_APPLICABLE.

## Sources
1. The title and the WHOLE body (`inputs/context/description.md`): every section, checklist, criteria block and expected-behaviour statement. It establishes a finish line you can quote. An image: its caption and the sentence around it. An external link: nothing.
2. The labels and title (`inputs/context/metadata.json`): the kind of issue, including whether it is an umbrella, epic or requirement card. They never establish a finish line by themselves.
3. The comments (`inputs/context/comments.json`): a finish line stated there counts. They never establish one you cannot quote.
4. A linked design or spec document the issue delegates to, materialised as a `.md` file under `inputs/context/outline/`: when it states a concrete, testable contract THIS work must satisfy — specific behaviours, status codes, API or state conditions — that contract IS a quotable finish line. Read and quote it before concluding none exists. A generic guideline, or a placeholder document that does not pin this deliverable's done-state, supplies nothing. A document never materialised is not evidence in either direction: when the issue delegates its finish line to a specific document you were not shown, report a collection gap and record no observation, never a claim against prose you were not shown.
5. Child work: sub-issues or a task list referenced in the body or comments, or child entries in `inputs/context/project_inventory.json` when captured. For an umbrella, they establish the decomposition that makes its outcome checkable.

## Judge
Test the cells in this order.
- PRESENT/GOOD (POSITIVE): the finish line is quotable from the body, a comment, or a materialised document; or, for an umbrella, children or tracked sub-issues already carry the decomposition — POSITIVE with no severity.
- PRESENT/BAD: no ordinary case. A checkable outcome is never undesirable.
- ABSENT/GOOD (NEGATIVE): a real deliverable to build, and no quotable outcome in the issue or any materialised document it delegates to. For an umbrella with substantive prose but no child-mapped done, this is a gentle decomposition nudge, not a hard failure; do not double-alarm.
- ABSENT/BAD: no ordinary case.
- UNDETERMINED: no ordinary case. A body read in full that states no finish line is ABSENT, not UNDETERMINED; a document you were not shown is a collection gap.
One observation per review, over the whole issue.

## Severity
Negatives only; never above MAJOR — a formative authoring habit, never a merge gate. MINOR, the usual band: everything softer is a single nudge, including the umbrella decomposition nudge. MAJOR: a maintainer genuinely cannot tell when ANY of the work is done — a real deliverable with neither a verifiable outcome nor a decomposition.

## Grounding
Quote the span you relied on: the checklist, criteria block, expected behaviour, the document sentence with its `inputs/context/outline/...` file path, or the child references. For ABSENT/GOOD, the citations show the boundary searched: the whole body, the labels, the comments, and the `inputs/context/outline/` documents or their absence. Never invent a checklist, a clean bill or an exoneration you did not read. Never assert technical feasibility, design correctness or the author's competence. Describe the observable gap in the issue, never the author's character or motive.

## Defer
Whether the problem itself is well stated — observed versus expected, who/what/why as a narrative — belongs to `issue-states-an-actionable-problem`; do not write that relationship into the feedback. Here only: is there a verifiable finish line?

practices.name: Point the issue to the context it depends on
practices.whyItMatters: An issue that silently depends on decisions made elsewhere forces every implementer to re-discover the context — or, worse, to guess it and build the wrong thing.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: When work depends on an existing design or decision, the issue links the document that holds it, so whoever picks it up starts with the evidenceRationale already in hand.
practices.criteria:
BEHAVIOR FOCUS: an issue that depends on a design, decision, spec, runbook or data model recorded elsewhere points the implementer to the document that holds it.

## The standard
Judge one thing: when an issue clearly depends on prior context an implementer would need to act on it correctly — an existing design, a decision record, a spec, a runbook, a data model — does the issue point them to that context with a link to the relevant wiki document, instead of assuming the reader already carries it? The signal is judged from the issue's own text: it leans on decisions or designs made elsewhere — "per our architecture", "following the agreed rollout plan", "as decided for the billing redesign", "must match the data model" — such that someone picking it up cold could not proceed correctly without finding that source. A link count is never the signal, and a link to an unrelated document is not credit. Do not infer a hidden dependency the text does not express.

## Occasion
This is a gate. Record NOT_APPLICABLE, name the fact, and stop — never ABSENT — when the issue is self-contained: a clear bug report, a small well-described change, a question. Most issues are; prefer NOT_APPLICABLE whenever the issue reads as self-contained, and never penalize a self-contained issue for lacking links.

## Sources
1. The title and the whole body (`inputs/context/description.md`, `inputs/context/metadata.json`): every phrase that appeals to context made elsewhere, and every link. It establishes whether the issue leans on external context and whether it points anywhere. It never establishes that a linked document is relevant; a bare link is not evidence on its own. An image: read its caption and the sentence around it. An external link outside the wiki: nothing.
2. The linked wiki documents materialized under `inputs/context/outline/`: read each to judge whether it is actually the context the issue leans on. A document establishes relevance when a passage in it carries the design, decision or spec the issue depends on. It never establishes relevance by its title alone.
When the issue links a specific document that was NOT materialized for you, you cannot tell whether it carries the context: report a collection gap and record no observation — neither credit nor criticism.

## Judge
Test the cells in this order.
- PRESENT/GOOD (POSITIVE): the issue genuinely rests on prior design, decision or spec context and links the specific materialized document that carries it, so an implementer can proceed without hunting or guessing.
- PRESENT/BAD: no ordinary case. A link to an unrelated document is not credit; judge that issue under ABSENT/GOOD.
- ABSENT/GOOD (NEGATIVE): the issue plainly leans on context made elsewhere but leaves the reader no pointer to it — nothing, or only a materialized document that does not carry that context — so they must reconstruct or reverse-engineer the intent.
- ABSENT/BAD: no ordinary case.
- UNDETERMINED: no ordinary case. Having read the whole issue and the materialized documents and found no pointer to the context it leans on is ABSENT/GOOD; a linked document that was not materialized is a collection gap, not an observation.
One observation per review, over the whole issue.

## Severity
Negatives only; never above MAJOR — a non-blocking authoring nudge, not a gate. MINOR, the usual band: a mild lean on unstated context — a nudge to link the source. MAJOR only when the missing context is load-bearing enough that an implementer would likely build the wrong thing without it. When unsure, prefer the lower severity.

## Grounding
For ABSENT/GOOD quote the exact phrase in the issue that appeals to external context ("as decided…", "per the design", "must match…") and state what context an implementer would need but is not pointed to. For PRESENT/GOOD cite the materialized document's `inputs/context/outline/` file path and quote or closely paraphrase the passage that shows it is the relevant context. Never invent a document, a decision or a dependency; talk about the issue's text, never the reporter's intent or character.

## Defer
Whether the issue is actionable on its own terms belongs to `issue-states-an-actionable-problem`; the two are disjoint. Here only: does an issue that depends on external design or decision context actually point to it?

groups.name: Reviewing a teammate's work constructively
groups.description: Review a teammate's change well. Leave specific, actionable comments, raise concerns as questions rather than commands, and read the change before approving it rather than waving it through.

practices.name: Leave specific, actionable review comments
practices.whyItMatters: 'This looks off' leaves the author guessing what to change and why. A comment that points at the exact line and names the concern gets fixed, while a vague one just slows the change down.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: A note anchored to the line that says 'this throws when items is empty, so guard the loop or return early on a null list', so the author knows exactly what to do next.
practices.criteria:
BEHAVIOR FOCUS: the substantive comments a reviewer wrote on this pull request each point at something concrete and tell the author what to do about it.

## The standard
Judge the craft of the comments a reviewer wrote — never whether the reviewer's claim about the code is correct, and never the author's code. A useful comment names a specific construct or anchors to a real line AND states an actionable substance: what is wrong, what to change, a concrete alternative, or a pointed question a maintainer can actually answer. A vague comment is a content-free gesture that leaves the author guessing: "this is messy", "fix this", "cleanup", a bare "?". Inline (diff-anchored) notes and conversation-tab notes meet the same standard. A blunt but specific comment is useful here; a polite but vague one is not. A reviewer comment is one whose author differs from the pull request author in the metadata.

## Occasion
This is a gate.
