The practice judges reviewer activity, not the changed code: "a big pull request got little review" is not an observation, and an unreviewed or draft pull request is never a substandard review. Build one list of every review note in your context, wherever it is carried — inline arrays, general or conversation notes, any discussion thread rendered in the artifact text. Set aside the notes that carry no reviewer-craft signal: the author's own self-notes; automation output (a comment the record flags `bot`: an access token, an app, a review service — the reviewer craft judged here is a person's); bare approvals or acknowledgements ("LGTM", "+1"); author-uptake or status replies that report what was done rather than ask for a change; off-topic chatter unconnected to anything this diff touches. When `inputs/context/review_threads.json` has no review decision and no substantive reviewer comment survives, the occasion never arose — the common case for a freshly opened pull request: record NOT_APPLICABLE, name the fact, and stop — never ABSENT. Do not abstain merely because a field name or flag is missing while a real reviewer comment is plainly visible: read it and judge it.

## Sources
1. The inline review threads (`inputs/context/review_threads.json`): each comment's author, body and path:line anchor, and the review decision. They establish the diff-anchored comments and their positions.
2. The conversation notes (`inputs/context/general_comments.json`): each note's author and body. A conversation note has no position; it establishes only author and body.
3. The pull request metadata (`inputs/context/metadata.json`): the pull request author, which separates reviewer comments from author notes.
4. The annotated diff (`work/change/diff.patch`): the hunk a comment anchors to. Read it to confirm the comment points at something real. It never establishes whether the comment's claim is correct; assess the comment, not the code.
If the artifact shows a review happened but the comment bodies were not materialized for you, reviewer craft exists that you could not read: report a collection gap and record no observation.

## Judge
Test the cells in this order over the substantive reviewer comments that remain.
- PRESENT/GOOD (POSITIVE): the clear majority are specific and actionable — the author can tell what to change.
- PRESENT/BAD (NEGATIVE): vague comments leave the author guessing — from a stray straggler among useful notes to a review that is predominantly empty gestures. Quote each one.
- ABSENT/GOOD and ABSENT/BAD: no ordinary case. With no substantive reviewer comment the occasion is NOT_APPLICABLE; with one, its craft is judged.
- UNDETERMINED: no ordinary case. A comment you can read is judged; one you cannot read is a collection gap.
One observation per review, over all the substantive reviewer comments together.

## Severity
Negatives only; never above MAJOR on comment quality alone — a workflow habit, not a merge gate. Scale to how much of the review is content-free. MINOR, the usual band: a stray vague straggler; a lone unhelpful comment is a light cost, never a serious one. MAJOR: a review that is predominantly empty gestures, leaving the author unable to act. Equivalent situations yield equivalent severity.

## Grounding
Quote verbatim every comment you call vague — with its path:line for an inline comment; by author and body for a conversation note, which has no position, so never invent a file:line for it. Quote at least one useful comment when one exists. Never call a comment vague without quoting it; never fabricate a comment to avoid looking idle. Talk about the comments; never grade the reviewer as a person or impute intent.

## Defer
Whether the author took the comments up or left threads open belongs to `engaging-with-inline-review-comments`; tone and politeness belong to `reviews-respectfully-asks-rather-than-demands`. Here only: could the author act on what the reviewer wrote?

practices.name: Comment on the code, not the person
practices.whyItMatters: The same point can be made as a question or as a put-down, and people remember which one you chose. A curious question gets acted on, while sarcasm and bare orders breed defensiveness and make the next review harder.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: 'What happens if this runs twice, could we hit a race here?' rather than 'this is obviously broken, did you even test it?', so disagreement lands on the code and never on the author.
practices.criteria:
BEHAVIOR FOCUS: how the REVIEWER's substantive comments are voiced — as questions, suggestions and reasoned disagreement aimed at the code, or as orders, sarcasm or contempt aimed at the person.

## The standard
Judge whether the reviewer's comments stay civil and collaborative: concerns raised as questions or suggestions, disagreement carrying a reason ("I'd prefer X because Y"), rather than bare orders, belittling, sarcasm, contempt, name-calling or hostility aimed at the author. This is about HOW feedback is voiced, never whether the technical point is correct. Directness, brevity and strong technical disagreement are not incivility: "This will NPE when items is empty" is blunt and civil. A command paired with a reason is fine. Do not flag a word like "just" or "obviously" when it reads neutrally; judge the whole phrasing in context as an experienced reviewer would. The subject is the reviewer, never the changed code: "a big pull request got little review" is not an observation.

## Occasion
This is a gate. A reviewer is anyone whose author differs from the pull request author; never grade the author's own words. Skip comments the record flags `bot` and bare approvals ("LGTM", "+1") — they carry no human reviewer tone. The flag is the provider's classification; never guess from the shape of a login: a numeric or token-like login without the flag is a real human reviewer, not automation. When no review decision exists and no substantive reviewer comment survives this filter — the common case for a freshly opened pull request, and always for an unreviewed or draft one — the occasion never arose: record NOT_APPLICABLE, say so, and stop. Never ABSENT; an unreviewed pull request is never a substandard review. This is the only NOT_APPLICABLE case.

## Sources
1. The pull request record (`inputs/context/metadata.json`): the author, to apply the filter, and the state. It establishes who is a reviewer. It never establishes tone.
2. Inline review comments (`inputs/context/review_threads.json`): each carries path, line, body and author. They establish what a reviewer said at a position in the code.
3. Conversation-tab comments (`inputs/context/general_comments.json`): author and body, no path or line. They establish what a reviewer said about the change as a whole.
Judge tone across both comment sources. An image in a comment: read its caption and the sentence around it. An external link: nothing. If the record shows a review happened but the comment bodies are not in your context, there was reviewer speech you could not read: report a collection gap and record no observation.

## Judge
Test the cells in this order.
- PRESENT/GOOD (POSITIVE): at least one substantive reviewer comment survives the filter and every one is civil and collaborative — a concern posed so the author can respond, disagreement kept on the code.
- PRESENT/BAD (NEGATIVE): one or more comments carry a quotable incivility marker: a bare order with no reason and no softening ("Change this."), belittling that implies the author should not have needed telling, sarcasm or contempt, name-calling, hostility aimed at the person.
- ABSENT/GOOD and ABSENT/BAD: no ordinary case. No surviving reviewer comment is NOT_APPLICABLE, not ABSENT.
- UNDETERMINED has no ordinary case: a marker you cannot quote is counted absent, never UNDETERMINED, and comment bodies you could not read are a collection gap, not an observation.
One observation per review, over every surviving reviewer comment.

## Severity
Negatives only; never above MAJOR on tone alone — a formative communication habit, not a merge gate. MINOR, the usual band: a single sharp-but-impersonal edge. MAJOR: a pattern across several comments, or contempt, name-calling or hostility aimed at the person. Identical comments yield identical severity.

## Grounding
Quote every marker you count verbatim, with its author; never fabricate a comment, a clean bill or an exoneration. Cite an inline comment only by the path and line it actually carries; cite a conversation-tab comment by author and quoted text and leave the location empty. Frame everything about the COMMENT — "this phrasing reads as a demand" — never about the reviewer as a person; no hunches, no psychoanalysing, no intent inferred beyond the words. For PRESENT/GOOD, cite the surviving comments you read.

## Defer
Whether a comment is specific, actionable or technically right belongs to `leaves-useful-specific-review-comments` and `reviews-substantively-with-understanding`; a vague-but-civil comment is still POSITIVE here. Here only: does the phrasing land on the code and not on the author?

practices.name: Explain consequential review judgments
practices.whyItMatters: A short explanation makes the basis of an important approval or concern available to the author and other reviewers. A bare approval alone does not show what was checked; it also does not prove that the reviewer failed to read the change.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: For a consequential authorization change, a reviewer names the permission check they considered and explains why it addresses the concern, or asks a specific unresolved question. A routine change with no material concern may need only a brief approval.
practices.criteria:
BEHAVIOR FOCUS: a review whose captured context called for written reasoning carries a substantive comment grounded in the change.

## The standard
Judge the written explanation accompanying a review, not whether the reviewer read or understood the change. A substantive comment makes the reviewer's reasoning inspectable: it names or quotes a concrete diff element — a path, a symbol or a term that actually appears in the diff or summary you can see — or asks a real clarifying question about the change. One such comment is enough; polish, tone and specificity are not graded here. A bare approval or acknowledgement ("LGTM", "+1", a lone thumbs-up) supplies no written reasoning, but it does not establish that the review was careless or superficial. Written reasoning is owed only when the captured context establishes an occasion for it: a request to explain a consequential trade-off, or a documented review requirement. Change size or risk alone does not make commentary mandatory. A reviewer is anyone whose login differs from the pull request author. Discount machine noise and empty ceremony: a comment or decision the record flags `bot` is not human review, and a content-free approval is not engagement. The flag is the provider's classification of the account; a login's shape decides nothing.

## Occasion
This is a gate. This practice judges REVIEWER activity, never the changed code; "a big PR got little review" is not an observation. Record NOT_APPLICABLE, name the fact, and stop — never ABSENT — when no review has happened yet (no reviewer comment and no approval), when `inputs/context/review_threads.json` has no review decision and no substantive reviewer comment survives the author-exclusion filter, or when the context demonstrates no need for an explanation and none was supplied. An unreviewed or draft pull request is never a substandard review; do not manufacture praise or criticism from a bare approval.

## Sources
1. The review threads (`inputs/context/review_threads.json`): the review decisions and the inline diff comments, with their authors. They establish who reviewed, what was approved, and any inline reasoning. An empty inline thread never establishes missing reasoning across the other sources, nor an unperformed review.
2. The general comments (`inputs/context/general_comments.json`): the conversation and discussion notes. The substance of a review may live here rather than inline; read whatever review notes are materialized, under whatever heading, before concluding nothing substantive exists. They also establish a request for an explanation, when one was made.
3. The description and metadata (`inputs/context/description.md`, `inputs/context/metadata.json`): the author's login for the reviewer filter, and any documented review requirement or trade-off the change raises. They never establish that reasoning was written.
4. The diff (`work/change/diff.patch`) and the checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): whether a comment's named path, symbol or term actually appears in the change, and the real size of the change once obviously generated or vendored bulk (lockfiles, generated clients, migrations, snapshots) is discounted — a "big" diff that is mostly generated is smaller than its line count. They never make commentary mandatory on their own.
Judge from the review notes and the change-size signals present in your context; do not claim per-comment or per-line facts you cannot see. Missing or incomplete required sources are a collection gap with no observation; never read a missing count as zero.

## Judge
Test the cells in this order, after inspecting every declared source of review comments.
- PRESENT/GOOD (POSITIVE): an applicable review includes a substantive comment grounded in the change, inline or in the discussion.
- PRESENT/BAD: no ordinary case. A grounded explanation is never undesirable here; its wording belongs to a sibling.
- ABSENT/GOOD (NEGATIVE): the captured context establishes that written reasoning was demonstrably required or requested, the review was approved without it, and every declared review-comment source holds nothing but bare approvals or acknowledgements.
- ABSENT/BAD: no ordinary case.
- UNDETERMINED only when the captured requirement or explanation remains genuinely ambiguous after every available source is inspected; name the unresolved question. Having read every source and found no reasoning where none was demonstrably required is NOT_APPLICABLE, not UNDETERMINED.
One observation per review. Equivalent inputs yield equivalent calls.

## Severity
Negatives only; never above MAJOR — a non-blocking practice. Severity reflects the concrete coordination or decision-recording consequence of the missing explanation, never an assumption about how carefully the reviewer read. MINOR, the usual band: the missing reasoning costs the team little to recover. MAJOR: the missing reasoning leaves a consequential decision with no inspectable basis for the author or other reviewers.

## Grounding
Cite the written comment for PRESENT/GOOD, and the diff element it names when it names one. For ABSENT/GOOD, cite the context that establishes why an explanation was needed, the approval that supplied none, and the boundary: every declared review-comment source inspected. Never invent a comment, a file, a size or a clean bill you did not verify. Neither a not-yet-reviewed change nor an approval without commentary establishes a superficial review; describe what was written, never how the reviewer read.

## Defer
Whether the comments were specific and well-worded belongs to `leaves-useful-specific-review-comments`; whether the author acted on them belongs to `engaging-with-inline-review-comments`. Do not double-flag them here. Here only: does the written explanation meet its demonstrated purpose?

groups.name: Testing your changes
groups.description: When a change adds or fixes behaviour, it comes with the tests that exercise it. And it never quietly deletes, skips, or weakens a test just to make the build pass.

practices.name: Include tests with the change
practices.whyItMatters: Code without a test is a promise nobody can check, and it is one careless refactor away from quietly breaking. Adding the test alongside the logic locks in the behaviour you just built, which matters most when you are fixing a bug.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: New logic arrives with a test beside it, and a bug fix comes with a test that fails on the old code and passes on the new, proving the behaviour is what you say it is.
practices.criteria:
BEHAVIOR FOCUS: a test for the changed production behaviour arriving in the same change.

## The standard
Judge one workflow habit: when the change introduces non-trivial production behaviour, does a test for THAT behaviour arrive in the same diff? You are not hunting for missing edge cases, doing a lint sweep or re-judging the change's size; you are asking whether the new logic ships locked in by a test that could observe it. Production behaviour: a new function or endpoint, a new branch or computation, a changed validation or state transition. A covering test plausibly exercises that behaviour: it touches the same symbol, endpoint or path, or asserts the corrected result. A bug fix is strongest when it ships a test that would fail on the old code and pass on the new. Judge the PRESENCE and plausible linkage of a covering test, never its naming, readability or assertion style.

## Occasion
This is a gate. Record NOT_APPLICABLE, name the fact, and stop — never ABSENT — when there is no production surface to judge: the diff is empty, or — after setting aside generated, vendored, lock and migration files, which are neither production logic nor a test of it — it is test-only, docs-only, config-only, or a pure rename, format or type-only change with no quotable added behaviour. Layout is not behaviour: a view, control or style change with no branch, computation or state transition — a button whose action is empty, a title, a colour, a spacing — leaves nothing a test could observe, and is NOT_APPLICABLE. A test-only change does not establish the occasion.

## Sources
This is decided from the diff alone.
1. The diff (`work/change/diff.patch`) with the file list (`work/change/files.json`): classify each changed file as production or test by its path and name, using judgment about test conventions across languages. The production hunks establish the behaviour added or changed; the test hunks establish whether a test names the same symbol, endpoint or path, or asserts the corrected result. Neither establishes that any test ran.
2. The commits (`inputs/context/commits.json`): subjects that say what the change does, such as naming a fix. They establish the shape of the change; they never establish a per-commit mapping, since per-commit patches are not in your context.
3. The checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): existing tests near the changed code, for context on where a covering test would live. The absence of a repository-wide test inventory is never a reason to abstain: load-bearing, testable logic shipped into a repository with no test target at all is the lesson, and is judged, not abstained from.
If a required part of the production or test diff is truncated or unavailable, report a collection gap and record no observation.

## Judge
Test the cells in this order.
- PRESENT/GOOD (POSITIVE): the diff adds or changes real production behaviour and the same diff adds or updates a test that plausibly exercises it. Quote the production line and the test span that names the shared symbol or asserts the corrected result.
- PRESENT/BAD: no ordinary case. A test that is added but plausibly does not exercise the changed behaviour leaves that behaviour untested; that is ABSENT/GOOD, not PRESENT/BAD.
- ABSENT/GOOD (NEGATIVE): the diff adds testable production behaviour, and no test in the same diff exercises it — after scanning every test file in the diff. Never manufacture untested logic to force this cell.
- ABSENT/BAD: no ordinary case.
- UNDETERMINED only when the complete captured evidence leaves the relationship between a test and the changed behaviour genuinely ambiguous; name what would settle it. Having scanned every test file in the diff and found none that covers a quotable behaviour is ABSENT, not UNDETERMINED. A truncated diff is a collection gap, not UNDETERMINED.
One observation per review, on the single most consequential untested behaviour when there are several.

## Severity
Negatives only; never above MAJOR on this alone — non-blocking. Reason about consequence, never a line count. MINOR, the usual band: a single small, focused piece of untested logic that one test would pin. MAJOR: a defect fix shipping with nothing to lock the corrected behaviour in, or substantial or branching untested logic. Identical evidence yields identical severity.

## Grounding
Quote the exact added span relied on: the `[L<n>]` production line embodying the behaviour, and for PRESENT/GOOD the `[L<n>]` test span naming the shared symbol. ABSENT/GOOD requires the quoted untested production line AND a stated scan of the diff's test files confirming that none covers it — that scan is the boundary. Never invent a test, a file or a clean bill you did not read. Never claim a test ran or passed, and never claim a per-commit mapping you did not observe. Describe the observable delivery; never impute intent or character.

## Defer
Change size belongs to `scope-one-reviewable-change`; weakening an EXISTING suite belongs to `keeps-the-test-suite-honest`. Here only: did a test for the new behaviour ship with it?

practices.name: Keep the test suite honest

appliesWhen.absentSays: the change touches no test file and neither adds nor removes a test declaration

practices.whyItMatters: Deleting or skipping a failing test to get a passing build hides the breakage instead of fixing it, and removes the alarm that would have caught it next time. The suite only protects you while it tells the truth.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: When a test starts failing, the change fixes the underlying cause, and if the test genuinely needs to go, it is removed with a one-line note on why, never quietly skipped to get a passing build.
practices.criteria:
BEHAVIOR FOCUS: weakening or bypassing an existing test — deleted, skipped, commented out or hollowed — with no quotable reason for why the check is gone.

## The standard
Judge ONE thing: does the change keep the existing test suite honest, or does it weaken the safety net to get a green build? An honest suite keeps telling the truth: when a test starts failing, the fix addresses the underlying cause, and when a test genuinely must go, it goes with a stated, quotable reason. A dishonest move silences the alarm instead: it deletes, disables or skips, comments out, or hollows out a test or its assertions so the build passes, without explaining why the check is gone. The test is one of judgment, not keywords: can the check still fail on the regression it guarded? A faithful migration that preserves assertion strength — a rename, a move, an API upgrade, splitting one test into several, or deleting a test whose subject under test is itself removed in this same diff — is not a suppression. This is a craft habit about how the change treats its safety net, not a line-by-line lint sweep and never a merge gate.

## Occasion
This is a gate. Record NOT_APPLICABLE, name the fact, and stop — never ABSENT — when there is no existing test the change could be lowering: the diff touches no hand-written test surface (docs, config or production-only), the patch is empty, or generated or vendored files dominate. A feature with no test changes is NOT_APPLICABLE here, not an assessed observation. An existing test surface makes the practice applicable; it does not make the behaviour PRESENT.

## Sources
1. The diff (`work/change/diff.patch`, read exhaustively, with `work/change/files.json` to find the test files): every test hunk — an added skip or disable, a removed assertion or test block, commented-out executable test code, an assertion made trivially true, and any adjacent comment naming a tracker or a `reason=` / `@Disabled("…")` argument. It establishes what happened to each check and any reason written beside it. It never establishes that the suite ran.
2. The commits (`inputs/context/commits.json`) and the description (`inputs/context/description.md`): a line explaining a removal or skip. They establish a quotable reason tied to the change; they never establish a reason they do not state.
3. The checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): the unchanged surroundings of a touched test, to tell a hollowed assertion from a faithful move or split, and whether a deleted test's subject is gone. It never supplies a justification nobody wrote.
When the change touches a test surface but the patch is truncated so those hunks cannot be read, report a collection gap and record no observation; unread required evidence is not a judgment.

## Judge
The undesirable behaviour is unjustified weakening. Test the cells in this order.
- PRESENT/BAD (NEGATIVE): a real assertion becomes trivially true, an entire test block is dropped, executable test code is commented out, or a test is skipped or disabled — and no quotable reason is tied to it anywhere in the sources above. Quote the deciding line(s).
- ABSENT/BAD (POSITIVE): the change touches real test code and, after a complete bounded search of every test hunk, every check is at least as strong as before, or each removal or skip carries a quotable reason. A faithful migration is ABSENT/BAD, not a suppression. Name the test file(s) you inspected.
- PRESENT/GOOD and ABSENT/GOOD: no ordinary case. A removal with a stated reason is not a suppression; it belongs under ABSENT/BAD.
- UNDETERMINED only when a read hunk genuinely cannot settle whether a check can still fail on what it guarded; name what would settle it. A missing or truncated patch is a collection gap, not UNDETERMINED.
One observation per review. Name the single most consequential suppressed test and show the shape of the fix: restore the assertion, or add the one-line reason or tracker.

## Severity
Negatives only; never above MAJOR on test suppression alone — formative, non-blocking. MINOR, the usual band: a single unexplained skip. MAJOR: a deleted test, a hollowed assertion, or several unexplained suppressions, since more of the suite's honesty is lost.

## Grounding
Every observation quotes the deciding test line(s) from the diff: the added skip or weakened assertion, or the removed line for a deletion. For ABSENT/BAD, cite the test hunks inspected and any quoted reason; never record it for a diff that touches no test surface. Never claim to have run, compiled or executed the suite; you see only the patch. Never assert a suppression, or a justification, you cannot point to in the captured files — if you cannot quote it, it does not exist. Describe the observable behaviour of the diff; never impute intent or character, and never grade the author.

## Defer
Whether NEW tests were added for new logic belongs to `ships-tests-with-the-change`. Here only: does the change WEAKEN the existing safety net without saying why?

groups.name: Writing maintainable code
groups.description: Keep the changed code easy for the next person to read and change. Factor out duplication, keep units small and single-purpose, and leave no clutter behind, such as dead code, debug leftovers, or comments that just restate the line.

practices.name: Factor out duplication instead of copy-pasting
practices.whyItMatters: Copy-pasted logic means every future fix has to land in every copy, and the copy you forget keeps the old behaviour, which is exactly the bug. Pull the shared part into one place and you fix it once.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: By the time the same validation logic shows up a third time, you stop copying it and lift the shared concept into one named helper every caller uses, leaving a single source of truth instead of copies that drift apart. You hold off when blocks only look alike by coincidence, since forcing a shared abstraction on them is worse than the duplication.
practices.criteria:
BEHAVIOR FOCUS: nontrivial logic duplicated among the lines this pull request adds, instead of lifted into one shared place.

## The standard
Judge one closed corpus: the lines this pull request adds. A senior reviewer flags copy-paste: two or more added blocks near-identical in shape that differ only in a few literals, identifiers or types — the kind of repetition an Extract Function, a shared constant, a loop or a small lookup table would collapse into one source of truth (Fowler; Hunt & Thomas, DRY; Martin). The harm is drift: a fix has to land in every copy, and the copy that is forgotten becomes the bug. Judge the repeated unit of knowledge — the same computation or rule expressed twice — not text that merely looks alike. A coherent multi-line computation, validation, mapping or transform, or constant or config block can be a flaggable copy. A one-liner, a guard clause, a field assignment or a forced-similar idiom (equals/hashCode, builder chains, switch arms, DI or route registrations) is not. Legitimately parallel repetition is not a defect: test cases, fixtures and table-driven or parametrized bodies are meant to look alike. Duplication can live within one function: sibling `if`, `case` or branch bodies that each repeat the same multi-line computation differing only in a constant are as flaggable as cross-function copies. Use judgment on whether two blocks are a genuine copy-paste or a coincidental shared idiom.

## Occasion
This is a gate. Record NOT_APPLICABLE, name the fact, and stop — never ABSENT — only when the change offers no surface to judge: a documentation, diagram, image or configuration-only diff, or one whose added lines are entirely generated, vendored or test fixtures. A diff you read and found clean is not one of these; NOT_APPLICABLE says the work had no subject here, which is false of it.

## Sources
1. The annotated diff (`work/change/diff.patch`): the `[L<n>]` new-side spans of the added hunks. It establishes every candidate pair — a flaggable pair must sit inside these lines. It never establishes duplication against unchanged repository code, which is out of scope either way; pre-existing duplication you cannot see being introduced here is not judged.
2. The file spread (`work/change/files.json`): which paths are generated or vendored (`*.gen.*`, lockfiles, OpenAPI specs, route trees, migrations and the like) or test fixtures. It establishes the hand-authored remainder you assess. It never establishes a pair.
3. The checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): the surrounding lines of a hunk cut off mid-block. It establishes the full shape of an added block. It never establishes a pair against code the change did not add.
Per-commit patches are not in your context. If the diff was not captured completely, report a collection gap and record no observation.

## Judge
Before choosing, scan every added hand-written block for structural sameness, including branch bodies, not just whole functions. Then test the cells in this order.
- PRESENT/BAD (NEGATIVE): you can quote a near-identical added pair. Cite both occurrences and name the small delta between them.
- ABSENT/BAD (POSITIVE): you read every added hand-written hunk and no near-identical pair is in them. This is a proof over a closed corpus, not a failure to find: the copy-paste that could have arrived with this change did not.
- PRESENT/GOOD and ABSENT/GOOD: no ordinary case.
- UNDETERMINED for a candidate pair you read and genuinely cannot call; quote it and name what would settle it. Do not resolve the doubt into an assessed observation, and not into NOT_APPLICABLE either. Having read every added hunk and found no pair is ABSENT/BAD, not UNDETERMINED.
One observation per review, covering every flagged pair.

## Severity
Negatives only; never above MAJOR on this signal alone — a formative habit, not a merge gate. Calibrate to consequence and spread. MINOR, the usual band: a duplicated pure-UI or markup block with no logic — a gentle "extract a component" nudge. Duplicated logic where a divergent copy is a real bug risk weighs more. MAJOR: a copy already spreading to several places, or several distinct duplicated blocks. Identical added code yields identical severity.

## Grounding
For PRESENT/BAD quote both occurrences by path and `[L<n>]` span and name the delta; a duplication claim you cannot ground in two quoted added spans is not made. For ABSENT/BAD record `evidence.search` over the diff, cite the repeated-looking blocks you actually checked, and state in the boundary that duplication against code outside the diff is out of scope either way. Describe only the observable copy-paste habit: never assert the code is buggy, will diverge or will break, and never impute intent or character.

## Defer
Whether one block is too long or does too many things belongs to `keeps-functions-small-and-single-purpose`; never flag a single block here. Here only: repetition across added blocks.

practices.name: Keep functions small and single-purpose
practices.whyItMatters: A function that does five things is hard to name, hard to test, and hard to change without breaking a part you forgot it touched. Small, focused functions are the ones you can actually hold in your head.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: Instead of one long method that parses, validates, saves, and notifies, you have a few short functions, each doing one clearly named step you can read and test on its own.
practices.criteria:
BEHAVIOR FOCUS: a function body this change introduces or substantially rewrites tangles several substantial, separable concerns, buries its core action in nesting, or runs so long its purpose stops being scannable.

## The standard
Ask of the largest function the change introduces or substantially rewrites what a senior reviewer asks: can I hold its purpose in my head, name it in a phrase, and follow it at a glance? A focused function does one nameable job. The defect is a single body that visibly interleaves several SUBSTANTIAL, separable concerns — each a real multi-step block, genuinely interwoven, not a short serialize/encode/respond tail on a coherent pipeline — OR nests control flow so deep the core action is lost in indentation, OR runs so long its purpose stops being scannable. Not a defect: a linear pipeline of single-purpose stages (guard → build → encode → return; validate → operate → respond) is ONE purpose even when it ends by serializing a result; a thin body that delegates each step to a named helper in one call each (parse → fetch → render) is ONE orchestration, because the responsibilities live in the helpers — counting one-line delegated calls as separate concerns is the false positive to avoid. A defect: one body that parses input AND performs I/O AND applies business rules AND formats output, each written out and tangled together; a handler whose real action sits four conditionals deep. Reason like an expert about THIS code's shape. Apply no line count and no fixed concern count, and never quote a threshold to the developer. Use your judgment for cases these examples do not cover.

## Occasion
This is a gate. Record NOT_APPLICABLE, name the concrete fact, and stop — never ABSENT — only when the change adds no function body that could carry the defect: a documentation, diagram, image or configuration-only diff, a pure deletion or rename, or a diff dominated by generated or vendored files with essentially no hand-written body. That value says the work had no subject here, which is untrue of a change whose bodies you read and found focused.

## Sources
1. The annotated diff (`work/change/diff.patch`): the added and rewritten bodies with their `[L<n>]` new-side markers — a closed set you can enumerate. It establishes each body's length, nesting and the concerns written out in it. It never establishes that a function is correct, or how it is factored against collaborators you cannot see.
2. The checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): the pinned source of a body the diff truncates. Read it to finish reading that body. It never adds an unchanged caller, or a function merely renamed or called but not shown, to what you judge.
If a required body cannot be captured from either, report a collection gap and record no observation.

## Judge
Read every added or substantially rewritten body through. Then test the cells in this order.
- PRESENT/GOOD and ABSENT/GOOD: no ordinary case.
- PRESENT/BAD (NEGATIVE): a quotable added body that carries the defect. Grade the single most consequential function; never sum across files, and never escalate because many separate small functions exist — many small focused units IS the baseline.
- ABSENT/BAD (POSITIVE): the change adds bodies, you read every one, and none sprawls, nests deeply or interleaves separable concerns. The sprawl that could have arrived with this change did not. Record it with `evidence.search` over the diff, cite the largest body you read, and say in the boundary that you judged shape, not whether the functions are correct or well factored against collaborators you cannot see.
- UNDETERMINED: no ordinary case. A body you can see is judged on its visible shape; a body you cannot see is a collection gap.
One observation per review.

## Severity
Negatives only; never above MAJOR on function shape alone — a craft habit about how work is shaped, never a correctness claim, non-blocking. MINOR, the usual band: a reader can still follow the body and a single extraction would help. MAJOR: a body that clearly does it all, or whose core action is genuinely obscured by nesting.

## Grounding
Every NEGATIVE quotes the specific `[L<n>]` added span and names the responsibilities to split out or the nesting to flatten; a sprawl you cannot anchor to a quoted hunk is not emittable. Judge only function bodies visible in the diff or its pinned source; never reason about an unchanged caller, a function merely renamed or called but not shown, or code you did not read. Never claim to compile or run anything. Describe the observable shape; never impute intent or character.

## Defer
Repeated or near-identical blocks belong to `removes-duplication-instead-of-copy-pasting`; dead, commented-out or leftover scaffolding belongs to `leaves-the-code-clean-with-intent-revealing-comments`. Do not repeat another practice's complaint. Duplication or dead code alone does not establish tangled responsibilities, but neither removes the function-body occasion: assess the shape on its own evidence, with ABSENT/BAD only after the full read. Here only: does each introduced body hold one nameable job a reader can follow?

practices.name: Leave the code clean and comment the why
practices.whyItMatters: Stray debug output, blocks of commented-out code, and comments that just echo the line all add noise the next reader has to wade through. Clean code with a comment that explains the why reads like someone meant it.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: No leftover print statements or commented-out branches, and where a line looks surprising, a short comment gives the reason, such as 'retry once: the upstream API drops the first call after an idle period', rather than restating what the line does.
practices.criteria:
BEHAVIOR FOCUS: residue from the writing process on the added lines of this diff — commented-out code, leftover debug output, throwaway scaffolding — or a comment that restates the line instead of explaining it: a comment that says in words what the next line does ("convert stored strings to enum" above the conversion) is a restatement whether or not it carries a marker or an emoji.

## The standard
Judge the added lines, every one, for code that ships clean and comments that earn their place. A senior reviewer scanning them should find no residue: no commented-out code, no leftover debug or trace output, no throwaway scaffolding shipped as if final. Any comment that IS present should explain the WHY — intent, a non-obvious constraint, a unit, a caveat, a reference — rather than restate the WHAT the next line already says. Blemishes, open and illustrative: an added line that is itself plausible source behind a comment marker (a commented-out assignment, call or control statement); a bare trace print or breakpoint; a "TEMP" or "remove before merge" stub; "// increment i" above `i++`; a comment that narrates the editing session rather than the code ("// FIX 1: added episodes and year", "// changed this to use X", "// moved from Foo"); a comment with no code under it, left where code was meant to follow; a scratch or empty file added to the tree (`File.txt` holding a copied line); a template placeholder left in a manifest the change edited (`# TODO: Adjust …`). A bare `print`, `NSLog`, `console.log`, `dump` or `debugPrint` added in normal method flow — not a logging abstraction, not test code — is a debug leftover. Clean, open and illustrative: a comment that gives a reason ("retry once: upstream drops the first call after idle"); output that is the file's deliberate purpose (a CLI's own stdout, a test's expected output); a logger call through a real logging facility; a sanctioned TODO referencing a tracked issue. Code-shaped text inside a comment is not sufficient evidence of debris: documentation examples, API usage, commands and explanations may legitimately quote executable syntax. Assess the surrounding purpose, and flag an inactive implementation only when the captured context establishes it is leftover rather than an intentional example.

## Occasion
This is a gate. Record NOT_APPLICABLE, name the fact, and stop — never ABSENT — when there were no hand-written added lines to read: an empty diff, or a diff that is all generated or vendored surface (lockfiles, `*.gen.*`, specs, build output, migrations). Exclude those files first; if no hand-written added surface remains, the work had no subject here. Source code is the subject: a change that adds no source-code line — a documentation, diagram, image or configuration-only diff — has no subject here and is NOT_APPLICABLE. When the diff is truncated where the added lines live, report a collection gap and record no observation.

## Sources
1. The diff (`work/change/diff.patch`): only the lines marked ADDED (leading `+`). Residue is visible in the line itself. Removed and unchanged lines are not graded; code the author commented out and DELETED is a cleanup, never a blemish.
2. The file list (`work/change/files.json`): which files are generated or vendored and so excluded.
3. The checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): the surrounding purpose of a file — whether its output is deliberate, whether a quoted snippet is an example. It never turns an unquotable line into a blemish.
An image or an external link: nothing.

## Judge
Test the cells in this order.
- PRESENT/GOOD: no ordinary case. A comment that explains the why is not residue; it contributes to ABSENT/BAD.
- PRESENT/BAD (NEGATIVE): a quotable blemish on an added hand-written line. The bare debug calls named above, in normal method flow, are always this cell. One blemish is enough: a single restating comment, marker or leftover you can quote is this cell at its lightest severity, never rounded down to ABSENT/BAD because it is alone.
- ABSENT/GOOD: no ordinary case.
- ABSENT/BAD (POSITIVE): you read all the added hand-written lines through and none carries a blemish. This is a covered search, not a lucky miss: the residue that could have shipped did not. Record it.
- UNDETERMINED only for a single candidate line you read and genuinely cannot call — a prose comment that may be restatement or explanation, or an inactive implementation that may be leftover or an example. Quote it and do not resolve the doubt in either direction.
One observation per review, over all added lines; a scatter of leftovers is one observation.

## Severity
Negatives only; never above MAJOR on this practice alone — a proportionate, non-blocking nudge about clarity and maintenance burden. MINOR, the usual band: a lone stray comment or marker is the lightest touch; a scatter of leftovers is a modest cleanup. MAJOR only for a demonstrated, consequential source of confusion about the maintained implementation. Line count never raises severity: a long commented-out block is still one cleanliness nudge. Do not borrow error-handling or security consequences from other practices. Identical added lines yield identical severity.

## Grounding
Quote the exact `[L<n>]` span and file path for every blemish; a blemish you cannot quote is not counted. For an inactive implementation, also quote the context that shows it is leftover. Never infer that a line is dead or debug-only unless its quoted text shows it. For ABSENT/BAD, cite the search over the diff and state the boundary you did not cover: unchanged lines, files this diff does not touch, generated and vendored surface. Never claim a build or test ran. Describe what was left in the code; never impute intent or character.

## Defer
Naming, function and file size belong to `keeps-functions-small-and-single-purpose`; scope to `scope-one-reviewable-change`; duplication to `removes-duplication-instead-of-copy-pasting`; swallowed errors to `handles-errors-instead-of-swallowing-them`. Dead branches in live code and runtime defects belong to other practices. Here only: residue on added lines, and WHAT-versus-WHY comments.

practices.name: Log through the platform logger, not print
practices.whyItMatters: A `print` is a debugging note that ships: it has no level, no category and no subsystem, cannot be filtered or turned off, and on a device it goes nowhere anyone reads. The platform logger — `Logger` on Apple platforms, `Log`/Timber on Android, SLF4J on the JVM, `logging` in Python, a logger module in Node — gives every message a level and a place, so the app can be diagnosed where it runs.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: Application code reports through the platform's logger with a level and a category; `print`, `console.log`, `println` and `System.out` are left to command-line output and scripts, and a debugging print is removed before the change lands.
practices.criteria:
BEHAVIOR FOCUS: diagnostic messages the change adds go through the platform's logger with a level and a category, not through print-style output, in application code.

## The standard
Judge one thing about the application code this change adds: when it reports a diagnostic — a state, an error, a step reached — does it use the platform's logger or print-style output? Print-style output is the closed list `print(`, `debugPrint(`, `dump(`, `NSLog(` (Swift and Objective-C), `println(`/`print(` and `Log.d/v` with an ad-hoc tag (Kotlin and Java on Android), `System.out.println`/`System.err.println`/`printStackTrace()` (JVM), `console.log/debug/info/warn/error` (TypeScript and JavaScript in application code), `print(` (Python). A logger is `Logger(subsystem:category:)` / `os_log`, Android `Log` behind a shared tag or Timber, SLF4J/Log4j/`java.util.logging`, a `winston`/`pino`/framework logger, Python `logging`. Print-style output is not a lapse where it is the program's output: a command-line tool, a script, a build step, a test, a playground, a `#Preview`, or a `DEBUG`-only block (`#if DEBUG`) that removes itself from release. Judge added lines only; an existing print the change did not touch is not this change's.

## Occasion
This is a gate. Record NOT_APPLICABLE, name the fact, and stop — never ABSENT — when the change adds no diagnostic line at all: no added print-style call and no added logger call in application code. A change that adds only logger calls is an occasion with a positive answer; a change whose only prints are the program's output (a CLI, a script) has no occasion. Added diagnostic lines are the occasion.

## Sources
1. The diff (`work/change/diff.patch`) with `[L<n>]` markers and the file list (`work/change/files.json`): each added print-style or logger call, the file it lands in, and whether a `#if DEBUG` or a test target encloses it. It establishes what was added where. It never establishes what an unchanged file does.
2. The checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): whether the project already has a logger (`Logger(` definitions, a logging dependency in the manifest) and whether the file is an application target or a tool. Read it to classify the file and to say whether the print was written beside an existing logger.
3. The precompute summary (`work/precompute-out/summary.md`): the print-style and logger calls it found per file, and whether the checkout defines a logger, as leads, never conclusions.
If the diff is truncated where the calls are added, report a collection gap and record no observation.

## Judge
Enumerate the added diagnostic lines first, then test the cells in this order.
- PRESENT/GOOD (POSITIVE): every added diagnostic in application code goes through the platform logger, and any print-style call is the program's output or `DEBUG`-only. Quote a representative logger call.
- PRESENT/BAD (NEGATIVE): the logger is used, but with no level distinction or no category where the platform has them — every message at the default level under one catch-all category, or an error logged as info. Quote the call and name what it lacks.
- ABSENT/GOOD (NEGATIVE): an added print-style call reports a diagnostic in application code that ships — outside a CLI, script, test, preview or `DEBUG` block. Quote the line and the file.
- ABSENT/BAD: no ordinary case.
- UNDETERMINED: whether a file is an application target or a tool cannot be told from the diff or the checkout; name the file.
One observation per review, on the single most consequential lapse when there are several; count the rest in the summary.

## Severity
Negatives only; never above MAJOR on this alone — non-blocking. MINOR, the usual band: one or two prints in application code, or a logger without categories. MAJOR: an error path reported only by print, or a print that emits personal or secret data. Identical evidence yields identical severity.

## Grounding
Quote the `[L<n>]` call and its file; for ABSENT/GOOD say why the file is application code (its target, its `import SwiftUI`/`UIKit`, its path). Never claim a print is debugging output without the line; never claim a file is a tool without the fact that makes it one.

## Defer
An error swallowed rather than reported belongs to `handles-errors-instead-of-swallowing-them`; a secret in a message to `avoids-insecure-defaults-and-over-broad-permissions`; a leftover debugging line of another kind to `leaves-the-code-clean-with-intent-revealing-comments`. Here only: does the diagnostic go through the logger?

groups.name: Handling failure well
groups.description: Fail safely when things go wrong. Handle errors instead of swallowing them, check inputs and edge cases where data enters, and do not crash on a problem the code could recover from.

practices.name: Handle errors instead of swallowing them
practices.whyItMatters: An empty catch block turns a failure into a silent one: the code carries on as if nothing went wrong, and you find out only when something downstream breaks with no clue why. Surfacing the error saves the 2am debugging session.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: A failed call either surfaces the error to a caller who can react or recovers safely, for example by rolling back the partial work and failing closed, instead of logging and then continuing (or silently continuing) with bad or missing data.
practices.criteria:
BEHAVIOR FOCUS: added code catches or receives a failure and then silently drops it, so downstream code carries on with bad or missing data.

## The standard
When this change introduces a failure path — a call that can throw, reject or return an error — the failure should stay visible: surfaced to a caller who can react, or recorded with enough context that someone can diagnose it later. Handled: the error propagates (rethrown, wrapped with context, returned or forwarded), is recorded meaningfully (logged at a level a human would notice, a failure metric, an error state the UI reads), or is deliberately absorbed with an in-diff comment naming WHY that is safe. Swallowed: the failure is discarded — an empty or no-op catch, a caught error variable that is never used, an ignored error return, a dropped async rejection. A handler that records the failure but then lets downstream code proceed on the missing or bad value is still a swallow: the error was detected, then no corrective action taken. These are illustrations, not a closed list; recognise the same shape in any language or idiom as an experienced reviewer would. Judge this as a craft habit in how the ADDED code handles errors, not a line-by-line lint sweep.

## Occasion
This is a gate. Record NOT_APPLICABLE, name the fact, and stop — never ABSENT — only when the hand-written change adds no failure path at all. That value says this work had no subject for the practice; saying it about a change with sound error handling tells the developer there was nothing here to see. It is valid only after the enumeration below finds no added error-handling construct. Source code is the subject: a change that adds no source-code line — a documentation, diagram, image or configuration-only diff — has no subject here and is NOT_APPLICABLE.

## Sources
1. The annotated diff (`work/change/diff.patch`): the added and modified lines with their `[L<n>]` new-side markers and the visible in-diff context. It establishes every failure path the change adds — a closed set you can enumerate from the added lines — and where each error goes. It never establishes that the handling is CORRECT, that the recovery works, or that paths outside the diff behave.
2. The checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): pinned source around a hunk. Read it when where a caught error goes, or what downstream does with the missing value, sits just outside the hunk. It never establishes that anything was run, compiled or tested.
Per-commit patches are not in your context; reason from what the diff shows. If the change adds a failure path but the relevant diff is truncated or unavailable, report a collection gap and record no observation: unread required evidence establishes neither absence nor uncertainty in the work.

## Judge
Enumerate, then classify. First list every added error-handling construct — `catch`, `try?` or `try!`, `guard … else`, `if let`, an early `return` or `throw`, `Result` or `.failure`, a `??` fallback on a failable call — quoting each added line; then classify each as handled (surfaced, logged, propagated) or swallowed. Do not assume a clean surface from a glance. Then test the cells in this order.
- PRESENT/GOOD and ABSENT/GOOD: no ordinary case. A swallowed failure is never desirable, and a handled one is never a lapse.
- PRESENT/BAD (NEGATIVE): a quotable swallowed failure. Quote the exact added hunk that shows the discard; if you cannot point to the dropped error in a quoted added line, you do not have an observation.
- ABSENT/BAD (POSITIVE): the change adds failure paths, you walked every one, and each propagates, records, or is deliberately absorbed with a stated why. The swallow that could have arrived with this change did not. Record it with `evidence.search` over the diff and say in the boundary what you did NOT establish, so the strength stays a claim about what is visibly there and not a warranty.
- UNDETERMINED: a failure path you did find whose handling the diff and pinned source genuinely do not show you; name the path and what would settle it. It is what you say after the scan, never a shortcut around it.
One observation per review. Name the single most consequential swallowed failure, not an exhaustive list.

## Severity
Negatives only; never above MAJOR on this practice alone — a formative habit to grow, never a merge gate. MINOR, the usual band: a swallow on a best-effort or clearly secondary path — cleanup, teardown, optional telemetry, or a failure merely logged a touch too quietly. MAJOR: a swallow that hides a real fault from the caller or user, on a path that persists, communicates, authenticates, parses or otherwise carries consequence. Several distinct swallows, together hiding more of the change's failures, lean MAJOR. Identical constructs yield identical severity.

## Grounding
Judge only constructs this diff adds or modifies (new-side `[L<n>]` markers); never grade pre-existing context or assume code you cannot see. For PRESENT/BAD, cite the added hunk with the discard. For ABSENT/BAD, cite the constructs you enumerated and state the boundary: not that the handling is correct, not that recovery works, not that code outside the diff behaves. Never claim to run, compile or test. Never invent a construct, an exoneration, or a clean bill you did not verify. Describe the observable behaviour; never impute intent or character.

## Defer
Whether inputs and edge cases are validated belongs to `validates-inputs-and-edge-cases-at-the-boundary`; a deliberate fail-fast crash on an unrecoverable state belongs to `avoids-unsafe-panics-and-chosen-crashes`. Here only: does an added failure stay visible, or is it dropped?

practices.name: Validate inputs and edge cases at the boundary
practices.whyItMatters: Data from a user, a file, or another service will not always arrive in the shape you expected: it can be empty, null, negative, or huge. Checking it where it enters means a clear rejection instead of a confusing crash three layers deep.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: Code that reads an external value first asks what happens if it is missing or out of range and handles that on purpose, so an empty list or a malformed payload meets a clean guard instead of a null-pointer surprise.
practices.criteria:
BEHAVIOR FOCUS: added or modified code consumes a value it does not control without a visible guard for the obvious failure case.

## The standard
Judge whether added or modified code that consumes a value it does not control handles the obvious failure case on purpose, instead of assuming a happy path. A boundary value enters from outside the local logic: a request param, body or header; a parsed string or number; a value fetched by key or index from a collection; a file, stream, env or config read; the result of a third-party or RPC call. A site is in scope only when the same change also USES that value — dereferences it, indexes it, computes on it, or passes it into logic that assumes a shape. A value merely forwarded untouched, or one whose shape its type already guarantees, is not a consuming site. A guard is a null, empty or missing-key check; a try/catch or error return around a parse that can fail; a bounds check before indexing; a range, sign or finite check before arithmetic; a default for an absent config; or a framework guard visible in the same hunk, such as a Bean Validation annotation or an early return on the bad case. Judge the HABIT — is the obvious failure handled at all — not an exhaustive lint of every conceivable input.

## Occasion
This is a gate. Record NOT_APPLICABLE, name the fact, and stop — never ABSENT — when the change consumes no boundary value at all: an empty diff, a diff with no consuming site, or only generated or vendored files remaining. Source code is the subject: a change that adds no source-code line — a documentation, diagram, image or configuration-only diff — has no subject here and is NOT_APPLICABLE. Never invent an input surface.

## Sources
1. The annotated diff (`work/change/diff.patch`): the added and modified lines with their `[L<n>]` new-side markers and the visible in-diff context. It establishes every consuming site the change introduces — a closed set you can enumerate from the added lines — and whether each meets a guard in the same hunk or its immediate visible context. It never establishes that the guards are sufficient, that they cover every case, or that callers beyond the diff are safe.
2. The checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): pinned source around a hunk. Read it when the guard that would decide a site could plausibly sit just above a truncated hunk. It establishes whether such a guard exists. It never establishes that anything was run, compiled or tested.
Per-commit patches are not in your context. If the context a deciding site needs remains unavailable after reading the pinned source, report a collection gap and record no observation, rather than asserting absence or inapplicability.

## Judge
Before choosing, actually scan the changed lines for an uncontrolled value that gets consumed; then test the cells in this order.
- PRESENT/BAD (NEGATIVE): a site reads an uncontrolled value and then dereferences, indexes or computes on it with no guard in the same hunk or its immediate visible context, so a malformed or absent input breaks the new path. Quote the exact `[L<n>]` span of each unguarded site and name the missing guard ("null check before .name", "catch around the parse").
- ABSENT/BAD (POSITIVE): you walked every consuming site the change introduces and each handles its obvious bad case. The unguarded boundary that could have arrived with this change did not; the claim is about the coverage of your reading, nothing about correctness.
- PRESENT/GOOD and ABSENT/GOOD: no ordinary case. An unguarded consuming site is never desirable here, and a guarded one is never a lapse.
- UNDETERMINED for a consuming site you can see whose guard the visible context does not settle; name the site and what would settle it. Having walked every site and found each guarded is ABSENT/BAD, not UNDETERMINED. Missing required context is a collection gap, not an observation.
One observation per review, covering every unguarded site found.

## Severity
Negatives only; never above MAJOR on this practice alone — a habit to grow, not a merge gate. Calibrate to the demonstrated consequence at the boundary and explain the observable risk. MINOR, the usual band: an omission on a low-impact operation. MAJOR: a missing check on a consequential operation, which one site can warrant; several harmless omissions do not escalate on their own. Identical hunks yield identical severity.

## Grounding
Judge only the added and modified lines and their visible in-diff context, plus pinned source you actually read. For PRESENT/BAD, cite the `[L<n>]` span of each unguarded site. For ABSENT/BAD, record `evidence.search` over the diff and state in the boundary what you did NOT establish: that the guards are sufficient, that they cover every case, that callers beyond the diff are safe. Never assert a missing guard you cannot point to; never claim to run, compile or test anything; never invent a clean bill of health. Describe the observable code behaviour, never intent or character.

## Defer
Whether untrusted input reaches a dangerous sink unescaped belongs to `validates-and-escapes-untrusted-input`. The quality of error handling once input is guarded belongs to `handles-errors-instead-of-swallowing-them`; a catch that merely prevents the crash satisfies the guard here regardless of its body. Do not repeat another practice's complaint, and do not let another kind of defect stand in for this one: an applicable consuming site still needs its own assessment, and another defect establishes neither a missing guard nor no occasion.

practices.name: Avoid crashing on recoverable problems
practices.whyItMatters: Reaching for a force-unwrap or a panic on a condition that can actually happen turns an ordinary hiccup into a hard crash for your users. A problem the code can recover from deserves a graceful path, not a deliberate stop.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: Where a value might legitimately be absent, the code unwraps it safely and falls back to a default or a clear error, instead of force-unwrapping and bringing the whole thing down.
practices.criteria:
BEHAVIOR FOCUS: added code deliberately crashes on a recoverable runtime condition — a force-unwrap, a force-cast or an abort on a value that rides an ordinary runtime path.

## The standard
Code degrades gracefully on ordinary, recoverable runtime failure rather than deliberately aborting. A chosen crash is an ADDED construct that hard-stops the process on a condition an ordinary program could survive: force-unwrapping or force-casting a value that can legitimately be absent, or a deliberate abort, panic, exit or fatal error, when that value rides an ordinary runtime path — parsed input, network, database, disk or environment, a decoded payload, a fallible API's result. Judge two things: was the failure recoverable, and did the change crash on it anyway. Bad, for example: force-unwrapping a value decoded from JSON or fetched from a server; panicking on a fallible parse; a fatal abort on a path that could return an error instead. Not a chosen crash, for example: a genuine programmer invariant that cannot fail unless surrounding code is already broken (an unreachable enum default, a precondition on a value just proven non-nil); a fail-fast at a CLI or startup entry point where aborting IS the contract; an operation total by language contract for its operand type (Swift `String.data(using: .utf8)` for a Unicode-capable encoding, indexing a literal-bounded array); force-unwrapping an author-controlled literal or constant. Reason about totality and provenance across languages and stacks as an experienced reviewer would, not about the spelling of the construct and not from a keyword list. A `!` alone is not the defect; whether the operation can ACTUALLY return nil or throw on some real input is. Crash-shaped constructs to enumerate: a force unwrap `x!`, a force cast `as!`, `try!`, `fatalError`, `precondition`, `assert`, `exit`, `abort`, an unchecked array subscript `a[i]` or `.first!`, integer conversion or arithmetic that traps. An array subscript on a runtime-sourced collection is one of them; on a literal-bounded or author-controlled collection it is total. Read every `[` before recording that no construct was added.

## Occasion
This is a gate, decided by a closed list. A crash-shaped construct is one of: a force unwrap (`x!`), `try!`, a force cast (`as!`), `fatalError`, `precondition`/`preconditionFailure`, `assert`/`assertionFailure`, `exit`/`abort`, an array or dictionary subscript whose index or key is not a literal (`items[i]`, `dict[key]!`, `.first!`), a lossy numeric conversion of a runtime value (`Int(someDouble)`, `UInt(x)`), and an integer division or modulo by a non-literal — or their equivalents in another language (`panic`, `unwrap()`, `process.exit`, a non-null assertion). Record NOT_APPLICABLE, name the fact, and stop — never ABSENT — only when the added source lines contain none of these: a docs-, config- or data-only diff, or a generated- or vendored-only diff, carries no surface. A construct the change guards on the same path — behind `guard let`, `if let`, `??`, `try?`, do/catch, a bounds check, a `Result` — is still a construct that is PRESENT and handled: the occasion holds and the cell is judged below, never NOT_APPLICABLE. The precompute lists the constructs it could find; the scan below is over the added lines themselves.

## Sources
1. The annotated diff (`work/change/diff.patch`): the added and modified lines with their `[L<n>]` new-side markers. It establishes the closed set of crash-shaped constructs the change adds and, where the hunk shows it, where each crashed-on value came from. It never establishes anything about removed lines, unchanged code or code outside the diff, and it never establishes that anything compiled or ran.
2. The checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): pinned source around a hunk. Read it only to trace the origin of a value the hunk crashes on but does not source. It never adds a construct to judge — only constructs the diff adds are judged — and it never establishes that unchanged code cannot crash.
If the diff is truncated or unavailable for a change that adds a crash-shaped construct, report a collection gap and record no observation.

## Judge
Scan first, then classify. Enumerate every crash-shaped construct in the added lines and trace where each crashed-on value came from; look before you leap. Then test the cells in this order.
- PRESENT/GOOD and ABSENT/GOOD: no ordinary case.
- PRESENT/BAD (NEGATIVE): a quotable added construct that crashes on a value with a named runtime source, where the operation can actually return nil or throw on a real input. Quote the deciding added line and name the source.
- ABSENT/BAD (POSITIVE): the change adds crash-shaped constructs from the closed list, you read every one, and each is guarded on its path, sits on a genuine programmer invariant, a total operation, an author-controlled constant or an entry-point contract rather than an ordinary runtime path. The chosen crash that could have arrived with this change did not. Record it with `evidence.search` over the diff and say in the boundary that you judged the constructs the diff adds, not whether unchanged code can still crash. A total conversion read as safe is one of the constructs this pass reports having read, never a negative.
- UNDETERMINED: a construct you can see whose value provenance the diff and pinned source do not settle — you see the diff, not the whole program. Name the construct and the fact that would settle it. It is earned by the trace running out of evidence, never by skipping the trace, and it is never filed under NOT_APPLICABLE, which claims no such construct was here. A crash you cannot tie to a runtime-sourced value is not groundable as a negative.
One observation per review. When NEGATIVE, name the single most consequential chosen crash and show the shape of the graceful alternative for that line — a guard or `if let`, try-with-fallback, return-an-error, `Result`; do not rewrite the whole change.

## Severity
Negatives only; never above MAJOR on this practice alone — a defensive-programming habit to grow, not a merge gate. MINOR, the usual band, and the ceiling whenever you cannot demonstrate a concrete input on which the unwrapped operation yields nil or throws. MAJOR: a clearly recoverable failure on a clearly ordinary runtime source — decoded or fetched input crashed on outright. Genuine uncertainty about recoverability lowers the band. Identical hunks yield identical severity.

## Grounding
Cite the exact added-line span and the value's origin from observable diff evidence. Judge only added or modified lines with new-side `[L<n>]` markers; never reason about removed lines or code outside the diff, and never claim to compile or run it. Never invent a file, a line, a value source or a clean bill you did not verify. For ABSENT/BAD, cite the constructs you enumerated and state the boundary you did not cross. Describe the observable behaviour of the code; never impute intent or character.

## Defer
Empty or swallowed catches and logged-and-continued errors belong to `handles-errors-instead-of-swallowing-them`; missing input validation belongs to `validates-inputs-and-edge-cases-at-the-boundary`. Here only: does an added construct deliberately crash on a recoverable runtime condition?

groups.name: Making changes secure by default
groups.description: Make each change secure by default. Validate and escape untrusted input before it reaches a dangerous sink, avoid insecure defaults and over-broad permissions, and change dependencies deliberately.

practices.name: Neutralize untrusted input before a dangerous sink

appliesWhen.absentSays: the added lines build no query, command, path, URL or markup from a value

practices.whyItMatters: Gluing raw user input straight into a query, a shell command, or a page is how injection bugs are born, the kind that leak a database or run an attacker's code. Parameterizing or escaping it first is what keeps that door shut.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: User-supplied values reach the database through bound parameters and the page through proper escaping, never concatenated into a SQL string or dropped into HTML as-is.
practices.criteria:
BEHAVIOR FOCUS: a value from outside the trust boundary that added code carries into a dangerous sink without neutralizing it first.

## The standard
When code added in this diff carries a value from outside the trust boundary into an operation where that value can change the operation's meaning, the value must be neutralized first — parameterized, escaped for the exact sink context, or validated against an allow-list or strict type — rather than concatenated or interpolated raw. Reason as an experienced security reviewer. A source is any externally-controlled value: a request param, header or body, an uploaded filename, a CLI arg, a remote service's response. A dangerous sink is any place where raw text changes execution: a built query string, a shell command, an HTML or template render, a filesystem path, a redirect target, a deserializer or eval, or a constructed URL whose path or query interpolates the value — `"/auth/\(token)"` then `URL(string: base + path)`, where the fix is percent-encoding via the platform URL builder, not raw interpolation. These lists are illustrative; recognize the shape in any language or stack, including sinks not named here. Neutralized looks like: bound as a parameter, run through a context-correct encoder, passed as an args array to exec, confined under a canonicalized base path, rendered through auto-escaping left on. Not neutralized looks like: string-concatenated or interpolated straight into the sink with nothing in the quoted hunk neutralizing it.

## Occasion
This is a gate. Record NOT_APPLICABLE, name the fact, and stop — never ABSENT — only when no untrusted value reaches a dangerous sink in the added lines at all. A dangerous sink is a query, command, path, URL or markup built from the value as text. A typed or parameterized API — an ORM or SwiftData store, a prepared statement, a URL built from components, a text control that does not interpret markup — is not one: a value that only ever reaches such APIs is no flow here, and a change with only those is NOT_APPLICABLE, not ABSENT/BAD. Scan the added lines for a source-to-sink flow before abstaining; do not skip the scan because the diff looks routine. When the diff contains a sink-shaped line — raw input concatenated into a query, command, path or markup — and you still abstain, name the single most suspicious line by file:line and state why it is safe.

## Sources
1. The annotated diff (`work/change/diff.patch`): the added and modified `[L<n>]` lines and their immediate in-diff context. It establishes the closed set of source-to-sink flows this change introduces and whether each is neutralized in those same lines. It never establishes that code outside the diff sanitizes — or fails to sanitize — the value; never assume either.
2. The file spread (`work/change/files.json`) and the checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): which paths are generated or vendored. They establish the hand-written remainder you assess. They never establish neutralization for a flow the added lines do not show.
Trace only what you can see. If the diff was not captured completely, report a collection gap and record no observation.

## Judge
Test the cells in this order.
- PRESENT/BAD (NEGATIVE): a quotable added hunk where a source reaches a sink unneutralized. Name the source and the sink end-to-end.
- ABSENT/BAD (POSITIVE): the added lines do carry untrusted input toward a sink, and you traced every introduced flow and each is neutralized before its sink. The injection that could have arrived with this change did not. This is a covered reading of the diff, never a security clearance.
- PRESENT/GOOD and ABSENT/GOOD: no ordinary case.
- UNDETERMINED for a flow you can see whose neutralization the added lines do not settle; name the flow and what would settle it. UNDETERMINED comes after the scan, never instead of it. No flow visible at all is NOT_APPLICABLE, not UNDETERMINED.
One observation per review, covering every unneutralized flow found; show the shape of the fix for the single most consequential one.

## Severity
Negatives only; never above MAJOR on this practice alone — a security habit to grow, not a merge gate. MINOR, the usual band: a render, redirect or header-style flow; the lightest nudge when the value is partly constrained but the context-correct escape is still missing. MAJOR: raw input that changes code or data execution — injection, traversal, RCE shapes. Identical hunks land at the same level.

## Grounding
For PRESENT/BAD quote the exact added `[L<n>]` hunk where the source reaches the sink and name both ends; if you cannot point to both on quoted added lines, it is not assertable. For ABSENT/BAD record `evidence.search` over the diff and state in the boundary what you did NOT establish: that the escaping is correct for every input, that sinks reached from unchanged code are safe, that the application has no other exposure. Never claim the code runs, compiles, is exploitable, or that a payload triggers; assert only the visible habit. Never invent a file, a line or a clean bill. Describe the observable behaviour — raw input flowing into a sink — never intent or character.

## Defer
A generic missing bounds, null or format check with no dangerous sink belongs to `validates-inputs-and-edge-cases-at-the-boundary`; a committed secret belongs to `avoids-insecure-defaults-and-over-broad-permissions`. Defer to the sibling rather than double-flag. Here only: a taint-to-sink injection flow.

practices.name: Avoid insecure defaults and over-broad permissions

appliesWhen.absentSays: the added lines touch no transport, origin, permission, file-mode, auth, credential, logging or debug setting

practices.whyItMatters: A default or permission that ships wider than it needs sits quietly until someone exploits it, and this kind of misconfiguration is among the most common security gaps there is. Starting locked down means you only open what you can justify.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: A new endpoint or credential grants exactly the access it needs and no more, with scoped permissions and a specific allowed origin from an allowlist, not an origin reflected back from the request or a blanket wildcard, instead of a permissive default dropped in to make things work.
practices.criteria:
BEHAVIOR FOCUS: an added line ships an insecure default or widens an access or exposure boundary without an evidenced justification.

## The standard
Code should start locked down and open only what it can justify. Hunt the added lines for a change that ships an insecure default or widens an access or exposure boundary without an adequate, evidenced justification. Judge the SETTING the change adopts, not the data flowing through it, and never as a blanket vulnerability scan. A sink-hunt, not a posture rating: do not read the top-level intent, conclude "looks secure" and stop. Walk these sink classes over the added lines; they are classes to think in, not a closed value list, so recognise the same shape on any stack:
1. transport, certificate or host verification toggled off;
2. cross-origin, CORS or permission scope widened — a credentialed response that reflects the request Origin back without an allowlist, or a bare wildcard on an authenticated route;
3. a file, resource or object mode made world-readable or world-writable, or otherwise over-broad;
4. an existing auth or authz guard removed or loosened;
5. secret or credential exposure — trace dataflow here, do not pattern-match names: inspect EVERY logging, string-interpolation, persistence and URL-building call in the added lines and ask what the interpolated value can hold at runtime. A print or log of a request or response body, a header, or any value derived from an auth, login, token or credential exchange is a leak even when the variable is not named "token" (a response body that carries the issued token, for example);
6. a debug, verbose-error or permissive default shipped to a non-test surface.
Spotting one tightened setting (an ATS flag removed, say) does not discharge the hunt; finish every class. A candidate sink class establishes what to inspect, not an automatic defect.
