Clean: a setting correctly scoped, least-privilege or tightened; a widening whose quoted purpose and captured constraints establish an appropriate exception. A reason, or a test, sample or local filename, does not by itself make exposure safe: verify the actual boundary, the permitted audience and the applicable safeguards from the captured evidence. The absence of an insecure setting is a clean baseline, not a hardening act.

## Occasion
This is a gate. Record NOT_APPLICABLE, name the fact, and stop — never ABSENT — when the added lines touch no setting of any sink class at all: a pure UI, layout, documentation, model or test change with no transport, origin, permission, file-mode, auth, credential, logging or debug setting in it. That value claims the work had no subject here; ABSENT/BAD is for a change that touches such a setting and does so securely. An added logging, print or persistence call that interpolates any runtime value touches class 5 (credential exposure) and is a setting of that class: a change with one is never NOT_APPLICABLE; walk the class and record what the value can hold. Never abstain on a shallow pass. When the diff contains a config-shaped line (a keychain, permission, CORS or allow-all setting, a token in a URL or path), NOT_APPLICABLE must name the single most suspicious line by file and `[L<n>]` and state why it is safe. Assess only the hand-written remainder of a generated- or vendored-dominated diff.

## Sources
1. The annotated diff (`work/change/diff.patch`): the added lines with their `[L<n>]` markers, and any removed or weakened guard line. It establishes every candidate sink the change introduces — a closed corpus you can walk — and any in-diff comment or profile guard that justifies a widening. It never establishes that the existing configuration is sound, that unchanged settings are safe, or that the system has no other exposure.
2. The checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): pinned source around a hunk. Read it when the boundary, audience or safeguard that would decide a candidate line sits outside the hunk (a dev profile, a network policy, the route's auth wrapper). It establishes the constraints an exception rests on. It never establishes that anything was run, compiled or tested.
3. Precompute hints (`work/precompute-out/summary.md`), when present: leads to inspect, never evidence. An absent or empty candidate list is never grounds for NOT_APPLICABLE while a candidate line is visible.
Never infer a setting from a filename or a count you cannot quote.

## Judge
Walk every sink class first; then test the cells in this order.
- PRESENT/GOOD and ABSENT/GOOD: no ordinary case. An insecure default is never desirable, and a locked-down setting is never a lapse.
- PRESENT/BAD (NEGATIVE): a concrete added setting whose exposure is inappropriate under the evidenced constraints. Quote the added `[L<n>]` line, or the removed or weakened guard line, and name the file.
- ABSENT/BAD (POSITIVE): the added lines touch at least one setting of a sink class, you walked every class over them, and none was touched insecurely. A COVERED search over a closed corpus, not an impression: an unwalked class makes it a false claim rather than an incomplete one. Record it with `evidence.search` over the diff, name the sink classes you walked in `lookedFor`, and state in the boundary what you did NOT establish. A report on a search, never a security clearance.
- UNDETERMINED: a candidate sink line is visible but the fact that would settle it is not; name the line and what would settle it. Never file an unreadable sink under NOT_APPLICABLE.
Before either abstention, state in the rationale what you found for the credential-exposure class (5). One observation per review; with several issues, name the single most consequential and mention the rest in a clause.

## Severity
Negatives only; never above MAJOR on this practice alone — a security-hygiene habit to grow, not a merge gate. MINOR, the usual band: a lower-blast-radius misconfiguration. MAJOR: a meaningfully widened blast radius — disabled verification, credentialed origin-reflection or wildcard exposure, a removed or loosened auth guard, or exposed credential material — when the captured boundaries establish consequential exposure. A merely asserted internal or dev rationale does not reduce that consequence; an evidenced appropriate exception is not a negative to grade at all. Do not sum severities.

## Grounding
Every observation quotes the exact added `[L<n>]` line, or the removed or weakened guard line, and names the file. A claim that a setting was added, removed, hardened or mitigated must quote the changed line that does it. An appropriate exception must quote both the justification and the constraints that support it, and it does not remove an otherwise present review occasion. Never claim to run, compile or test; never invent a file, a line or a clean bill of health. Point forward to the safer default: verification on; the exact origin named instead of `*`; the toggle behind a dev profile; the least-privilege mode; the guard restored or its reason recorded. Talk about the configuration, never the contributor.

## Defer
Whether untrusted input is escaped or validated belongs to `validates-and-escapes-untrusted-input`. This practice is the terminal owner of exposed credential material — a hardcoded secret, token, API key or password on a non-test path, or in a URL or log: report it here at MAJOR, never defer it and never NOT_APPLICABLE it.

practices.name: Change dependencies deliberately

appliesWhen.absentSays: the change touches no dependency manifest or lockfile

practices.whyItMatters: Every dependency you add is code you now trust and have to keep patched, and many malicious packages slip in disguised as a real name a letter or two off. A one-line note on why a package is there, plus a lockfile that moves with the manifest, lets a reviewer sanity-check the addition and keeps the build reproducible.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: A new package arrives with a sentence on what it is for, and the lockfile is updated in the same change as the manifest so the build still resolves the same way.
practices.criteria:
BEHAVIOR FOCUS: a dependency edit whose manifest and lockfile stay coherent under the ecosystem's resolution rules, with a recorded reason for a notable addition or bump.

## The standard
Judge whether this pull request edits its dependencies deliberately. Two things hold together: the manifest and any lockfile remain consistent with the ecosystem's resolution rules and the repository's documented policy, and a notable new dependency or version bump carries a one-line reason a reviewer can read — in the manifest context, the title or body, or a commit subject. This is a supply-chain workflow habit about how a dependency edit is justified and kept coherent. It is never a claim about the dependency's own correctness, its CVEs, or whether the chosen version is the "right" one. The principle — coherence plus a traceable reason for notable changes — decides, not a fixed file list: reason as an experienced reviewer about manifests, lockfiles and ecosystems not named here. A patch or minor bump and a transitive-only delta need no prose. A large generated lockfile delta is normal evidence of coherence, not a problem. A supported version range is not itself a defect: libraries may deliberately declare compatible ranges, and a manifest edit need not change an already compatible locked resolution.

## Occasion
This is a gate. Record NOT_APPLICABLE, name the fact, and stop — never ABSENT — when the change touches no dependency manifest or lockfile (in any ecosystem: package, build, module, container, workflow pin), or when the deciding hunk is not quotable.

## Sources
1. The annotated diff (`work/change/diff.patch`) and the file spread (`work/change/files.json`): the manifest hunks and the matching or missing lockfile spans. They establish what changed on the dependency surface and whether manifest and lockfile move together. They never establish the dependency's quality or the correctness of the chosen version.
2. The title (`inputs/context/metadata.json`) and the whole description (`inputs/context/description.md`): where an explaining sentence for a notable add or bump may live. An image: its caption and the sentence around it. An external link: nothing.
3. The commit subjects and bodies (`inputs/context/commits.json`): a subject can carry the reason. Per-commit patches are not in your context; judge from subjects, the file spread and the quoted hunks.
4. The checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): the repository's documented policy — a stated reproducibility requirement, a lockfile rule, a pinning convention. It establishes the policy a constraint removal is measured against. It never establishes a defect on its own.
Before calling a notable change unexplained you must have read the diff, the title, the body and the commit subjects. If one of those surfaces was not materialized for you, your search is incomplete: report a collection gap and record no observation.

## Judge
Test the cells in this order.
- PRESENT/GOOD (POSITIVE): the dependency edit is coherent and, where a notable add or bump needs one, explained. A new direct runtime dependency arrives with a sentence on what it is for and any required resolution update is present; a routine transitive resolution refresh is internally consistent.
- PRESENT/BAD (NEGATIVE): the captured manifest and lockfile contradict one another under the ecosystem's resolution rules, with the deciding entries quoted; or a resolution constraint is removed in conflict with an evidenced repository reproducibility requirement. Establish the ecosystem's semantics and the captured policy before reporting inconsistency.
- ABSENT/GOOD (NEGATIVE): a notable add or bump is coherent but lands as an unexplained pin — no quotable why in the manifest context, the title, the body or the commit subjects. Name the pin and the surfaces you read.
- ABSENT/BAD: no ordinary case.
- UNDETERMINED when the deciding policy or resolution context remains ambiguous after reading the sources; name the question. An unchanged or absent lockfile alone proves neither coherence nor a defect. A required source that was not captured is a collection gap, not an observation.
One observation per review. Identical hunks yield identical assessments.

## Severity
Negatives only; never above MAJOR on dependency deliberateness alone — a non-blocking habit to grow, not a merge gate. Scale to how much reproducibility is actually at risk. MINOR, the usual band: an unexplained but coherent notable pin — a formative nudge. MAJOR: manifest and lockfile out of step on something that ships — the most serious case here.

## Grounding
Quote the manifest line, the matching or missing lockfile span, and the explaining sentence or commit subject verbatim. For ABSENT/GOOD the citations show the pin and the boundary searched: the diff, the title, the body, the commit subjects. Never invent a file, a reason, a CVE, or a clean bill you did not verify. Never claim a build resolved or ran. Describe the observable edit; never impute intent or character.

## Defer
Artifact hygiene about generated churn belongs to `excludes-generated-and-build-artifacts`; review size belongs to `scope-one-reviewable-change`. Here only: is the dependency edit coherent, and is a notable change explained?

groups.name: Recording decisions and documenting changes
groups.description: Capture the why. Record the evidenceRationale behind significant design decisions, and document changes to public APIs and shared behaviour, so the people who maintain or build on the code later can understand it.

practices.name: Record significant decisions and the evidenceRationale
practices.whyItMatters: When you pick one design over another, the evidenceRationale is the first thing to fade. A maintainer who cannot find why you chose it will either undo a good decision or be too afraid to touch it, and both cost the team later.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: A meaningful design choice arrives with its evidenceRationale written down, in the description or a short architecture decision record (ADR), such as 'chose an event queue over direct calls so a slow consumer cannot block checkout', not just the code that does it.
practices.criteria:
BEHAVIOR FOCUS: a written rationale for the architecturally significant decision this change makes, recorded where a future maintainer can find it.

## The standard
Judge one thing: when this pull request makes an architecturally SIGNIFICANT decision, is the WHY recorded — a constraint, a trade-off, or an alternative rejected — rather than left to be reverse-engineered from the code? A recorded WHY may be one clause: naming the need the decision serves ("to show a confirmation banner after checkout", "a stored type for the attachments a user uploads", "so a customer can save a draft") or the constraint that forced it ("the platform only ships the SDK as a package") records it; the lapse is silence about the decision, not brevity, and a clause quoted for the description's WHY may be the same clause. Never demand the alternatives considered or the reason this framework over another: the need served is the rationale a maintainer needs. Significance is a closed list, so two readers find the same subject: a new third-party dependency or framework added by hand to a manifest; a change to a PERSISTED model or schema (a stored type, a migration, a field that is saved); a public-contract or wire-API change (an endpoint, a message format, an exported library API); a new cross-cutting mechanism the rest of the app plugs into (a shared aspect, interceptor or event bus, a base class many types extend); an auth or security mechanism; the removal of a feature and its stored data. Not on the list, and never significant on their own: a call to an external web service (an HTTP API consumed at runtime is a mechanism used, not a dependency added to a manifest); a view or view model and how screens navigate; an in-memory draft, cache or value type; adopting the stack the project already uses (its persistence framework, UI framework or map kit); a helper, extension or calculation; a rename. When the only candidate is one of these, stage 1 fails and the cell is NOT_APPLICABLE. Work in two stages, in order. (1) Decide whether the hand-written diff contains a significant decision. (2) Only if it does, check whether its rationale is recorded in the title, the description, a commit subject, or a linked ADR or design document. A reason given in a review comment or the conversation is not recorded where a maintainer finds it and does not count; the discussion is where a rationale was asked for, not where it lives. A rationale clause counts in prose or inside a bullet or checklist item — "chose X because Y", "an event queue so a slow consumer can't block checkout", "to avoid Z" — so scan the whole body. Restating WHAT changed, an empty or template body, or a bare "added dependency X" does not record a why.

## Occasion
This is a gate. Record NOT_APPLICABLE, name the fact, and stop — never ABSENT — when the change is routine and carries no architectural decision: tests, formatting, docs, a rename without a contract change, a version bump of an already-present dependency, a tuned constant or threshold on an internal symbol, or an empty diff. Significance comes from hand-written hunks only: a dependency echoed solely in a lockfile with no manifest edit is not an independent decision; a hand-authored migration changeset is. When the diff is unreadable, the change still made whatever decisions it made and you could not read them: report a collection gap and record no observation, never a routine or a significant verdict.

## Sources
1. The diff (`work/change/diff.patch`, with `work/change/files.json`): the added lines that establish significance, and any ADR or design document added in the same change. It establishes what was decided; it never supplies the why by itself.
2. The title (`inputs/context/metadata.json`) and the WHOLE description (`inputs/context/description.md`): every paragraph, bullet and checklist item. They establish a recorded rationale you can quote. An image: its caption and the sentence around it. An external link: nothing.
3. The commit subjects and bodies (`inputs/context/commits.json`): a rationale stated there counts. Per-commit patches are not in your context; never claim a per-commit file mapping.
4. A linked ADR or design document materialised as a `.md` file under `inputs/context/outline/`: read it before concluding the why is absent. Cite its file path together with the quoted or closely paraphrased rationale sentence; a bare URL is not evidence the why was recorded. When the change names a specific document that was not materialised, the rationale may be there: report a collection gap and record no observation, never a claim against prose you were not shown.
5. The checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): what a changed symbol or mechanism means, and an in-repository ADR the change points to. It never supplies a rationale the change did not write.

## Judge
Test the cells in this order.
- PRESENT/GOOD (POSITIVE): a significant decision is present and its rationale is written down in one of the sources above, so the intent survives without re-reading the code.
- PRESENT/BAD: no ordinary case. Text that only restates what changed is not a rationale; treat it as ABSENT.
- ABSENT/GOOD (NEGATIVE): a significant decision ships with no recorded why anywhere in the description, the commit subjects, or a linked ADR or materialised document. Name the decision.
- ABSENT/BAD: no ordinary case.
- UNDETERMINED: no ordinary case. Having searched every source and found no why is ABSENT, not UNDETERMINED; a document you were not shown is a collection gap.
One observation per review. When several significant decisions co-occur, judge them together in one observation.

## Severity
Negatives only; never above MAJOR on rationale alone — non-blocking. MINOR, the usual band: a single contained unexplained decision — one new dependency, one isolated column, one app-internal class. MAJOR: the genuinely consequential — an unexplained auth or security mechanism, a persistence, public-API or wire-contract change, a real cross-cutting mechanism others build on, or several significant decisions co-occurring unexplained. When unsure, prefer the lower severity.

## Grounding
Quote the exact added `[L<n>]` line(s) that establish significance in every cell. For PRESENT/GOOD, also quote the verbatim rationale sentence, commit subject or document reference and where it lives. For ABSENT/GOOD, the citations show the search: the description, the commit subjects, and the referenced rationale sources or their absence. Never invent a rationale, never infer the why from the code itself, and never assert that the dependency, schema or endpoint is wrong — judge only whether the why is recorded. Never claim a build or test ran. Describe the observable record; never impute intent or character.

## Defer
The overall adequacy of the description — a clear title and a why for the change as a whole — belongs to `describe-what-and-why`; here judge only whether THAT significant decision's rationale is recorded, so the two never double-flag. Whether a public-surface change is documented for its consumers belongs to `documents-public-api-and-behaviour-changes`; whether a linked wiki document now contradicts the code belongs to `change-keeps-linked-docs-consistent`.

practices.name: Document public API and behaviour changes
practices.whyItMatters: People outside your code depend on what you export. Change a public function or endpoint without a note and they find out at runtime, in their own project, with no warning, and they trust your library a little less each time.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: A renamed parameter or a changed response shape lands with its reference docs and a changelog line updated in the same change, so the people building on your API hear about it from you, not from a broken build.
practices.criteria:
BEHAVIOR FOCUS: consumer-facing documentation of the changed public surface — a downstream caller hears what moved from the change itself.

## The standard
Judge one habit: when the change alters a PUBLIC or SHARED surface — something a SEPARATE consumer depends on and compiles or integrates against — does the change carry, in the same diff or in the description, documentation that tells consumers what moved? Public surfaces: a library's or framework's exported symbols, a published package's API, a documented HTTP or RPC contract, a persisted or wire schema, an error or response shape callers branch on, a config default a consumer sets. Good: the renamed parameter, new endpoint, changed response field or breaking removal lands with its doc-comment, a changelog line, or a description sentence naming the consumer-facing effect. Bad: a real exported-surface change ships with nothing a consumer could read to adapt. A generated API specification or reference documents a contract when its authoritative source and meaning are captured: judge the contract and the information a consumer receives, not whether the text was handwritten. Irrelevant generated output is not documentation, and generated churn alone never establishes an authored contract decision.

## Occasion
This is a gate. Establish the separate consumer from the captured contract or usage, never from package type alone: an application can expose HTTP endpoints, configuration or wire formats to other consumers without publishing a library. Record NOT_APPLICABLE, name the fact, and stop — never ABSENT — when the changed symbols are internal types, private signatures, local refactors or app-only fields with no separate consumer, or when no public-surface change is observable in the diff and description at all. Decide whether a changed symbol is actually exported and consumer-facing as an experienced reviewer would, not by keyword; a plainly internal symbol is NOT_APPLICABLE.

## Sources
1. The diff (`work/change/diff.patch`, with `work/change/files.json`): the surface change itself, and any documentation shipped beside it — a doc-comment on or above the surface, a changelog or docs addition, an updated reference. It establishes what changed and what documentation arrived with it. It never establishes a consumer by itself.
2. The description (`inputs/context/description.md`): a sentence naming the consumer-facing effect. It establishes documentation a consumer would read on the change; it never establishes a surface change the diff does not show.
3. The checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): the contract and its usage — who depends on the surface, and the existing reference docs the diff leaves untouched. It establishes whether a separate consumer exists and where the documentation would live. It never supplies the note the change failed to write.
4. A linked wiki document the change references, when it was materialised as a `.md` file under `inputs/context/outline/`: its body may hold the documentation consumers need. Cite its file path together with the quoted or closely paraphrased sentence relied on; a bare URL is not evidence that the document says it. When the change points at a specific document that was not materialised for you, the documentation may live there: report a collection gap and record no observation, never an undocumented surface.
An image: its caption and the sentence around it. An external link: nothing.

## Judge
Test the cells in this order.
- PRESENT/GOOD (POSITIVE): the public-surface change carries documentation naming what moved — quote the surface change and the documenting text.
- PRESENT/BAD (NEGATIVE): documentation exists for the change yet never names the specific changed parameter, field, route or default a consumer must adapt to. Quote both.
- ABSENT/GOOD (NEGATIVE): a real public-surface change and, after looking in every place a consumer would — the doc-comment on or above the surface, a changelog or docs addition, the description, and a materialised wiki document — nothing a consumer could read to adapt.
- ABSENT/BAD: no ordinary case.
- UNDETERMINED only when the evidence genuinely cannot settle whether the one symbol this practice turns on crosses a module or service boundary; name the question. Do not resolve that doubt into an observation or into a claim that no public surface was here. Having looked everywhere and found no documentation for an established public surface is ABSENT, not UNDETERMINED.
One observation per review. When several surfaces change, grade by the least-documented one.

## Severity
Negatives only; never above MAJOR on documentation alone — a formative habit, not a merge gate. MINOR, the usual band: a new additive surface with no documentation, since nothing breaks but consumers cannot discover it; lighter still, documentation that exists yet never names the specific changed parameter or field. MAJOR: a breaking change — a removed or renamed symbol, route or field, a narrowed type, a changed default — shipping with no documentation anywhere, so callers break without a migration note. Equivalent situations land at equivalent severity.

## Grounding
Cite the diff lines of the observable surface change in every cell. For PRESENT/GOOD, quote the documenting text and its file. For PRESENT/BAD, quote the documentation and the changed element it omits. For ABSENT/GOOD, cite the surface change and name the boundary searched: the surface's doc-comment, the changelog and docs in the diff, the description, and any materialised wiki document. Never invent a symbol, an export marker, a changelog or a clean bill you did not see. Never assert the compile or runtime correctness of the surface, and never impute intent or care; describe the documentation habit on the observable artifact only.

## Defer
The pull request's general what-and-why narrative belongs to `describe-what-and-why`; whether a design decision's rationale is recorded belongs to `records-significant-decisions-with-rationale`. A thin description or an unjustified choice is not an observation here. Here only: is the public-surface change documented for its consumers?

practices.name: Keep linked wiki docs consistent with the change
practices.whyItMatters: A wiki that contradicts the code is worse than no wiki: teammates act on documented behaviour that no longer holds, and the drift compounds silently until someone is burned by it.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: When a change alters something the team's design or reference doc describes, the same PR brings the doc along, so the wiki keeps telling the truth about the system.
practices.criteria:
BEHAVIOR FOCUS: a specific contradiction between what this change does and what a linked wiki document still asserts about the same behaviour.

## The standard
Judge one thing: when this pull request changes a documented behaviour — a config default, a public API or wire contract, a CLI flag, an error or return code, an operational step — AND a linked wiki document describes that same behaviour, does the document still agree with the code, or has the diff left it contradicting reality? Work in two stages, in order. (1) From the hand-written diff, identify a concrete behaviour, contract or config the change alters. (2) Only if a materialised document describes that same thing, check whether the document now asserts something the code contradicts: an old default, a removed flag, a renamed field, a changed status code, a superseded step. The signal is a genuine contradiction between a specific document passage and a specific diff hunk — never staleness in the abstract, and never "the code changed, so the document is probably old". The presence or absence of a wiki link is never itself the observation; a change with no relevant document is not a weakness.

## Occasion
This is a gate. Record NOT_APPLICABLE, name the fact, and stop — never ABSENT — when: the pull request (its description or a linked issue) references no wiki document; the diff is empty; or the diff does not touch anything the materialised document describes. A document is available to you only when the pull request references it and its body was materialised as a `.md` file under `inputs/context/outline/`. When the pull request references a specific document that a reader would expect to describe the behaviour this diff changes, and that document was not materialised, you cannot tell whether it now contradicts the code: report a collection gap and record no observation. An unreadable diff is the same collection gap.

## Sources
1. The description (`inputs/context/description.md`) and each linked issue (`inputs/context/linked_work_items/<n>.md`): which wiki documents the change references, and any sentence saying the document was updated. They establish that a document is in scope; they never establish what the document says. A bare URL is not evidence of a document's content. An image: its caption and the sentence around it. An external link: nothing.
2. The materialised documents (`inputs/context/outline/<document>.md`): the passages that describe the behaviour. They establish what the wiki asserts today. Read the file before concluding anything about it.
3. The diff (`work/change/diff.patch`, with `work/change/files.json`): the hand-written hunks that alter a behaviour, contract or config, and any documentation the same change updates. It establishes what the code now does; it never establishes what the wiki says.
4. The checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): context for what a changed symbol, flag or step means. It never supplies a document passage.

## Judge
Test the cells in this order.
- PRESENT/GOOD: no ordinary case. A document contradicting the code is never desirable.
- PRESENT/BAD (NEGATIVE): the diff changes a documented behaviour and the materialised document still asserts the old behaviour, so a reader who trusts the wiki is misled. Quote both sides.
- ABSENT/GOOD: no ordinary case.
- ABSENT/BAD (POSITIVE): the diff changes something the document describes AND the same pull request updates that document, or the document already reflects the new behaviour, so code and document do not contradict.
- UNDETERMINED: no ordinary case. A referenced document you were not shown is a collection gap, not UNDETERMINED. Having read the materialised document and found no passage the diff makes false is ABSENT/BAD, not UNDETERMINED.
One observation per review, over the whole change.

## Severity
Negatives only; never above MAJOR — the aim is a trustworthy wiki, not a merge gate. MINOR, the usual band: a contradiction on a minor or internal-facing detail, a nudge to update the document. MAJOR: a contradiction a consumer would act on wrongly — a wrong documented default or limit, a removed API or flag the document still offers, a changed auth, security or data-handling step. When unsure, prefer the lower severity.

## Grounding
Ground every NEGATIVE in both sides: the exact added or removed `[L<n>]` diff line that changes the behaviour, and the verbatim sentence from the materialised `.md` document that still asserts the old behaviour, cited with its `inputs/context/outline/...` file path. If you cannot point to a specific document passage the diff makes false, do not raise the observation: never infer a contradiction you cannot cite, and never fabricate a document quote. For ABSENT/BAD, cite the diff line of the changed behaviour and the document line (in the diff or in the materialised file) that now agrees with it. Never claim a build or test ran, and never impute intent or care; describe what the document says and what the code does.

## Defer
Whether a change was documented at all, in any surface, belongs to `documents-public-api-and-behaviour-changes`. Whether the WHY of a decision is recorded belongs to `records-significant-decisions-with-rationale`. Here only: does a specific linked wiki document now contradict the code?

practices.name: Say what else you considered
practices.whyItMatters: A decision record that names only the winner tells the next person what was done, not what it cost. When a constraint later changes — a library is deprecated, the traffic grows, the team shrinks — the first question is always "what else did we look at, and does that reason still hold?". If the alternatives were never written down, that question can only be answered by redoing the whole investigation, and usually it is not answered at all: the decision quietly becomes something nobody feels able to revisit.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: A record that names the two or three options that were genuinely in play and gives each one a sentence saying what ruled it out — the constraint it failed, the cost it carried, the thing the team was not willing to trade. Written for someone who arrives a year later with a changed constraint, so they can tell in a minute whether the decision still stands.
practices.criteria:
BEHAVIOR FOCUS: a published decision record names at least one alternative that was genuinely considered and says why that alternative lost.

## The standard
Judge whether a decision record says what else was seriously considered and why those options were not chosen. A record that states only the chosen option records an outcome; a later reader needs the reasons the others lost, because that is the only part that tells them whether the decision still holds once a constraint changes. PRESENT means the document names at least one alternative that was genuinely on the table and gives a reason it was not chosen — a constraint it failed, a cost it carried, a trade-off the team was unwilling to make — and that reason is about that alternative specifically. A reason that only restates the chosen option's merits says nothing about why the others were worse and does not count. No template or heading name is required: a document that gives the reasons in prose satisfies this as fully as one with a headed section.

## Occasion
This is a gate. The practice applies only when the document is recognisably a decision record: it names a single decision and takes a position on it. Signals: a title or heading naming a decision; a status line (proposed, accepted, superseded); a section headed with words like decision, context, consequences, options, alternatives, trade-offs. Record NOT_APPLICABLE, name the kind, and stop — never ABSENT — for a design overview, a runbook, a how-to guide, a meeting note, an index page, or a specification that decides nothing. Stay silent rather than asking such a document to be a decision record.

## Sources
1. The document body (`inputs/context/document.md`): the whole authored text. It establishes whether an alternative is named and whether a reason is given for it. It never establishes whether the decision was right, whether the rejected options deserved rejection, or whether the document is still current.
2. The document metadata (`inputs/context/document.json`): the title. It establishes only whether the title names a decision, for the occasion. It never establishes what the body says.
Judge the text in front of you and nothing else. An image you cannot open: read its caption and the sentence around it. An external link: nothing. Two cases are not absence: a record that defers its options discussion to another document you were not given, and a body that visibly breaks off before any options section. If either reflects incomplete capture, report a collection gap and record no observation. If the complete authored document itself ends without discussing alternatives, judge that omission; do not mistake unfinished writing for missing capture.

## Judge
Read the whole body before deciding. Then test the cells in this order.
- PRESENT/GOOD (POSITIVE): at least one alternative is named and a reason specific to it is given. Quote the span naming the alternative and the span giving the reason.
- PRESENT/BAD: no ordinary case. Whether a stated reason was a good one is not observable here.
- ABSENT/GOOD (NEGATIVE): the document states a decision and its rationale but names no alternative at all; or it lists alternatives with no reason any of them lost (a bare bullet list of technology names); or the only reason given restates the chosen option's merits. A section headed "Alternatives considered" that is empty, or contains only "none", is ABSENT unless the document explains why there was genuinely no other option.
- ABSENT/BAD: no ordinary case.
- UNDETERMINED: no ordinary case. A complete document either names an alternative with its reason or does not; an incomplete or deferring document is a collection gap, not an open question. Having read the whole body and found no alternative with a reason is ABSENT, not UNDETERMINED.
One observation per review, on the document as a whole.

## Severity
Negatives only; MINOR is the usual band: a bounded addition fixes it — one alternative and the sentence that ruled it out. Do not raise the band on this practice alone; the weight of the decision is not something the text lets you judge.

## Grounding
For PRESENT/GOOD, cite the exact lines naming the alternative and the exact lines giving its reason. For ABSENT/GOOD, cite the decision statement and the boundary you searched: the whole body, including any options or alternatives section quoted or stated to be empty. Never claim the decision was correct or incorrect, never claim a rejected alternative deserved its fate, and never claim the document is or is not up to date. Describe what the record says; never impute intent or character.

## Defer
Whether a pull request records the decisions it makes belongs to `records-significant-decisions-with-rationale`. Whether the decision was right, whether the alternatives deserved rejection, and whether the document is current are not judged by any practice here. Here only: does the record name what else was considered and why it lost?

groups.name: Disciplined delivery and version control
groups.description: Keep your delivery clean. Make each commit one self-contained change, leave generated and build files out of the diff, and branch from the shared integration branch so your work stands on its own.

practices.name: Keep each commit to one logical change
practices.whyItMatters: Mixing unrelated changes in a commit makes selective review, reverts and backports harder. Keeping changes separable makes the history more useful; clear commit subjects help a reader understand that intended separation.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: Separate commits for separate ideas, such as 'Fix off-by-one in pagination' in one and 'Rename helper for clarity' in another, so each can be reviewed, reverted, or backported on its own.
practices.criteria:
BEHAVIOR FOCUS: how the pull request's commits are partitioned — each commit one cohesive logical change, as its authored subject and body describe it.

## The standard
Judge one thing: whether the commits are SPLIT so each one captures a single logical change, rather than one commit tangling unrelated kinds of work into a bundle a reviewer cannot follow, revert, or cherry-pick on its own. Cohesive: a fix and the test that covers it together; a single change described in two clauses about the same step ("parse the header and validate it"). Several cohesive feature commits in one pull request is fine here. A tangle: a subject that plainly conjoins distinct concerns — a behavioural fix with an unrelated reformat or lint sweep, a rename sweep, a merge-conflict resolution, a dependency bump — or a series that obviously braids process or chore work through behavioural work. Decide what counts as "unrelated" as an experienced reviewer would; there is no fixed word list, and a conjunction joining clauses about the SAME change is not a tangle. This is a workflow habit about how the history is partitioned, never a code-defect claim.

## Occasion
This is a gate. Record NOT_APPLICABLE, name which case, and stop — never ABSENT — when there was no split to judge: only a single non-merge commit, or every entry is an automatic merge commit (`parent_count` of 2 or more, or a "Merge ..." subject).

## Sources
1. The commits (`inputs/context/commits.json`): each subject, full body, `parents` and the `files` it touched against its first parent, with status and line counts. They establish the author's partition — what each commit says it contains and which files it actually touched. A commit whose files span concerns its subject does not name is the observation; `git show <sha>` in the checkout gives its patch when the file list is not enough.
2. The per-file changed-line spread of the whole change (`work/change/files.json`, `work/change/diff.patch`): the overall breadth the commits together cover. It establishes the spread the partition must account for.
Read subjects, bodies and each commit's files together and judge conservatively. The precompute summary (`work/precompute-out/summary.md`) lists every authored commit as one row with the shape of its subject — bare, a repeat, a list of concerns, cut off — and the files and kinds of file it touched, as places to look, never verdicts. If `inputs/context/commits.json` is unavailable, report a collection gap and record no observation; uncollected subjects are never authored silence and never UNDETERMINED.

## Judge
Test the cells in this order.
- PRESENT/GOOD (POSITIVE): every commit reads as one cohesive logical unit. Scope the claim to the described partition: the subjects and bodies establish what the author says each commit holds, not what it holds.
- PRESENT/BAD (NEGATIVE): the split itself is wrong — a subject plainly conjoins distinct concerns, or the series braids chore work through behavioural work. Read a list literally: a subject that joins two or more concerns with "and", commas or bullets ("add search, caching, and icon cleanup"; "refactor X, add logging, and add a permission key") conjoins them, and is this cell however natural the combination reads. Two clauses are two CONCERNS when they name different subjects — different features, screens, files of different kinds, or a chore beside a behaviour change. Two verbs on ONE subject are one concern and never this cell: "recolour and centre the button", "refine the diagram and update the path that embeds it", "add the view and its navigation entry" each describe one artifact and what was done to it. Quote the deciding subject(s) and name the two subjects they join.
- ABSENT/GOOD and ABSENT/BAD: no ordinary case. With two or more non-merge commits a partition exists and is judged; with fewer, the occasion is NOT_APPLICABLE.
- UNDETERMINED when vague descriptions leave the partition unresolved; name the missing distinction. Do not infer atomicity from the absence of an obviously mixed subject: missing evidence of unrelated concerns is not proof of cohesive commits.
One observation per review, over the whole series.

## Severity
Negatives only; never above MAJOR on commit atomicity alone — a formative habit, not a merge gate. MINOR, the usual band: a single commit bundles unrelated work, and splitting it would isolate each concern. MAJOR: the history broadly tangles, so a reviewer cannot reason about or revert one concern at a time.

## Grounding
Every claim cites the authored commit descriptions that support it: quote the deciding subject(s) for PRESENT/BAD; cite the subjects and bodies whose described partition you accepted for PRESENT/GOOD. Never claim a per-commit file mapping you cannot observe. Commit messages are not citable lines, and `inputs/context/commits.json` being derived here rather than staged is not a collection gap: the subjects were read. Quote the deciding subjects verbatim in the rationale, each with its short SHA, and cite `inputs/context/metadata.json` (`scm.pull-request.core`, the `title` line) as the location: the pull request the commits belong to. Never cite a diff line or a repository file for this observation — its evidence is subject text — and never record UNDETERMINED because the subjects have no line of their own to cite. Describe the observable split; never impute intent or character, and never frame a tangle as a defect in the code.

## Defer
Overall pull request size and file spread belong to `scope-one-reviewable-change`; a large but demonstrably cohesive described partition can be a strength here. Subject wording and legibility belong to `commit-subjects-explain-each-change`; a vague subject alone establishes neither cohesion nor a tangle. Here only: does each commit hold one logical change?

practices.name: Keep generated and build files out of the diff
practices.whyItMatters: A reviewer catches the most problems in the hand-written lines they can read closely, and a committed build output or editor config buries that source under machine noise nobody reviews. Leaving generated files out keeps the diff to the change a person can actually check, and spares everyone the odd conflict in a file no human wrote.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: The diff holds only the source you hand-wrote, with build outputs, logs, and editor files kept out through .gitignore. If the repo deliberately tracks a generated file, such as a committed API spec or client, that is fine as long as it was regenerated and moves in step with the source change that drives it, not hand-edited.
practices.criteria:
BEHAVIOR FOCUS: generated or build artifacts committed with the change where no repository policy or source-to-artifact workflow justifies tracking them.

## The standard
Judge one thing: does the change include generated or build artifacts only where the repository's captured policy or its source-to-artifact workflow justifies tracking them? This is a repository-hygiene habit about what gets committed — never a code-defect claim about a file's contents, and generated output is not itself the defect. Judge from the file paths in the diff. Machine noise being reviewed as if it were source has a recognisable shape across any stack or language — a location or a banner that says "a tool wrote this": a build-output directory, an editor or OS cruft file, a coverage dump, a vendored or cached blob, a minified single-line bundle, or a tracked generated file someone hand-edited instead of regenerating. These are open examples, not a closed list. A repository may deliberately version-control some generated sources — a committed OpenAPI spec, a generated client, an ERD, a route tree. When such a tracked artifact moves in step with the hand-written change that drives its regeneration, that is intended, regeneration-consistent movement: do not flag it. An intentional regeneration may be appropriate without a simultaneous hand-written edit. Flag only output that is not meant to be tracked, or a tracked generated file left hand-edited or stale relative to its source.

## Occasion
This is a gate. Record NOT_APPLICABLE, name the fact, and stop — never ABSENT — only for an empty change. A change whose files are all generated still has content whose inclusion can be reviewed; it is judged, not ruled out.

## Sources
1. The file spread (`work/change/files.json`) and the per-file headers of the diff (`work/change/diff.patch`): the paths. They establish which paths changed and where they sit — the primary evidence. A path never establishes compile, build or runtime behaviour.
2. The patch body (`work/change/diff.patch`): open it only to confirm a flagged path is machine-emitted when the path alone is ambiguous — a "DO NOT EDIT", "@generated" or "auto-generated" banner, a minified single line. The evidence is the path plus that confirming line, never a line-by-line review of the file's contents.
3. The checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): the ignore rules, the documented generation workflow, and whether an artifact is tracked and which source drives it. It establishes whether tracking a generated file is intended. It never establishes manual editing or stale generation from an unchanged source file alone.
If the policy or source evidence a flag needs was not acquired, report a collection gap and record no observation.

## Judge
Test the cells in this order.
- PRESENT/BAD (NEGATIVE): a quoted repository policy or an observable workflow establishes that an added artifact should not be tracked, or a tracked generated file was hand-edited or left stale relative to the source that drives it. Quote each offending path.
- ABSENT/BAD (POSITIVE): a complete bounded search over every changed path establishes that the changed artifacts are appropriately tracked — every path is something a person authored or intended: source, tests, docs, hand-written config, a lockfile moving in step with its manifest, or a tracked generated artifact moving in step with its source.
- PRESENT/GOOD and ABSENT/GOOD: no ordinary case. A justified tracked artifact is not the behaviour; an unjustified one is never desirable.
- UNDETERMINED when the one path this practice turns on is genuinely ambiguous — the path, any banner and the patch together cannot tell you whether it is machine-emitted, or whether a tracked generated artifact moved in step with the source that drives it. Say so rather than let the doubt pass as a clean bill; name what would settle it. Having walked every path and found each justified is ABSENT/BAD, not UNDETERMINED.
One observation per review, covering every flagged path.

## Severity
Negatives only; never above MAJOR on this practice alone — a habit to grow, not a merge gate. MINOR, the usual band: a lone stray artifact. MAJOR: a committed build-output directory, several leaked artifacts, or a hand-edited generated file that should have been regenerated. Identical situations land identically.

## Grounding
Every NEGATIVE names each offending path verbatim and, for a generated-file flag, quotes the confirming banner or names the tracked artifact and its driving source. If you cannot name an offending path there is nothing to flag; do not invent one. Cite a line of the flagged file from `work/change/diff.patch` (`scm.pull-request.diff`, the pinned `inputs/context/change.json`): `work/change/files.json` is derived here and is not citable. For ABSENT/BAD the citations show the boundary: `changed_files` in `inputs/context/metadata.json` (`scm.pull-request.core`) and the paths you walked, listed in the rationale. Describe the observable fact ("this path is machine-emitted") and the next step (ignore it and drop it, or regenerate from source). Never assert compile, build or runtime behaviour from a path; never impute intent or character.

## Defer
Whether a dependency change was deliberate or justified belongs to `changes-dependencies-deliberately`; a lockfile moving in step with its manifest is its concern. Do not infer that a lockfile was hand-edited merely because its manifest did not change — an intentional resolution refresh may update a lockfile alone. Here only: does the diff carry machine output that should not be tracked?

groups.name: Tracking work from issue to merge
groups.description: Plan and track the work so a maintainer can route it and watch it progress, and keep the issue and the change that answers it linked: split genuinely large issues into trackable sub-tasks, triage each one, name the issue the change implements, and confirm the issue's outcome when the change lands.

practices.name: Break large work into trackable subtasks
practices.whyItMatters: A big ask written as one wall of text is either 0% or 100% done, with no way to see progress or split the load. Breaking it into checkable steps turns a daunting job into pieces people can pick up and finish one at a time.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: A genuinely large issue split into a task list or linked sub-issues, such as 'design the schema', 'add the endpoint', and 'wire up the UI', so progress is visible and pieces can be worked in parallel.
practices.criteria:
BEHAVIOR FOCUS: a trackable breakdown of work that is large enough to need one — checkable sub-units a maintainer can watch reach done, rather than one monolithic ask.

## The standard
Judge ONE thing: when the issue describes genuinely LARGE or multi-part work, is that work broken into explicit, trackable sub-units, rather than left as a single undivided block? Trackable means the parts are individually checkable or addressable: a task list of checkboxes that name work to do, a tracked sub-issue tree, or enumerated child or tracking issues the body frames as parts. Reason like a senior reviewer scanning a backlog: a big ask written as one block is either 0% or 100% done with no visible progress; a decomposed one lets pieces be picked up in parallel and tracked to done. What counts as LARGE is a judgment, not a word count: the signal is two or more SEPARABLE deliverables that could ship or be assigned independently, or an explicit epic, initiative, meta or tracking framing the issue itself chose. Two or more such deliverables joined by commas or "and" in one sentence — a rename, a new tab, a theme, a changed default — are large work by this test however short the body is; the body's length is never the test. Sequential steps of ONE cohesive flow described as a journey are a single deliverable, not several parts. A checklist of verification items is not a work breakdown unless it also names concrete implementation sub-steps.

## Occasion
This is a gate. Record NOT_APPLICABLE, name the case, and stop — never ABSENT — when: the issue is a pure question, a support request or an open discussion with no concrete deliverable; the body is empty, title-only or an unmodified template, so nothing is quotable; or the work is a focused single-concern deliverable (one feature, one bug), which neither needs a breakdown nor is penalised for lacking one. Never manufacture a strength from the mere absence of largeness, and never make the single-concern scope judgment here — that belongs to `issue-scoped-to-single-concern`.

## Sources
Your context is the issue only; there is no diff or code.
1. The title and the WHOLE body (`inputs/context/description.md`): every section, checklist and enumerated list. It establishes whether the work is large (separable deliverables, epic framing) and whether a checklist or a set of framed child issues breaks it down. It never establishes largeness from title length or tone alone.
2. The labels and the sub-issue rollup (`inputs/context/metadata.json`): a label such as epic or tracking, and the `sub_issues_total` / `sub_issues_completed` figures. A non-zero rollup is a tracked sub-issue tree. The labels establish the framing the issue chose; they never by themselves establish that a breakdown exists.
3. The comments (`inputs/context/comments.json`): a later comment can supply the breakdown or the child issues. They establish a breakdown on that surface; they never establish one the text does not show.
An image in the body: read its caption and the sentence around it. An external link: nothing. Before concluding that no breakdown exists, scan ALL three surfaces. If the body or the comments were not captured, report a collection gap and record no observation.

## Judge
Test the cells in this order.
- PRESENT/GOOD (POSITIVE): the work is genuinely large AND a trackable breakdown is quotable — named sub-steps as a checklist ("design the schema", "add the endpoint", "wire up the UI"), a non-zero sub-issue rollup, or child issues the body frames as parts. Sibling issues in the project inventory that this body never names are not its breakdown, however well they match its sentences.
- PRESENT/BAD and ABSENT/BAD: no ordinary case. A breakdown that exists is the behaviour; its quality is not judged here.
- ABSENT/GOOD (NEGATIVE): the work is clearly large AND no trackable breakdown exists on any of the three surfaces — an epic or tracking-framed issue with nothing tracked under it, or a body that enumerates several independent deliverables as prose with no way to track each. An element you cannot quote counts as absent.
- UNDETERMINED only when the text genuinely cannot settle whether its spans are one journey or several separable deliverables AND no breakdown exists on any surface; quote the ambiguous span and say what would settle it. Do not resolve that doubt into silence. Having scanned every surface and found no breakdown for clearly large work is ABSENT, not UNDETERMINED.
One observation per review, over the whole issue. Identical evidence yields the same call.

## Severity
Negatives only; never above MAJOR on decomposition alone — a non-blocking workflow habit, not a merge gate. MINOR, the usual band: only a couple of parts go untracked, and a short checklist would fix it. MAJOR: an issue the text itself frames as an epic, initiative, meta or tracking issue has nothing tracked under it at all.

## Grounding
Every "large" claim and every "no breakdown" claim quotes the exact span: a label name, a body sentence naming each separable deliverable, the rollup figure, or a comment. For PRESENT/GOOD, quote the checklist lines, the rollup figure or the framed child references. For ABSENT/GOOD, cite the spans that establish largeness and name the boundary searched: the body, the rollup, and the comments. Never invent largeness, never fabricate a breakdown you did not see. Never assert technical feasibility, hour estimates or design correctness, and never grade the reporter as a person; describe the observable artifact state only.

## Defer
Whether the work SHOULD have been one concern belongs to `issue-scoped-to-single-concern`; treat a multi-part ask as legitimately large work needing a breakdown, and do not re-judge its scope. Whether acceptance criteria or a Definition of Done are present belongs to `issue-has-checkable-outcome`; do not re-flag a verification checklist here. Here only: is large work DECOMPOSED into trackable parts?

practices.name: Classify the issue the way the project classifies issues
practices.whyItMatters: A label kind the project filters and groups by — type, priority, size — routes the issue to the board column, the person and the sprint it belongs to. An issue outside that scheme is the one nobody's filter shows, so it waits.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: In a project that labels its issues, each issue carries one label of every kind the project uses (`type::`, `priority::`, `size::`), and an owner or milestone where the project assigns them, so every view of the queue sees it.
practices.criteria:
BEHAVIOR FOCUS: the issue carries the classification the project's own convention gives every issue — the label kinds the project uses, and an owner or milestone where the project assigns them.

## The standard
Judge whether this issue follows the labelling convention the project actually keeps, not whether every metadata field is filled. A project has a convention when its issues carry labels as a rule — most issues labelled, with a recognisable scheme such as scoped labels (`type::Bug`, `priority::Major`, `size::S`) or a stable set of kinds. Within such a project, an issue that carries one label of each kind the scheme uses is classified; one that carries none, or misses a kind the scheme gives every issue, is not, and the queue that filters or groups by that kind does not see it. Ownership and milestones follow the same rule: judged only where the project assigns them as a rule. A native issue type that stands for a label kind satisfies that kind. Never demand a classification the project does not use.

## Occasion
This is a gate. Record NOT_APPLICABLE, name the fact, and stop — never ABSENT — when the project keeps no labelling convention: the inventory's `labelScheme` shows fewer than a third of the project's issues labelled and no scoped label kind in use, or the inventory was not captured. A project whose issues are labelled as a rule is the occasion, whatever the issue's own text says about routing. When required issue metadata is unavailable, report a collection gap and record no observation.

## Sources
1. The inventory (`inputs/context/project_inventory.json`, `labelScheme`: `issuesTotal`, `issuesLabelled`, `labelsInUse`): whether the project labels its issues as a rule and which kinds it uses — a scoped kind is the text before `::`. It establishes the convention; it never establishes this issue's labels.
2. The metadata (`inputs/context/metadata.json`): this issue's native type, labels, assignees and milestone. It establishes what classification is present. A label such as `stale` is not a kind of the scheme.
3. The title and body (`inputs/context/description.md`): a stated request to classify or route, which raises severity, never the occasion.

## Judge
Test the cells in this order.
- PRESENT/GOOD (POSITIVE): the issue carries a label of each kind the scheme uses, or a native type standing for one, and an owner or milestone where the project assigns them as a rule. Quote the labels and the scheme.
- PRESENT/BAD: no ordinary case.
- ABSENT/GOOD (NEGATIVE): the project labels its issues as a rule and this issue carries no label of a kind the scheme uses — none at all, or a kind every other issue carries is missing. Quote `labelsInUse` and the issue's `labels`.
- ABSENT/BAD: no ordinary case.
- UNDETERMINED: no ordinary case. Metadata read in full that lacks the kind is ABSENT; metadata you could not read is a collection gap.
One observation per review, over the whole issue.

## Severity
Negatives only; never above MINOR — non-blocking feedback about routing, not a merge gate. MINOR: no label at all in a labelled project, or the body asks to be routed and no label answers it. INFO: one kind of several missing.

## Grounding
Quote the scheme from `labelScheme.labelsInUse`, the issue's `labels` array as captured, and the counts that establish the convention. Never infer a convention from the number of people in a project; never assess whether the work is worth doing.

## Defer
Problem framing belongs to `issue-states-an-actionable-problem`, scope to `issue-scoped-to-single-concern`, and the definition of done to `issue-has-checkable-outcome`. Here only: is the issue classified the way this project classifies its issues?

practices.name: Confirm the outcome before closing the issue
practices.whyItMatters: Closing an issue tells the whole team it is handled. Closing it with a checklist item still unticked or sub-issues still open drops that work quietly, and someone hits the gap later expecting it to be done.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: Before closing, every acceptance item is checked and every tracked sub-issue is finished, or a comment says plainly what is being dropped and why, so 'closed' honestly means done.
practices.criteria:
BEHAVIOR FOCUS: closing the issue as done while a stated outcome of its own — an acceptance item or a tracked sub-issue — was still visibly open at the close.

## The standard
When an issue is CLOSED as done, judge whether its own stated definition of done was confirmed before the close — every checkable acceptance item ticked and every tracked sub-issue finished — or whether it was closed with a done-condition still visibly open. Assess this single closure decision only, never the work: an empty checkbox may simply never have been ticked while the work was genuinely done, or the remainder may be tracked elsewhere. A closing comment that says plainly what is being dropped or deferred and why accounts for the remainder. Never assert compile, runtime or correctness behaviour; there is no diff or code here.

## Occasion
This is a gate. Record NOT_APPLICABLE, name the fact, and stop — never ABSENT — when: the issue is not closed; it was closed as not-planned, wontfix, duplicate, superseded or deferred, since an unmet checklist is the expected state of deliberately abandoned work; or it stated no checkable outcome you can quote (a task list, an acceptance or Definition-of-Done block, a Given-When-Then, or a non-zero sub-issue rollup). Read the disposition from the observable fact: prefer an explicit `state_reason`, else an explicit closing-comment or body signal; a bare close with no not-planned signal defaults to done. Never invent a `state_reason` the record does not carry. NOT_APPLICABLE belongs to these scope rules, never to evidence you could not read.

## Sources
1. The issue record (`inputs/context/metadata.json`): state, `state_reason`, `closed_at`, labels, and the sub-issue rollup (completed of total). It establishes that the issue is closed, how, and when. A missing or absent rollup is unknown, never zero. `closed_at` never establishes when the body checkboxes or the rollup had their present values.
2. The title and the WHOLE body (`inputs/context/description.md`): the checkable outcome — each checkbox line, each acceptance item. Current body checkboxes are a current-state fact, not automatically the state at close.
3. Every comment (`inputs/context/comments.json`, read exhaustively): dated closing comments and any disposition that explains a remainder — "deferred to #123", "covered by !45", "done, forgot to tick". They establish, when dated, what was said at the close. They never establish a disposition nobody wrote.
4. The workspace inventory (`inputs/context/project_inventory.json`): open it and state either the overlapping or closing artifact you found — quote its `#number "title" (state)` — or that you scanned the inventory and found none.
An image: its caption and the sentence around it. An external link: nothing. When the comments or the body were not captured, report a collection gap and record no observation; unread required evidence is a readiness limitation, not a judgment.

## Judge
The undesirable behaviour is closing with a stated outcome unmet. Test the cells in this order.
- PRESENT/BAD (NEGATIVE): closed as done while a stated done-item was still open at the close — an unchecked acceptance or Definition-of-Done line, or a rollup short of complete — and nothing at the close names where that remainder went. Quote the deciding span.
- ABSENT/BAD (POSITIVE): closed as done and the complete outcome record establishes that nothing remains unmet — every checkable item ticked and every tracked sub-issue completed. Cite the record that shows it.
- PRESENT/GOOD and ABSENT/GOOD: no ordinary case. Closing over an open done-item is not desirable, and a confirmed outcome is not a lapse.
- The capture is read after the close, and ticks are only ever added: an item still unticked at capture was unticked at the close, so a done-close over an unticked list is decided from the current body and the closing comments — never UNDETERMINED for want of a dated tick. UNDETERMINED only when the body was truncated where the checklist stands, or the closing disposition is stated in a source that was not captured; name what is missing. Closure alone establishes neither presence nor absence. A missing required source is a collection gap, not UNDETERMINED.
One observation per review, on the single at-close question. Do not infer a longitudinal habit or a developer-wide pattern from this one issue.

## Severity
Negatives only; never above MAJOR on outcome confirmation alone — non-blocking. MINOR, the usual band: an open sub-issue rollup alone, or an open done-item whose disposition was named at the close, so the remainder was accounted for. MAJOR: an unconfirmed acceptance or Definition-of-Done condition with nothing anywhere — closing comments or body — accounting for it. Identical inputs yield identical severity.

## Grounding
Every claim cites an exact quoted span: the unchecked line, the "N of M" rollup, the state or `state_reason` value, the dated closing comment. For PRESENT/BAD, quote the open item and the dated evidence that it stood at the close. For ABSENT/BAD, cite the complete record — every item ticked, the rollup complete — and name what you scanned: body, comments, rollup, state. State the inventory result in every observation. Describe only observable state — "closed as done with '<quoted line>' still unchecked" — never a charge against the closer. Never fabricate a checklist, a clean bill or a disposition.

## Defer
Whether a NEW or OPEN issue defines a checkable outcome belongs to `issue-has-checkable-outcome`. Here only: was the stated outcome confirmed at the close?

practices.name: Link the change to the issue it implements
practices.whyItMatters: A change that names the issue it answers can be read against what was asked, closes that issue when it lands, and leaves a trail anyone can follow later. One without it makes the reviewer guess what the work was for, and leaves the issue open or closed by hand.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: The title, the description or the branch names the issue by number, with a closing keyword in the body when the change completes it, so the issue closes with the merge and the two stay linked.
practices.criteria:
BEHAVIOR FOCUS: the pull request names the issue it implements, so the work can be read against what was asked and the issue closes with the merge.

## The standard
Judge one thing: does this pull request say which issue it implements, in a way the platform links? A link is the issue's number in the title (`#12: …`), a closing reference in the body (`Closes #12`, `Fixes #12`, `Resolves #12`, or the provider's equivalent), a branch created from the issue (`12-add-login`), or a captured linked work item. A link makes the issue readable from the review and closes it when the change merges; a change with none of these stands alone. Judge the presence of the link, never the quality of the issue it points to or whether the change fulfils it.

## Occasion
This is a gate. Record NOT_APPLICABLE, name the fact, and stop — never ABSENT — when the work has no issue to link: the repository tracks no issues (`inputs/context/project_inventory.json` lists none), or the change is of a kind that answers no issue by convention — a release or version bump, a dependency update from a bot, a revert, a merge of one long-lived branch into another. A change a person made to the product is expected to answer an issue; a missing issue is then the lapse, not the absence of an occasion.

## Sources
1. The title, source branch and body (`inputs/context/metadata.json`, `inputs/context/description.md`): the number references and closing keywords as written. They establish the link the author made. They never establish that the issue exists or that the change fulfils it.
2. The linked work items (`inputs/context/linked_work_items/<n>.md`) when captured: the items the platform resolved from those references. They establish that a reference resolves; their absence establishes nothing when no reference was written.
3. The inventory (`inputs/context/project_inventory.json`): whether the project tracks issues at all, and, for a change with no reference, whether an open issue plainly describes this work — quote its `#number "title"` if you find one, or say you scanned it and found none.
4. The commits (`inputs/context/commits.json`): a further place an issue number may appear. They establish a reference the author left in history, nothing more. The precompute summary (`work/precompute-out/summary.md`) lists every number referenced, where it was written, and whether the inventory or the linked items hold an issue of that number with its title and state.
If the record or the inventory is unavailable for a change with no reference, report a collection gap and record no observation.

## Judge
Test the cells in this order.
- PRESENT/GOOD (POSITIVE): the title, body, branch or a captured linked item names an issue of this project by number, or a closing keyword names one. Quote the reference.
- PRESENT/BAD (NEGATIVE): a reference is written but cannot be what it claims — it names an issue of another project or none that exists, or the body closes an issue the change plainly does not touch (a closing keyword on an unrelated number). Quote the reference and name the fact that breaks it.
- ABSENT/GOOD (NEGATIVE): the change is product work by a person and no title, body, branch, commit or linked item names an issue, after scanning all of them. Say what you scanned.
- ABSENT/BAD: no ordinary case.
- UNDETERMINED: a reference whose target you cannot resolve because the inventory was not captured and the number could be a pull request as well as an issue; name what would settle it.
One observation per review.

## Severity
Negatives only; never above MAJOR on this alone — non-blocking. MINOR, the usual band: product work with no reference where an open issue for it plainly exists in the inventory, or a reference in the wrong form. MAJOR: a closing keyword that will close an issue the change does not fulfil, or product work with no issue at all in a project that tracks its work in issues. Identical evidence yields identical severity.

## Grounding
Quote the reference as written in the title, body, branch name or commit subject, or the linked item's `#number "title"`. ABSENT/GOOD names every source scanned. Never invent an issue number, and never claim an issue's content from its number alone.

## Defer
Whether the change fulfils the issue's acceptance criteria belongs to `honours-linked-issue-acceptance-criteria`; the description's what and why belong to `describe-what-and-why`. Here only: is the change linked to the issue it implements?

practices.name: Confirm the issue's outcome when the change lands
practices.whyItMatters: An issue that closes with its acceptance items untouched, or stays open after the work merged, tells the next person nothing about what was actually done. Confirming the outcome at the merge — ticking what landed, saying what did not — is how the tracker stays true.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: When the change merges, the linked issue's checkable outcome reflects it: the items the change delivers are ticked or the closing comment says what was delivered and what moves elsewhere, and the issue's state matches.
practices.criteria:
BEHAVIOR FOCUS: at the merge, the linked issue's stated outcome is confirmed — its checkable items ticked or the remainder named — so the tracker says what the merge delivered.

## The standard
Judge one thing about the moment this pull request merged: was the linked issue's own definition of done brought into line with what landed? An issue that stated a checkable outcome (an acceptance checklist, a Definition of Done, a Given-When-Then block, tracked sub-issues) is confirmed when the items the change delivers are ticked and any remainder is named — in the issue, in the pull request body, or in a closing comment. Assess only this bookkeeping act, never whether the work is correct: an unticked item may describe delivered work, and a ticked one may not. A closing sentence that says plainly what is done and what is deferred confirms the outcome as well as ticks do; a sentence that names the feature ("added the glossary") without naming the items confirms nothing.

## Occasion
This is a gate. Record NOT_APPLICABLE, name the fact, and stop — never ABSENT — when: the pull request is not merged; no linked work item was captured, or the linked item states no checkable outcome you can quote (a task list, an acceptance or Definition-of-Done block, a Given-When-Then, or a non-zero sub-issue rollup); or the linked item was closed as not planned, duplicate or superseded, since its outcome was deliberately abandoned. A linked item with an outcome and a merge are the occasion — every captured linked item that states one, the item the body closes and the items it only names alike; the precompute summary lists each with its items and ticks. A user story without a task list, an outcome heading or sub-issues is no occasion, however plainly the diff delivers it.

## Sources
1. The pull request record (`inputs/context/metadata.json`): `state` and `merged_at`. It establishes that and when the change merged. It never establishes the issue's state.
2. Each linked item (`inputs/context/linked_work_items/<n>.md`: number, title, state, body): the checkable outcome as written, with its ticks as captured. It establishes what was stated and which items are ticked. The capture is read after the merge, and a tick made after it still confirms the outcome: the lapse is bookkeeping never done, not bookkeeping done late. A closed state alone confirms nothing; the ticks or the words do.
3. The body (`inputs/context/description.md`) and the discussion (`inputs/context/general_comments.json`): a done/deferred mapping or a closing sentence. They establish what the author said was delivered. They never establish that it was.
4. The diff (`work/change/diff.patch`): read only to ground a heavier severity when a named item is plainly not touched. It never establishes that an item is met.
If the linked item's body or the record's merge time is unavailable, report a collection gap and record no observation.

## Judge
Test the cells in this order.
- PRESENT/GOOD (POSITIVE): every item the change delivers is ticked, or a closing sentence names what was delivered and what moves elsewhere. Quote the ticked items or the sentence. The ticks are the item's own: a checked box in the merge request's body ticks nothing on the item, and an item the diff plainly delivers that nobody ticked or named is still unaccounted — the practice is the bookkeeping, not the delivery.
- PRESENT/BAD: no ordinary case.
- ABSENT/GOOD (NEGATIVE): the change merged, the linked item states a checkable outcome, and neither ticks nor a closing sentence account for it — items stay unticked with no word, whether the issue was closed by the merge or left open. Quote the unticked items and the merge time.
- ABSENT/BAD: no ordinary case.
- UNDETERMINED: the linked item's outcome is captured only in part — a truncated body that cuts the checklist — so the ticks cannot be counted; name what is missing.
One observation per review.

## Severity
Negatives only; never above MAJOR on this alone — non-blocking. MINOR, the usual band: one or two items left unticked with the work plainly delivered, or a closing sentence that names the outcome loosely. MAJOR: the issue closed by the merge with most of its stated outcome untouched and unmentioned, or left open with nothing said. Identical evidence yields identical severity.

## Grounding
Quote the outcome items from the linked item as written, the tick state, the merge time from the record, and any closing sentence. Never claim an item is met or unmet from the code; never infer a tick that is not in the capture; never read a closed state as a tick.

## Defer
Whether the change fulfils the acceptance criteria belongs to `honours-linked-issue-acceptance-criteria`; the issue's own closing decision, when someone closes it by hand, belongs to `issue-closed-with-unmet-outcome`. Here only: did the merge leave the issue's stated outcome confirmed?

practices.name: Track the review asks you defer
practices.whyItMatters: A reviewer's ask answered with 'later' and nothing else is a promise that evaporates at the merge. Turning a deferred ask into a tracked issue, or getting the reviewer's explicit agreement to drop it, keeps the review's value after the thread is resolved.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: Every review ask the author does not address in the change is either turned into an issue the thread links, or explicitly waived by the reviewer; nothing is resolved with a bare 'will do later'.
practices.criteria:
BEHAVIOR FOCUS: a review ask the author defers rather than addresses is turned into tracked work or explicitly waived by the reviewer, never resolved on a bare promise.

## The standard
Judge one thing: when a reviewer asked for something in a thread and the author did not do it in this change, what happened to the ask at the merge?
