A deferral is tracked when the thread, the body or a comment names an issue for it (`#number`, a link, "tracked in …") or the reviewer explicitly agrees to drop it ("fine to skip", "not needed", an approval after the author's stated reason). An approval given on the condition that the ask be done later ("I'll approve it, with the condition that you add it in your next MR") keeps the ask alive: it is a deferral that needs a tracked item, never a waiver. A deferral is bare when the ask is resolved or the change merged with only "later", "next PR", "will do" or silence. Judge only asks the author deferred; an ask the author addressed in the diff, or answered with a reason the reviewer accepted, is not a deferral.

## Occasion
This is a gate. Record NOT_APPLICABLE, name the fact, and stop — never ABSENT — when: the pull request is not merged; no review thread was captured, or no thread contains an ask the author left unaddressed in the change — every ask was addressed in the diff or answered with a reason the reviewer accepted. A question that requests no change ("what is this for?") is not an ask, whether or not it was answered, and neither is a remark aimed at later work ("something to keep in mind next time"): it asks nothing of this change. The author is the `author` login of `inputs/context/metadata.json`; a comment by any other login is a reviewer's, and a reviewer's own "ignore" or "fine" on an ask — theirs or a bot's — is a waiver. A merged change with at least one deferred ask is the occasion.

## Sources
1. The inline review comments (`inputs/context/comments.json`: `path`, `line`, `body`, `author`, `created_at`) and the conversation (`inputs/context/general_comments.json`): every ask and every reply, with authors and dates. They establish which asks were made, which were answered, and with what words. The threads (`inputs/context/review_threads.json`) carry each thread's path, line and resolution and no words; a resolution by the author establishes nothing about the substance, and a resolution by the reviewer after the author's stated reason is the reviewer accepting it. The precompute summary (`work/precompute-out/summary.md`) lists every comment by someone other than the author, one row each, with whether the change touches its file, whether the author replied, whether the reviewer had a later word on the thread or approved after it: decide every row that asks something.
2. The diff (`work/change/diff.patch`): whether an ask was addressed in the change — the file and line the thread anchors to, read as changed or not. It establishes addressed versus not; it never establishes a waiver.
3. The body and the discussion (`inputs/context/description.md`, `inputs/context/general_comments.json`): a follow-up list, an issue reference for the deferral, or the reviewer's agreement. They establish tracking or a waiver when quotable.
4. The linked work items (`inputs/context/linked_work_items/<n>.md`) when captured: an issue that names the deferred ask. It establishes the tracking; its absence establishes nothing when a comment names an issue by number.
If the change merged but the threads are absent or truncated, report a collection gap and record no observation.

## Judge
Enumerate every ask by someone other than the author first and decide each against the diff — a two-part ask half-addressed leaves one part deferred, and a thread marked RESOLVED decides nothing. An ask is addressed only by a changed line that does what was asked; where the line the ask points at still stands unchanged in the head diff, the ask was not addressed, whatever the thread's state. An ask the author answered with a reason is deferred bare unless the reviewer's next word accepts the reason or the approval follows it. Then test the cells in this order.
- PRESENT/GOOD (POSITIVE): every deferred ask is tracked by a named issue or explicitly waived by the reviewer. Quote the ask and the tracking reference or the waiver.
- PRESENT/BAD: no ordinary case.
- ABSENT/GOOD (NEGATIVE): at least one ask was deferred on a bare promise or in silence — resolved or merged past with no issue and no reviewer waiver. Quote the ask and the author's last word on it, or note the silence.
- ABSENT/BAD: no ordinary case.
- UNDETERMINED: the thread's last word could be a waiver or a deferral and the reviewer's approval carries no comment; name the fact that would settle it.
One observation per review, on the single most consequential bare deferral when there are several.

## Severity
Negatives only; never above MAJOR on this alone — non-blocking. MINOR, the usual band: a small ask (a rename, a comment, a nit) deferred bare. MAJOR: a correctness, safety or test ask deferred on a bare promise and the change merged. Identical evidence yields identical severity.

## Grounding
Quote the reviewer's ask and the author's reply verbatim with their authors and dates, and the issue reference or waiver when there is one. Never infer a waiver from an approval alone, and never claim an ask was addressed without the changed line that addresses it.

## Defer
Whether the author replied to comments at all belongs to `engaging-with-inline-review-comments`; a thread left unresolved at the merge belongs to `merged-past-unresolved-review-threads`. Here only: where did the deferred asks go?

practices.name: Merge only after someone else approved
practices.whyItMatters: A change merged before anyone approved it skips the one check the team agreed on: a second pair of eyes before the code is everyone's. It is also how a reviewer's outstanding request for changes gets buried. Waiting for the approval, and re-requesting it after a rework, is what keeps the review real.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: The person who merges does so after an approval from someone other than the author that is still current — no later request for changes, no dismissal — and after a rework asks for the approval again before merging.
practices.criteria:
BEHAVIOR FOCUS: the merge happens after a current approval from someone other than the author, and never over an outstanding request for changes.

## The standard
Judge one thing about the moment this pull request merged: was there, at that moment, an approval from someone other than the author that still stood? An approval stands when it was submitted before the merge and nothing later withdrew it — no dismissal, no revocation (`UNAPPROVED`) and no request for changes by the same reviewer after it. A request for changes stands when it was submitted before the merge and no later approval by the same reviewer replaced it. A record that lists no dismissal, revocation or request for changes shows that none happened: the absence of a withdrawal is a fact read from the record, never an unknown. Merging with a standing approval and no standing request for changes is the practice; merging with none, or over a standing request for changes, is the lapse. Judge the decisions as recorded, never whether the review was thorough — that belongs to the review practices. That the author presses the merge button on their own pull request is the ordinary course in most teams and is never the lapse here; the only lapse is merging without another person's standing approval. The subject is the person who merged; when that person is not the author, this review says nothing.

## Occasion
This is a gate. Record NOT_APPLICABLE, name the fact, and stop — never ABSENT — when: the pull request is not merged; or the repository plainly works without review — no reviewer was requested, no review decision or review thread exists on this pull request, and the inventory shows a single-person project. A pull request with a reviewer requested, a review decision or a review comment is the occasion.

## Sources
1. The pull request record (`inputs/context/metadata.json`): `merged_at`, `merged_by`, `author`. It establishes who merged and when. When `merged_by` is absent or differs from `author`, record no observation: the review cannot name the merger.
2. The review decisions (`inputs/context/review_threads.json`, `reviewDecisions` oldest first: `state`, `author`, `submittedAt`, `body` when one was written, `dismissed`) and the threads: each decision with its author and time. They establish which approvals and requests stood at the merge. A `truncated` record is a collection gap for this practice. The precompute summary (`work/precompute-out/summary.md`) lists the merge and one row per decision with `beforeMerge`, `isAuthor`, `dismissed` and `bot` computed, and each reviewer's last decision apart: decide from the rows, and quote the decision and the merge from the record.
3. The inventory (`inputs/context/project_inventory.json`): whether other people work in this project, for the occasion only.
If `merged_at` or the decisions are unavailable, report a collection gap and record no observation.

## Judge
Test the cells in this order.
- PRESENT/GOOD (POSITIVE): at least one APPROVED decision by someone other than the author, submitted before `merged_at`, with no later dismissal, revocation or request for changes by that reviewer, and no other reviewer's request for changes still standing. Who pressed merge does not enter into it. Quote the approval and the merge time.
- PRESENT/BAD: no ordinary case.
- ABSENT/GOOD (NEGATIVE): merged with no standing approval from another person, or over a standing request for changes. Quote the merge time and the decisions that stood, or the absence of any.
- ABSENT/BAD: no ordinary case.
- UNDETERMINED: the decisions record is truncated or a decision carries no time; name what is missing.
One observation per review.

## Severity
Negatives only; never above MAJOR on this alone — non-blocking. MINOR, the usual band: merged with no approval where a reviewer was requested and had not answered. MAJOR: merged over a standing request for changes, or after an approval was dismissed and not renewed. Identical evidence yields identical severity.

## Grounding
Quote `merged_at`, `merged_by` and each decision as recorded with its `author`, `state` and `submittedAt`. Identity is the login as recorded, compared as text: the same login is the same person and different logins are different people. Never infer that a reviewer is the author from a display name, a repository path or a namespace; never infer an approval from a comment or a thumbs-up; never treat the author's own approval as one.

## Defer
Whether review threads were resolved belongs to `merged-past-unresolved-review-threads`; whether the pipeline was green has no source here. Here only: did someone else approve before the merge?

practices.name: Plan the work in an issue before starting it
practices.whyItMatters: An issue written before the first commit is a plan: it says what will be built and how anyone will know it is done, and it can be discussed before the code exists. An issue created after the work is finished, to give the merge request something to close, is paperwork — the decision it should have recorded was made in the code.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: The issue the change implements exists before the change's first commit, states what is to be done, and the branch and merge request are opened from it.
practices.criteria:
BEHAVIOR FOCUS: the issue the change implements was opened before the work on the change began.

## The standard
Judge one thing: did the issue this pull request implements exist before the work started? The work starts at the change's first commit (`inputs/context/commits.json`, the earliest `authoredAt`), or at the pull request's creation when the commits carry no dates. The issue's opening is its `createdAt` in the linked work item. An issue opened before the first commit is a plan the work followed; an issue opened after it is a record written to fit the work. An issue opened within one hour of the first commit, before or after it, is one sitting — the developer wrote the plan and started in the same stretch — and counts as planned first. The hour is measured from the first commit and from nothing else: the pull request's creation is when the work was handed off, and an issue opened minutes before the pull request but a day after the first commit was written to fit the work. Judge only the order and distance of the two dates, never the quality of the issue or of the change.

## Occasion
This is a gate. Record NOT_APPLICABLE, name the fact, and stop — never ABSENT — when: no linked work item was captured, or none is an issue this pull request implements (adopted with a closing keyword, in the title, or by the branch); or the change is of a kind that answers no issue by convention — a release, a bot dependency update, a revert. Whether an issue is linked at all belongs to `links-the-change-to-its-issue`; here the linked issue is the occasion.

## Sources
1. The linked work item (`inputs/context/linked_work_items/<n>.md`, its opening line `Opened <time>`, and `linked_work_items.json`, `createdAt`): when the issue was opened. It establishes the plan's date.
2. The commits (`inputs/context/commits.json`, `authoredAt`): when the work began. The earliest authored commit of the range establishes it; a rebased history keeps the author dates, so it is the author date, not the commit date, that is read.
3. The pull request record (`inputs/context/metadata.json`, `created_at`): the fallback start when the commits carry no dates.
4. The precompute summary (`work/precompute-out/summary.md`): the adopted issue's opening time, the earliest commit's author date and the hours between them, computed; read the two dates from it and check them against the sources above.
If the linked item carries no opening time, or the commits are absent, report a collection gap and record no observation.

## Judge
Test the cells in this order.
- PRESENT/GOOD (POSITIVE): the issue's `createdAt` is earlier than the first commit's `authoredAt` (or the pull request's creation when no commit is dated), or within one hour after it. Quote both times.
- PRESENT/BAD (NEGATIVE): the issue was opened more than an hour after the work began — its `createdAt` is later than the first commit's author date by more than an hour. Quote both times.
- ABSENT/GOOD and ABSENT/BAD: no ordinary case. A change with no issue is decided by `links-the-change-to-its-issue`.
- UNDETERMINED: no ordinary case. Two dated records always order, and the one-hour window decides the close ones.
One observation per review, on the issue the change adopts (the closing reference, else the title's, else the branch's).

## Severity
Negatives only; never above MINOR on this alone — non-blocking. MINOR: the issue was opened more than a day after the first commit, or after the pull request itself. INFO: the issue was opened more than an hour but less than a day after the first commit, and before the pull request. Identical evidence yields identical severity.

## Grounding
Cite the linked item's `Opened <time>` line and the pull request record's `created_at`; the earliest commit's author date is read from `inputs/context/commits.json`, which is derived and not an artifact to cite, so quote it in the rationale with the commit's short SHA. Never infer an order from issue and pull request numbers; never read a commit date where an author date exists.

## Defer
Whether the change names its issue belongs to `links-the-change-to-its-issue`; whether the issue states a checkable outcome belongs to `issue-has-checkable-outcome`. Here only: was the plan written before the work?

groups.name: Building iOS apps well
groups.description: Write SwiftUI the way it is designed to be written: views that describe the screen from state they are handed, state owned where it belongs, concurrency that is structured, an interface everyone can use, a preview for every screen, and permissions declared truthfully. These practices run only on changes that touch Swift code.

practices.name: Keep networking and persistence out of views

appliesWhen.absentSays: the change adds no SwiftUI view code

practices.whyItMatters: A SwiftUI view that fetches, decodes or saves is a view nobody can preview, test or reuse, and its logic is invisible to the next screen that needs the same data. Keeping that work in a model or store is what lets the view stay a description of the screen.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: Views describe the screen from state they are handed; requests, decoding and file or preference access live in a model, store or service the view talks to through a method or a binding, and SwiftData is used through its own view-side idiom.
practices.criteria:
BEHAVIOR FOCUS: networking, decoding or persistence performed inside a SwiftUI view type — the undesirable behaviour; a view that delegates that work is the good case, recorded as ABSENT/BAD.

## The standard
Judge one thing about the SwiftUI code this change adds: does a `View` type perform I/O itself? I/O in a view is a `URLSession` or `URLRequest` call, `JSONDecoder`/`JSONEncoder` use, `UserDefaults` or `FileManager` access, `Data(contentsOf:)`, a Core Data fetch request, or a `fetch`/`load`/`save` implemented inside a `struct … : View` — in `body`, a modifier closure (`.task`, `.onAppear`, a button action) or a method of the view. A view that calls a model's method (`store.load()`, `viewModel.save(item)`) or passes a `Binding` is not performing I/O, and SwiftData's own idiom — `@Query`, and `modelContext.insert`/`delete` through `@Environment(\.modelContext)` — is the framework's designed use of a view, not I/O the view took on. The judgement is about where the work lives, never about the architecture's name.

## Occasion
This is a gate. Record NOT_APPLICABLE, name the fact, and stop — never ABSENT — when the change adds no code inside a SwiftUI view type: no added line lies within a `struct … : View` (or a `some View` computed property) — a model-only, service-only, test-only or non-Swift change carries no surface. Added lines inside a view type are the occasion, whether or not they perform I/O.

## Sources
1. The diff (`work/change/diff.patch`) with `[L<n>]` markers: the added lines and the type each hunk lies in, read from the hunk header and the surrounding declaration. It establishes which added lines are inside a view type and which call I/O. It never establishes what unchanged code does.
2. The checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): the enclosing type of a hunk when the diff context does not show it, and whether a called method belongs to a model or store. Read it only to place a line; it never adds an I/O call the diff does not show.
3. The precompute summary (`work/precompute-out/summary.md`): the I/O calls it found inside view types, as leads to inspect, never as conclusions.
If the diff of a Swift file is truncated where a view type is edited, report a collection gap and record no observation.

## Judge
Scan the added lines inside view types first, then test the cells in this order.
The undesirable behaviour is I/O inside a view. Test the cells in this order.
- PRESENT/BAD (NEGATIVE): an added line inside a view type performs I/O itself — a `URLSession`/`URLRequest` call, `JSONDecoder`, `UserDefaults`, `FileManager`, `Data(contentsOf:)`, a Core Data fetch or an inline fetch-and-parse. Quote the line and name the view type.
- ABSENT/BAD (POSITIVE): the change adds view code and every request, decode, save or storage access it needs is delegated to a model, store or service — the view calls a method or reads state — so no I/O is inside a view. Quote the delegating call. "Absent" here means the I/O is absent from the view, which is the good case.
- PRESENT/GOOD and ABSENT/GOOD: no ordinary case. I/O inside a view is not desirable, and a view that delegates is not a lapse.
- UNDETERMINED: the hunk shows the call but neither the context nor the checkout shows whether the enclosing type is a view; name the declaration that would settle it.
One observation per review, on the single most consequential I/O line when there are several.

## Severity
Negatives only; never above MAJOR on this alone — non-blocking. MINOR, the usual band: one read (`UserDefaults`, a decode) inside a view, or I/O in a small preview-only or prototype view. MAJOR: a network request or a persistence write implemented inside a shipped view, or the same I/O repeated in several views. Identical evidence yields identical severity.

## Grounding
Quote the `[L<n>]` added line that performs the I/O and the `struct … : View` declaration it lies in, or for the positive the delegating call; for ABSENT/BAD, record the diff as the source you searched — every added line inside a view type was read. Never claim I/O from a method name alone (`load()` may be a model call); never claim a type is a view without its declaration; never count a SwiftData `modelContext` call as I/O.

## Defer
Duplicated logic across views belongs to `removes-duplication-instead-of-copy-pasting`; oversized view bodies to `keeps-functions-small-and-single-purpose`. Here only: does the view do I/O itself?

practices.name: Own SwiftUI state at the right level

appliesWhen.absentSays: the change adds no SwiftUI view code

practices.whyItMatters: State declared in the wrong place is the root of the bugs that make SwiftUI feel unpredictable: a model recreated on every render, a value copied into two views that drift apart, a derived value stored and forgotten. Declaring each piece of state where it is owned keeps the screen a function of its data.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: Value state a single view owns is `@State`; a shared model is `@Observable` and injected through the environment or passed down, never recreated in a child; a child that edits a parent's value takes a `Binding`; a derived value is computed, not stored.
practices.criteria:
BEHAVIOR FOCUS: each piece of SwiftUI state declared where it is owned — view-local values as `@State`, shared models observed and injected, edits through `Binding`, derived values computed rather than stored.

## The standard
Judge the state declarations this change adds to SwiftUI views against four rules. (1) A value one view owns and mutates is `@State` (or `@AppStorage` for a persisted setting); a `let` or plain `var` that the view mutates is a lapse. (2) A model shared by more than one view is one object: `@Observable` (or `ObservableObject`) created once by its owner and reached through `@Environment`, `@Bindable` or a passed reference — a child view that creates its own instance of a shared model (`@State private var store = Store()` in a child, `StateObject` for a model the parent already holds) is a lapse. (3) A child that edits a parent's value takes a `Binding` (`@Binding`, `$value`), not a copy it mutates. (4) A value derivable from other state (a count, a filtered list, a formatted string) is a computed property, not a second stored variable kept in sync by hand. Judge declarations and how they are wired, never naming or file layout.

## Occasion
This is a gate. Record NOT_APPLICABLE, name the fact, and stop — never ABSENT — when the change adds no state declaration or state wiring to a SwiftUI view: no added `@State`, `@Binding`, `@Environment`, `@Bindable`, `@AppStorage`, `@Observable`, `ObservableObject`, `StateObject`, `ObservedObject`, or a mutable stored property inside a view type. A change to a view's layout alone carries no surface.

## Sources
1. The diff (`work/change/diff.patch`) with `[L<n>]` markers: the added declarations and the wiring that hands state between views (`init` arguments, `.environment(…)`, `$` bindings). It establishes what was declared where. It never establishes what unchanged views hold.
2. The checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): whether a model type is `@Observable`, whether a parent already owns an instance a child recreates, and whether a stored value is derivable from other declared state. Read it to place a declaration; it never adds a declaration the diff does not show.
3. The precompute summary (`work/precompute-out/summary.md`): the declarations it found inside view types, as leads, never conclusions.
If the diff is truncated where a view's declarations are edited, report a collection gap and record no observation.

## Judge
Enumerate the added state declarations first, then test the cells in this order.
- PRESENT/GOOD (POSITIVE): every added declaration follows the four rules — local values `@State`, shared models observed once and injected, edits through bindings, derived values computed. Quote the declaration you accepted as the representative.
- PRESENT/BAD (NEGATIVE): a declaration breaks a rule — a mutable stored property in a view without `@State`; a child creating a second instance of a model the parent owns; a copied value the child mutates where a `Binding` was needed; a stored value kept in sync by hand with the state it derives from. Quote the declaration and name the rule.
- ABSENT/GOOD and ABSENT/BAD: no ordinary case. A view with added declarations always has state to judge; a change with none is NOT_APPLICABLE.
- UNDETERMINED: whether a model is shared or owned by this view alone cannot be told from the diff and the checkout; name the type and the fact that would settle it.
One observation per review, on the single most consequential declaration when several break a rule.

## Severity
Negatives only; never above MAJOR on this alone — non-blocking. MINOR, the usual band: a derived value stored, or a mutable `var` that should be `@State` in a leaf view. MAJOR: a shared model recreated in a child (state that silently resets or diverges), or a copied value edited where the parent's value was meant to change. Identical evidence yields identical severity.

## Grounding
Quote the `[L<n>]` declaration and, for a shared-model lapse, the parent's declaration of the same model. Never claim a model is shared without a second view that holds it; never claim a value is derivable without naming the state it derives from.

## Defer
I/O inside views belongs to `keeps-views-free-of-networking-and-persistence`; concurrency belongs to `uses-structured-concurrency-safely`. Here only: is the state declared where it is owned?

practices.name: Make the UI accessible by default

appliesWhen.absentSays: the change adds no SwiftUI view code

practices.whyItMatters: A control a screen reader cannot name, a label that cannot grow with the user's text size, an image that says nothing — each locks a group of people out of the screen, and each is a line the author could have written when the view was made. Accessibility added later is the expensive kind.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: Every icon-only control and meaningful image has a label; text uses semantic fonts so Dynamic Type works; nothing is fixed to a size that clips at larger text; colour is never the only signal.
practices.criteria:
BEHAVIOR FOCUS: the added SwiftUI interface is usable with a screen reader and at large text sizes — icon-only controls and meaningful images labelled, text sized semantically, layout free of size caps that clip.

## The standard
Judge the interface code this change adds against a closed list of accessibility facts. (1) An icon-only control — a `Button`, `Toggle`, `Link` or tappable `Image` whose visible content is an `Image(systemName:)` or an asset image with no text — carries an `accessibilityLabel` (or a `Label` with a text title). (2) A meaningful image (an asset that carries information) carries a label or is marked `.accessibilityHidden(true)` when decorative. (3) Text, and an SF Symbol shown with it, use a semantic font (`.font(.body)`, `.headline`, `.title2`, …) or a scaled custom font, not `.font(.system(size: 14))` or a fixed-size custom font — a symbol sized in points stays small when the text around it grows. (4) No text container is capped in height (`.frame(height:)`, `.lineLimit(1)` on body copy) in a way that clips at larger text. (5) A state shown by colour alone (red for error, green for done) is also shown by text, an icon or a trait. Judge added lines only; an existing lapse the change did not touch is not this change's.

## Occasion
This is a gate. Record NOT_APPLICABLE, name the fact, and stop — never ABSENT — when the change adds no interface code: no added `Image`, `Button`, `Toggle`, `Text`, `Label`, `.font(`, `.frame(` or colour-state line inside a SwiftUI view. Added interface lines are the occasion, whether or not they carry a lapse.

## Sources
1. The diff (`work/change/diff.patch`) with `[L<n>]` markers: the added interface lines and the modifiers attached to them in the same expression. It establishes what each control and text carries. A modifier on the same view chain counts; one on a distant ancestor does not establish a label for an inner icon.
2. The checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): whether an asset image is decorative or informative, and whether a custom font is scaled with `relativeTo:`. Read it to classify; it never adds a control the diff does not show.
3. The precompute summary (`work/precompute-out/summary.md`): the icon-only controls, fixed-size fonts and height caps it found, as leads, never conclusions.
If the diff is truncated where a view body is edited, report a collection gap and record no observation.

## Judge
Enumerate the added controls, images and text first, then test the cells in this order.
- PRESENT/GOOD (POSITIVE): every added icon-only control and meaningful image is labelled, added text is sized semantically, no added cap clips text, and no added state relies on colour alone. Quote a representative labelled control or semantic font.
- PRESENT/BAD: no ordinary case.
- ABSENT/GOOD (NEGATIVE): at least one added item breaks the list — an unlabelled icon-only control or informative image, a fixed-size font, a clipping cap, a colour-only state. Quote the line and name the rule.
- ABSENT/BAD: no ordinary case.
- UNDETERMINED: an image whose informative or decorative role the checkout does not settle; name the asset.
One observation per review, on the single most consequential lapse when there are several; count the rest in the summary.

## Severity
Negatives only; never above MAJOR on this alone — non-blocking. MINOR, the usual band: one unlabelled icon or one fixed-size font. MAJOR: a primary action of the screen unreachable by screen reader, or a screen whose main text cannot scale. Identical evidence yields identical severity.

## Grounding
Quote the `[L<n>]` line of the control, image, font or cap. Never claim a label is missing without reading the whole view chain the control sits in; never claim clipping from a `.frame` on a non-text container.

## Defer
Localisation of the strings belongs to no practice here; magic numbers in layout to none. Here only: can everyone use what was added?

practices.name: Use structured concurrency safely

appliesWhen.absentSays: the change touches no Swift source file

practices.whyItMatters: An unstructured task that outlives its view, UI state mutated off the main actor, a fire-and-forget request that cannot be cancelled — these are the crashes and stale screens that appear only on a slow network. Swift's structured concurrency prevents them when it is used the way it is designed.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: Async work a view starts runs in `.task` so it is cancelled with the view; UI state is mutated on the main actor; a detached or unstructured `Task` exists only with a reason and a handle; errors from async work are handled, not swallowed.
practices.criteria:
BEHAVIOR FOCUS: async work tied to the lifetime that owns it, UI state mutated on the main actor, and no fire-and-forget task where structure was available.

## The standard
Judge the concurrency code this change adds against a closed list. (1) Async work a view starts runs in `.task { }` (cancelled when the view disappears), not in `Task { }` inside `.onAppear` or a button action unless the work must outlive the view — and only a stored task handle or a reason written in the code or a comment shows that intent; a reviewer's own inference that the work ought to outlive the view ("a user-initiated save should complete") is not a stated reason, and a `Task { }` in an action with none is the lapse. (2) State the UI reads is mutated on the main actor: a type that holds view state is `@MainActor`, or the mutation is `await MainActor.run`; a mutation of `@Published`/`@Observable` UI state from a background context is a lapse. (3) `Task.detached` and `DispatchQueue` appear only with a reason the code or a comment states. (4) A `Task` whose result matters is awaited or stored, not dropped. Judge added lines; existing concurrency the change did not touch is not this change's.

## Occasion
This is a gate. Record NOT_APPLICABLE, name the fact, and stop — never ABSENT — when the change adds no concurrency: no added `async`, `await`, `Task`, `.task`, `@MainActor`, `MainActor.run`, `Task.detached`, `DispatchQueue` or actor declaration. Added concurrency is the occasion, whether or not it carries a lapse.

## Sources
1. The diff (`work/change/diff.patch`) with `[L<n>]` markers: the added concurrency constructs and where they sit (a view modifier, a model method, a service). It establishes what was written. It never establishes the actor a type is isolated to when that declaration is outside the diff.
2. The checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): the declaration of the type a mutation lands in (`@MainActor` or not), and whether a `Task` handle is stored. Read it to place a construct; it never adds one.
3. The precompute summary (`work/precompute-out/summary.md`): the `Task {` blocks, `.onAppear` with async work, detached tasks and dispatch queues it found, as leads, never conclusions.
If the diff is truncated where async code is added, report a collection gap and record no observation.

## Judge
Enumerate the added constructs first, then test the cells in this order.
- PRESENT/GOOD (POSITIVE): every added construct follows the list — view work in `.task`, UI state mutated on the main actor, unstructured tasks justified and held. Quote a representative construct.
- PRESENT/BAD: no ordinary case.
- ABSENT/GOOD (NEGATIVE): an added construct breaks the list — a `Task { }` started from `.onAppear` or an action with no handle and no reason, UI state mutated off the main actor, an unexplained detached task or dispatch queue, a dropped task whose result matters. Quote the line and name the rule.
- ABSENT/BAD: no ordinary case.
- UNDETERMINED: an added line mutates UI state from an async context and the isolation of its type is in neither the diff nor the checkout; name the type. An added call into an unchanged method is judged as a call, never by what that method does inside.
One observation per review, on the single most consequential lapse when there are several.

## Severity
Negatives only; never above MAJOR on this alone — non-blocking. MINOR, the usual band: a `Task` in `.onAppear` for a quick local read, or a dispatch queue with an obvious reason left unstated. MAJOR: a network request in an uncancelled task that writes view state, or UI state mutated from a background context. Identical evidence yields identical severity.

## Grounding
Quote the `[L<n>]` construct and, for an actor lapse, the declaration of the type mutated. Never claim a mutation is off the main actor without the type's isolation; never claim a task is fire-and-forget when a handle is stored in the same hunk.

## Defer
Swallowed errors in async code belong to `handles-errors-instead-of-swallowing-them`; crash-shaped constructs to `avoids-unsafe-panics-and-chosen-crashes`. Here only: is the concurrency structured?

practices.name: Ship a preview with each new view

appliesWhen.absentSays: the change adds no SwiftUI view code

practices.whyItMatters: A SwiftUI view without a preview is a screen nobody can see without running the whole app to it, and the first thing the next person deletes when it breaks. A preview with representative data is the cheapest verification a view can have, and the way a reviewer sees what changed.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: Every new view type ships a `#Preview` that renders it with representative sample data — including an empty or error state when the view has one — so the screen can be seen and checked without launching the app.
practices.criteria:
BEHAVIOR FOCUS: a `#Preview` (or `PreviewProvider`) arriving with each new SwiftUI view type, rendering it with representative data.

## The standard
Judge one thing: when this change adds a new SwiftUI view type, does the same change ship a preview for it? A preview is a `#Preview` block or a `PreviewProvider` that constructs the view; it is representative when it hands the view sample data of the shape it renders (a filled model, a non-empty list) rather than defaults only, and it is complete when a view that has an empty, loading or error state previews that state too. A preview that constructs the view with a fresh or live view model and no sample shows only the view's first state — a spinner, an empty list, a prompt — and a live fetch inside a preview is not sample data; such a preview exists but is not representative. A preview for an existing view the change edits is welcome but not required. Judge presence and representativeness of the preview, never its layout or naming.

## Occasion
This is a gate. Record NOT_APPLICABLE, name the fact, and stop — never ABSENT — when the change adds no new view type: no added `struct … : View` declaration in a non-test file. An edit to an existing view, a model-only change or a preview-only change carries no surface.

## Sources
1. The diff (`work/change/diff.patch`) with the file list (`work/change/files.json`): the added `struct … : View` declarations and the `#Preview`/`PreviewProvider` blocks in the same change. It establishes which new views have a preview and what data the preview passes. It never establishes that a preview renders.
2. The checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): a preview that lives in another file of the same change, or sample-data helpers the preview uses. Read it to find the preview; it never supplies one the change did not add.
3. The precompute summary (`work/precompute-out/summary.md`): the new view types and the previews it found, as leads, never conclusions.
If the diff is truncated where a new view is declared, report a collection gap and record no observation.

## Judge
Enumerate the new view types first — every added `struct … : View`, `private` and file-scoped ones included; a parent's preview does not preview the child, and a helper's smallness goes to the severity, not to the cell. Then test the cells in this order.
- PRESENT/GOOD (POSITIVE): every new view type has a preview in the same change, and the preview hands it representative data. Quote the declaration and its preview.
- PRESENT/BAD (NEGATIVE): every new view has a preview, but a preview renders the view with nothing representative — an empty list for a list screen, a placeholder model with default values — or omits a state the view plainly has. Quote the preview and name what it lacks.
- ABSENT/GOOD (NEGATIVE): at least one new view type has no preview in the change, after scanning every Swift file in the diff. Quote the declaration and say what you scanned.
- ABSENT/BAD: no ordinary case.
- UNDETERMINED: a preview exists in the checkout but the diff does not show whether this change added it; name the file.
One observation per review, on the single most consequential view when there are several.

## Severity
Negatives only; never above MINOR on this alone — non-blocking. MINOR: a new view with no preview or with an unrepresentative one. INFO: a small helper view (a row, a badge) without a preview while its parent screen has one. Identical evidence yields identical severity.

## Grounding
Quote the `[L<n>]` `struct … : View` declaration and the `#Preview` line, or for ABSENT the declaration and the scan. Never claim a preview renders or compiles; never claim a view is a helper without its parent's preview.

## Defer
How to verify the change as a whole belongs to `states-how-to-verify-the-change`; tests for logic to `ships-tests-with-the-change`. Here only: can the new screen be seen?

practices.name: Declare permissions truthfully and ask at the point of use

appliesWhen.absentSays: the change touches no Swift source file

practices.whyItMatters: A capability the app requests without a usage description crashes on the device; one with a boilerplate description fails App Review and the user's trust; one requested at launch instead of at the moment it is needed is denied and never asked again. The declaration and the ask are part of the feature.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: When a change adds a capability that needs the user's permission, the `Info.plist` usage description arrives in the same change, says truthfully what the app does with the access, and the permission is requested where the feature needs it, not at launch.
practices.criteria:
BEHAVIOR FOCUS: a capability that needs the user's permission arriving with a truthful usage description and a request made where the feature needs it.

## The standard
Judge the permission-bearing capabilities this change adds against three facts. (1) Declaration: the matching usage-description key is present — `NSLocationWhenInUseUsageDescription` for `CoreLocation`, `NSPhotoLibraryUsageDescription` for `PhotosUI`/`PHPickerViewController` with library access, `NSCameraUsageDescription` for the camera, `NSMicrophoneUsageDescription`, `NSCalendarsUsageDescription`, `NSContactsUsageDescription`, `NSHealthShareUsageDescription`/`NSHealthUpdateUsageDescription` for HealthKit, `NSUserTrackingUsageDescription` for ATT, notification authorization needing no key — in `Info.plist`, `project.yml` or the target's build settings. (2) Truth: the description names what the app does with the access, not a placeholder ("needed", "for the app", an empty string). (3) Point of use: the authorization request (`requestWhenInUseAuthorization`, `requestAuthorization`, `PHPhotoLibrary.requestAuthorization`, …) is made from the feature that needs it, not from app launch or a root view's `onAppear`. Judge added capabilities; an existing one the change did not touch is not this change's.

## Occasion
This is a gate. Record NOT_APPLICABLE, name the fact, and stop — never ABSENT — when the change adds no permission-bearing capability: no added import or use of `CoreLocation`, `PhotosUI`, `AVFoundation` capture, `UserNotifications`, `EventKit`, `Contacts`, `HealthKit`, `AppTrackingTransparency` or an authorization request. `SwiftUI`'s `PhotosPicker` alone needs no permission and is not the occasion.

## Sources
1. The diff (`work/change/diff.patch`) with the file list (`work/change/files.json`): the added capability code, authorization requests, and usage-description keys in `Info.plist`, `project.yml` or `*.pbxproj`. It establishes what was added where. It never establishes what the app already declared.
2. The checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): the existing `Info.plist`/`project.yml` for a key the change relies on but did not add, and the call site of the request. Read it to complete the picture; a key present there satisfies the declaration.
3. The precompute summary (`work/precompute-out/summary.md`): the capabilities, requests and usage keys it found, as leads, never conclusions.
If the diff is truncated where the capability is added, or the project's plist is unreadable, report a collection gap and record no observation.

## Judge
Enumerate the added capabilities first, then test the cells in this order.
- PRESENT/GOOD (POSITIVE): every added capability has its usage key (in the change or the checkout), the description says what the app does with the access, and the request is made from the feature. Quote the key and the request.
- PRESENT/BAD (NEGATIVE): the key is present but the description is a placeholder, or the request is made at launch or from a root view rather than the feature. Quote the description or the request site.
- ABSENT/GOOD (NEGATIVE): an added capability has no usage key anywhere in the change or the checkout. Quote the capability line and say where you looked.
- ABSENT/BAD: no ordinary case.
- UNDETERMINED: the usage keys live in a build setting or generated file the checkout does not carry; name it.
One observation per review, on the single most consequential capability when there are several.

## Severity
Negatives only; never above MAJOR on this alone — non-blocking. MINOR, the usual band: a placeholder description, or a request made one screen early. MAJOR: a capability with no usage key at all (a crash on device), or a request made at launch for a feature the user has not reached. Identical evidence yields identical severity.

## Grounding
Quote the `[L<n>]` capability or request line and the plist/project key as written. Never claim a key is missing without stating the files scanned; never claim a request site is launch without the call chain that reaches it.

## Defer
Over-broad permissions and insecure defaults belong to `avoids-insecure-defaults-and-over-broad-permissions`. Here only: is the permission declared truthfully and asked for at the point of use?

practices.name: Use adaptive colors so every appearance works

appliesWhen.absentSays: the change adds no SwiftUI view code

practices.whyItMatters: A screen built from literal colors is right in one appearance and wrong in the other: white text vanishes on a light background, a hard-coded card stays white in Dark Mode, and every screen has to be revisited when the palette changes. Semantic and asset colors adapt on their own, and the whole app follows one palette.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: Text, backgrounds and fills use semantic colors (`.primary`, `.secondary`, `Color(.systemBackground)`), materials, the accent color or named asset colors with light and dark variants; a literal is used only where the color is part of the content, such as text over a fill the same view sets.
practices.criteria:
BEHAVIOR FOCUS: the added interface takes its colors from the system's semantic set, materials, the accent color or asset colors with both appearances, not from literals that hold one appearance.

## The standard
Judge the color choices the change adds to SwiftUI views against a closed list. A literal is `Color.white`, `Color.black`, `.white` or `.black` as a foreground, background or fill, `Color(red:green:blue:)`, `Color(hex:)` or a hex-parsing initializer, `UIColor(red:)`, `Color(uiColor: .white/.black)`, and a color from `.gray`/`.systemGray` when it stands for text on a background. An adaptive color is a semantic one (`.primary`, `.secondary`, `.tertiary`, `Color(.systemBackground)`, `.secondarySystemBackground`, `.label`), a material (`.ultraThinMaterial`, `.regularMaterial`), the accent (`.accentColor`, `.tint`) or a named asset color (`Color("Card")`, `Color(.card)`) — an asset color is adaptive when its colorset carries a dark appearance. A literal is not a lapse where the color is the content: text or a symbol over a fill or image the same view sets, a brand color deliberately constant, a shadow. Judge the added lines only.

## Occasion
This is a gate. Record NOT_APPLICABLE, name the fact, and stop — never ABSENT — when the change sets no color in a SwiftUI view: no added `.foregroundStyle`, `.foregroundColor`, `.background`, `.fill`, `.tint`, `.shadow(color:` or `Color`/`UIColor` expression inside a view type. Added color lines are the occasion, whether or not they carry a lapse.

## Sources
1. The diff (`work/change/diff.patch`) with `[L<n>]` markers: each added color expression and the modifier chain it sits in — what it colors (text, background, fill) and what fill the same view sets around it. It establishes the literal and its role. It never establishes an unchanged view's colors.
2. The checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): the asset catalog (`*.xcassets/<name>.colorset/Contents.json`) for a named color's appearances, and a color extension (`Color+App.swift`) a name may resolve to. Read it to classify a name; a `Color("x")` whose colorset has only one appearance is a literal in disguise.
3. The precompute summary (`work/precompute-out/summary.md`): the literal and adaptive color lines it found and, for each named asset color, whether its colorset has a dark appearance, as leads, never conclusions.
If the diff is truncated where a view body is edited, report a collection gap and record no observation.

## Judge
Enumerate the added color expressions first, then test the cells in this order.
- PRESENT/GOOD (POSITIVE): every added color is adaptive, or a literal only where the color is the content. Quote a representative adaptive color.
- PRESENT/BAD: no ordinary case.
- ABSENT/GOOD (NEGATIVE): an added literal colors text on a system background, a screen or card background, or a fill the rest of the interface adapts around — one appearance baked in. Quote the line and name what it colors.
- ABSENT/BAD: no ordinary case.
- UNDETERMINED: a named color whose colorset the checkout does not carry and whose appearance the diff does not show; name the asset.
One observation per review, on the single most consequential literal when there are several; count the rest in the summary.

## Severity
Negatives only; never above MAJOR on this alone — non-blocking. MINOR, the usual band: one literal text or fill color on a secondary element. MAJOR: a screen or card background, or the primary text of a screen, hard-coded to one appearance. Identical evidence yields identical severity.

## Grounding
Quote the `[L<n>]` color line and, when the role matters, the fill or background line of the same view; for an asset color, the colorset's appearances. Never call a color a literal without its line; never call a named color adaptive without its colorset or its definition.

## Defer
Labels, fonts and colour-only state belong to `makes-ui-accessible-by-default`. Here only: does the color hold in both appearances?

groups.name: Communicating in the open
groups.description: How you talk to teammates in shared channels: ask questions someone can actually answer, give answers people can act on, and keep others informed about where the work stands and what is blocking it. This is about the clarity of the exchange, not the correctness of the code being discussed.

practices.name: Ask questions a teammate can answer
practices.whyItMatters: A vague question forces the person helping you to stop and ask what you actually mean before they can even start, turning a one-message answer into a slow exchange. A question that carries its own context gets answered on the first reply.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: A question that says what you are trying to do, what you already tried, and exactly where it broke, so a teammate can answer it in a single reply without asking you anything first.
practices.criteria:
BEHAVIOR FOCUS: a question posed in the captured exchange carries enough context — the goal, what was tried, what happened — for a teammate to answer it in one reply.

## The standard
Judge whether a question raised in this conversation gives a teammate enough to answer it in a single reply, rather than forcing a round of clarifying questions first. A well-formed ask names the concrete goal, what was already tried, and what actually happened or is blocking. A bare "it doesn't work" or "how do I do this?" with no context makes the responder guess. Judge only the observable habit of how the question is posed; never whether the underlying problem is real, hard or worth solving. Use judgment about how much context the question genuinely needs: a quick clarification among people who plainly share the context is not a defect.

## Occasion
This is a gate. Record NOT_APPLICABLE, name the fact, and stop — never ABSENT — when the turn is not actually a question (a statement, an acknowledgement, social chat), or when there is no settled conversation to read. A real question whose needed context is supplied by the surrounding turns is not NOT_APPLICABLE; it is PRESENT/GOOD.

## Sources
1. The turn that poses the question (`inputs/context/conversation_thread.json`): its stated objective, what was tried, the exact behaviour seen or the specific point of confusion. It establishes how the question is posed. It never establishes whether the problem is real or worth solving.
2. The surrounding turns of the same thread (`inputs/context/conversation_thread.json`): earlier turns may supply the context the question leans on; a later reply that has to ask what was meant shows what the responder had to extract first. They establish what context was shared inside the captured thread and nothing outside it.
An image or attachment in a turn: read its caption and the sentence around it. An external link: nothing. When the thread begins mid-conversation, so you cannot tell whether what the question leans on was supplied in a turn you never saw, report a collection gap and record no observation; that is neither ABSENT nor UNDETERMINED.

## Judge
Test the cells in this order.
- PRESENT/GOOD (POSITIVE): a knowledgeable teammate could answer the question from the message alone, or from the message plus the surrounding turns, because it states the objective and the specific point of confusion or the exact behaviour seen. A quick clarification between people who share obvious context belongs here.
- PRESENT/BAD: no ordinary case. A question that can be answered in one reply is never undesirable.
- ABSENT/GOOD (NEGATIVE): the question is so thin on context that answering it requires asking the author what they mean, what they tried, or what they expected — and no surrounding turn supplies it. Name the missing element.
- ABSENT/BAD: no ordinary case.
- UNDETERMINED only when every declared turn was captured and the meaning still genuinely admits incompatible readings; quote the ambiguity and say what would settle it. Having read the whole thread and found the context missing is ABSENT/GOOD, not UNDETERMINED. A thread that begins mid-conversation is a collection gap, not an observation.
One observation per review, on the question turn you assessed.

## Severity
Negatives only. Scale to how much a responder must extract before they can help. MINOR, the usual band: a little more detail would sharpen the ask. MAJOR: the question as written cannot be answered without a full exchange of clarifications first. Never above MAJOR on question phrasing alone; this is a formative habit, never a gate.

## Grounding
Quote the exact turn you assessed. For PRESENT/GOOD where the surrounding turns supply the context, quote those turns too. For ABSENT/GOOD, the citations show the question and the boundary you searched: the whole captured thread, with no turn supplying the goal, the attempt or the observed behaviour. Describe the observable gap — "the question names no goal and no attempt" — never laziness or intent. Never invent missing context, grade an exchange you cannot quote, or claim the problem is or is not real.

## Defer
Whether the reply moves the asker forward belongs to `gives-actionable-answers`. Here only: does the question, as posed, let a teammate answer it in one reply?

practices.name: Give answers people can act on
practices.whyItMatters: When someone asks for help, a reply that only gestures at the problem leaves them exactly as stuck as before and burns another round of messages. An answer with a concrete next step lets them get moving right away.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: A reply that either solves the question outright or points to the exact next step or place to look, so the person who asked can act on it immediately instead of asking again.
practices.criteria:
BEHAVIOR FOCUS: a reply to a question in the captured exchange gives the asker something to act on now — the answer, the exact place to look, or the next step.

## The standard
Judge whether a reply to someone's question actually moves them forward, rather than leaving them where they started. A useful answer either resolves the question directly or names a concrete next step the asker can take. A reply that only restates the problem, points vaguely at "the docs", or answers a different question does not. A short answer can be fully actionable; length is not the signal. Judge only the observable helpfulness of the reply as written, never whether its technical content is ultimately correct. Use judgment about what the asker needed.

## Occasion
This is a gate. Record NOT_APPLICABLE, name the fact, and stop — never ABSENT — when the turn is not answering a question; when no question was actually asked; when the reply is a reasonable partial step in an ongoing exchange; or when there is no settled conversation to read.

## Sources
1. The question turn (`inputs/context/conversation_thread.json`): what was asked and what the asker needed. It establishes the question the reply is measured against. It never establishes whether the problem is real or hard.
2. The reply turn (`inputs/context/conversation_thread.json`): the answer given, the place named, the step proposed. It establishes what the asker can do next. It never establishes that the answer is technically right.
3. The surrounding turns (`inputs/context/conversation_thread.json`): whether the exchange is still in progress, and whether the answer had already been given elsewhere in the thread. They establish the state of the exchange inside the captured thread and nothing outside it.
An image or attachment in a turn: read its caption and the sentence around it. An external link: nothing; judge the reply by its own words. When a real question and its reply are both in front of you but the thread begins mid-conversation, so you cannot tell whether the answer had already been given elsewhere in it, report a collection gap and record no observation; that is neither ABSENT nor UNDETERMINED.

## Judge
Test the cells in this order.
- PRESENT/GOOD (POSITIVE): the asker could act on the reply immediately because it gives the answer, the specific place to look, or the exact next step.
- PRESENT/BAD: no ordinary case. A reply the asker can act on is never undesirable.
- ABSENT/GOOD (NEGATIVE): a genuine question was met with a reply that leaves the asker still stuck — too vague to act on, or it sidesteps what was asked. Name what the asker still lacks.
- ABSENT/BAD: no ordinary case.
- UNDETERMINED only when every declared turn was captured and the meaning still genuinely admits incompatible readings; quote the ambiguity and say what would settle it. Having read the reply and the surrounding turns and found no actionable content is ABSENT/GOOD, not UNDETERMINED. A thread that begins mid-conversation is a collection gap, not an observation.
One observation per review, on the question-and-reply pair you assessed.

## Severity
Negatives only. Scale to how stuck the asker remains after the reply. MINOR, the usual band: the answer is nearly there and one pointer would land it. MAJOR: a real question is met with a reply that cannot be acted on at all. Never above MAJOR on reply clarity alone; this is a formative habit, never a gate.

## Grounding
Quote the question and the reply you assessed. For ABSENT/GOOD, the citations show the question, the reply, and the boundary you searched: the surrounding captured turns, with no other turn supplying the answer. Describe the observable gap — "the reply names no place to look and no step" — never dismissiveness. Never fabricate an answer the reply did not give, and never claim the reply's content is correct or incorrect.

## Defer
Whether the question itself carried enough context to be answerable belongs to `asks-answerable-questions`. Here only: does the reply, as written, let the asker move forward?

practices.name: Post clear status and blocker updates
practices.whyItMatters: When work stalls quietly, the people depending on it keep waiting without knowing anything is wrong, and a blocker someone else could have cleared in minutes sits for days. A plain update on where things stand and what you need keeps the team moving.
practices.whatGoodLooksLike: An update that says where the work stands and, when you are stuck, names the blocker and what would unblock it, so teammates can plan around it or step in to help.
practices.criteria:
BEHAVIOR FOCUS: an update about ongoing work says where things stand and, when stuck, names the blocker and what would clear it.

## The standard
Judge whether an update about ongoing work tells the team where things stand and, when the author is stuck, names the blocker plainly along with what is needed to clear it. A clear update lets teammates plan around the work or step in to unblock it; an update so vague no one can tell whether help is needed leaves the team guessing. Judge only the observable clarity of the update, never whether the work itself is on track. Use judgment about how much an update needs to say: a brief "still on it, no blockers" among teammates already in sync is fine, and a real update made clear by its surrounding context is a good update, not a missing one.

## Occasion
This is a gate. Record NOT_APPLICABLE, name the fact, and stop — never ABSENT — when the turn is not a status update, when there is no in-flight work or blocker to report, or when there is no settled conversation to read. A real update whose standing or blocker is established by the surrounding turns is not NOT_APPLICABLE; it is PRESENT/GOOD.

## Sources
1. The update turn (`inputs/context/conversation_thread.json`): what it says about the current standing, whether it reports being blocked, what it names as the blocker and what it asks for. It establishes the clarity of the update as posted. It never establishes whether the work is actually on track or whether the blocker is real.
2. The surrounding turns of the same thread (`inputs/context/conversation_thread.json`): earlier turns may already establish the standing an update omits, or show that the teammates are in sync; a later turn that has to ask what is needed shows what the update left unsaid. They establish what was shared inside the captured thread and nothing outside it.
An image or attachment in a turn: read its caption and the sentence around it. An external link: nothing. When an update IS posted but the thread begins mid-conversation, so you cannot tell whether the standing it omits was already established, report a collection gap and record no observation; that is neither ABSENT nor UNDETERMINED.

## Judge
Test the cells in this order.
- PRESENT/GOOD (POSITIVE): the update states the current standing and, if blocked, says what is blocking and what would unblock it — from the turn alone or from the turn plus the surrounding thread.
- PRESENT/BAD (NEGATIVE): an update on stalled or in-flight work that hides a blocker behind a vague line, or reports being stuck without naming what is actually needed, so no one can plan or help. Quote the vague line and name what the team cannot tell from it.
- ABSENT/GOOD and ABSENT/BAD: no ordinary case. A turn that carries no status update is NOT_APPLICABLE, never a missing update; a silent stall is not a turn you can judge.
- UNDETERMINED only when every declared turn was captured and the update's meaning still genuinely admits incompatible readings; quote the ambiguity and say what would settle it. A thread that begins mid-conversation is a collection gap, not UNDETERMINED.
One observation per review, on the update turn you assessed.

## Severity
Negatives only; never above MAJOR on update clarity alone — a formative habit, never a gate. Scale to how much the update leaves the team unable to plan or help. MINOR, the usual band: the standing is clear but the ask is fuzzy. MAJOR: a real blocker is present yet the update gives the team nothing to act on.

## Grounding
Quote the update you assessed. For PRESENT/GOOD where the surrounding turns supply the standing or the ask, quote those turns too. For PRESENT/BAD, quote the vague line and the turns you read around it. Describe the observable gap — "the update says it is blocked and names no blocker" — never avoidance or intent.
